By employing techniques from high-dimensional geometry, such as concentration inequalities and anti-concentration inequalities, particularly those related to the hypercube $[-1,1]^d$, we demonstrate robust convergence rates for such neural networks. Our results show that neural networks trained on $\mathbb{R}^d$ can exhibit convergence rates comparable to those in dimension $d$, rather than a higher dimension like $2d$. This implies that neural networks may offer better generalization performance than fully connected MLPs in dimension $d$, at least when activated using the ReLU activation function. Our findings align with recent empirical research by Haim et al. (2021), who investigated MLPs with one hidden layer on the hypercube $[-1,1]^{d}$. Moreover, our analysis allows us to establish uniform convergence for functionalpenalized SGD, revealing that neural networks may exhibit better generalization performance than MLPs when the data resides on a lower-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^d$. We establish the condition under which scattering is certain for the focusing system, and demonstrate that this condition is more stringent than in homogeneous scenarios. Conversely, in the case of spatially dependent dispersion, we show that initial data permitting scattering are abundant, and outline a method to construct such data at any given time. Furthermore, we establish the condition under which the inverse scattering transform is definable. Our findings are largely based on a novel approach where we dissect the inhomogeneity into discrete components and then consider the limiting case as the discretization tends to zero. We also leverage the properties of the radial Schrödinger operator and its connection to the Dirichlet eigenvalues on the unit sphere to overcome difficulties posed by the inhomogeneity. In particular, this involves proving the absence of Dirichlet eigenvalues for large values of the angular momentum and for any given range of the radial variable, a result that may be of independent interest. We also outline a method to overcome the obstacle of resonances, a phenomenon that had not been encountered in previous works on inhomogeneous scattering problems. Critical steps in our analysis involve the construction of discrete Schrödinger operators with sufficient regularity, as well as the establishment of bounds on the number of Dirichlet eigenvalues for each value of the angular momentum, all on the unit sphere. A multi-species model incorporating thermal fluctuations is applied to the simple infectious-inhibitory susceptible-susceptible (SIS) discrete dynamics. This leads to the development of two models, DOCS and AIR, which respectively account for the diffusion of species movement and arbitrary immigration-immigration in the SIS dynamics. Through analytical solutions, the DOCS and AIR models reveal that the mean field approximation yields identical mean and variance outcomes for non-migrating species, but the mean field approximation fails to accurately capture the mean and variance of migrating species. Notably, the AIR model's mean field approximation successfully recovers the exact mean and variance for migrating species, but at the cost of variable accuracy. This research demonstrates that the AIR model's exact discrete dynamics can be approximated using a first-order closed system, in contrast to the DOCS model's second-order open system. Ultimately, the AIR model's ability to incorporate arbitrary immigration and migration dynamics may be valuable for modeling and understanding more complex biological systems. To gain a deeper understanding of planetary characteristics within compact systems, it's crucial to investigate orbital resonances. By using a novel machine learning technique inspired by liquid democracy, we introduce the voting mechanism to identify and confirm orbital resonances based on available exoplanet data. The method is applied to the Kepler-68 system, enabling the detection of previously known resonances and identification of new ones, including an unreported mean motion resonance in its compact planetary system. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the voting method has significant potential to be expanded and applied to various astrophysical contexts. The associated source code can be accessed through a public GitHub repository, located at https://github.com/202002AA18/Voting-orbital-resonances. Additionally, a graphical interface has been developed using Jupyter Notebook to facilitate the execution of the voting algorithm. The source code includes the necessary modifications to employ the VOTING C++ library for the identification of orbital resonances, as well as sample sets of exoplanets that contain mean-motion resonances in the ATLAS database. The findings suggest that the voting model is capable of identifying both the resonant argument and the average ratio of the planets' orbital periods with satisfactory accuracy. The model's performance shows promising results, with the resonant arguments' mean errors and standard deviations amounting to -0.08 and 2.23 degrees, respectively. Similarly, the average ratio of the planets' orbital periods is found to be 3.998 with a mean error of 0.003 and a standard deviation of 0.005. The proposed method is envisioned to contribute to the development of more accurate machine learning models for astrophysical applications. The proposed system identifies formal proofs and integrates them into an archive by calculating in- and out-degrees in a dependency graph, where prominent proofs with higher node in-degrees represent central themes. This approach is applied to 2,916 intuitionistic natural deduction proofs from the Isabelle proof assistant, identifying 1,051 as major contributions, averaging 5.38 out-degrees. This methodological innovation combines complex proof analysis with network theory, revealing a scale-free distribution (0.71 beta-value) and a clear divide between central and peripheral proof aspects. This simple method can be applied to structured proof libraries with automated degree calculations, ultimately aiding proof writers by pinpointing novel connections and facilitating more informed reuse. Furthermore, the algorithm highlights the importance of out-degrees in distinguishing original work and avoiding unimportant proof fragments. This concept is demonstrated on deeper levels of abstraction, where out-degrees help distinguish highly original components within individual proofs. The study also discusses the computational feasibility of this approach, combined with human judgment, enabling the effective reuse of proven mathematical concepts. We developed the FF-CUBED model to simplify the free-free emission components generated by stellar photoionization in protostellar disks and circumstellar disks, enabling efficient computation. The model accounts for ionization driven by wind, photoionization from the star, and photoionization from the midplane's irradiated surface due to free-free emission. We integrated this model into DISCO, a two-dimensional radiative transfer code, and validated it using simulations of a uniform disk. The model reveals complex phenomena including the wind's ionized surface producing a distinct emission layer and photoionization from the free-free emission itself, resulting in a pattern of red and blue shifts. We observed that photoionization from the free-free emission is negligible unless the free-free emission is intense, such as in the case of a disk surrounding a high-mass star. We analyzed the potential importance of free-free emission driven photoionization for various star masses and discovered it can be a major energy source for high-mass stars but is negligible for lower-mass stars. The model also shows that the photoionization from the free-free emission can impact the continuum shape, particularly for disks surrounding low-mass stars where the photoionization from the free-free emission is significant. Applying the model to observations of high-mass stars reveals that the free-free emission is a major energy source across the entire disk. Therefore, simplifying the free-free emission could lead to significant errors in estimating the star's luminosity and mass accretion rate. Utilizing the simplified FF-CUBED model can greatly improve computational efficiency by a factor of a thousand compared to comprehensive free-free emission calculations. The model is available for public use.

Researchers have experimentally achieved a novel Pauli crystal by utilizing a two-dimensional Fermi gas of ultracold $^{40}$K atoms. In this setup, an interface with a semiconductor material creates a tunneling barrier, allowing the study of Fermi gas behavior as it approaches the interface. By carefully adjusting the laser beam intensity, a Pauli crystal forming multiple rotation domains was obtained, each of which induces distinct, rotating spinor fields that strongly interact with the adjacent semiconductor material. This groundbreaking combination of quantum Hall regimes in ultra-cold atoms with the unique properties of semiconductors opens up new avenues in research. As predicted by theoretical studies, the achieved setup exhibits significant changes in the semiconductor material's electrical spin resonance, as well as substantial modifications to Pauli qubits and Fermi gas behavior near the interface. Our work presents a new approach to realizing topological systems with cold atoms and offers a platform for exploring quantum electronics based on the Pauli crystal principle. Furthermore, the demonstrated setup serves as a foundation for studying quantum entanglement between semiconductors and the multiple-rotation Pauli crystal formed by Pauli spinor fields. This setup also enables the control of heat transfer in connected semiconductor systems, which shows distinct differences from the standard Fermi gas thermal behavior. Additionally, the setup allows for the creation of a unique Pauli crystal on a semiconductor surface, where the crystal's spinor fields induce significant changes in the adjacent quantum Hall regimes and the semiconductor material's electrical properties. By leveraging this interaction, researchers have achieved precise control over the semiconductor interface's spin resonance, the movement of electrons within the semiconductor, and the transfer of heat between connected semiconductor systems. This control is shown to have substantial effects on the multiple-rotation Pauli crystal forming near the interface. Furthermore, the demonstrated setup serves as a foundation for realizing a new type of quantum electronics based on the Pauli crystal principle, which could be used to build advanced devices such as ultra-fast logic gates, devices that manipulate quantum states based on collisionless modes, and devices that transfer quantum information via collisions. This setup also provides a unique platform for studying novel phenomena such as the multiple-rotation Pauli crystal forming Pauli crystal, the unique properties of semiconductors in contact with superconductors, and the exceptional stability of electron beams in the quantum Hall regimes. By integrating research on ultra-cold atoms with semiconductor materials, the setup offers a new approach to realizing topological systems with cold atoms and offers promising avenues for future research.

It is proposed that $Z_{F\bar{F}} = \beta$ in QCD, providing a link between the renormalization constants of the fermion fields and the $\beta$-function. If this relationship holds, it would follow that the anomalous dimensions $[\gamma_1, \gamma_2, \gamma_3]$ for the operators $F\bar{F}$, $F\bar{F}^5$, and $F\bar{F}^6$ are all zero to one-loop order in the $\epsilon$-expanded scheme. If so, it would be possible to calculate the renormalization constants of the three-loop level using the anomalous dimensions at one-loop order and the $u$-expansion technique. Furthermore, it would be possible to calculate the $\beta$-function at the three-loop level using the anomalous dimensions at one-loop order and the $u$-expansion technique. We provide mathematical evidence to support these statements and offer a possible approach for calculating the renormalization constants at the three-loop level. Our findings have significant implications for precision calculations in the $[g_N, \alpha_S]$ regime and identify a key challenge for future calculations. We also extend the proposed relationship to include the case where $n_f > 6$ and perform an analysis of the anomalous dimensions for the $[J_P, J_S]$ operators, drawing on the knowledge that the anomalous dimensions for these operators are zero in QCD. We provide mathematical evidence to support this case and offer insights into the possible approaches for future calculations. Our findings prompt a call for action: they suggest that the relationship between $Z_{F\bar{F}}$ and $\beta$ should be verified through a three-loop calculation in order to inform precision calculations in $[g_N, \alpha_S]$ regime calculations and related $B$-physics applications. Our findings provide an important challenge for future calculations. We also use our findings to encourage further research into the relationship between the anomalous dimensions for the $[J_P, J_S]$ operators, drawing on the knowledge that the anomalous dimensions for these operators are zero in QCD. Our findings provide an important challenge in this area and offer insights into the relevant computational tools. We also provide a mathematical framework for calculating the anomalous dimensions at higher orders in QCD and extended $U(1)$ models, and offer insights into the role of anomalous dimensions in the context of renormalization and precision calculations

This research presents a novel framework addressing the problem of outlier samples in the sub-branch learning framework for few-shot learning. The framework consists of the combination of two networks: 1) a primary network designed with the standard five-shot learning protocol, and 2) a secondary network trained on an minimal set of data which classifies unfamiliar classes while mitigating the influence of noisy samples. The proposed method incorporates an out-of-class loss in the secondary network to effectively eliminate outlier samples. Furthermore, the concept of data-dependent uncertainty, derived from predictive uncertainty generated by the primary and secondary networks, is introduced to accurately handle class labels for unfamiliar classes. Experimental evaluations conducted on benchmarks such as miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cifarfs demonstrate the proposed framework's superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods. In recent years, SUKP and BMCP have gained significant attention in the machine learning community, given their utility in modeling diverse real-world problems. However, these problems are NP-hard, making it essential to develop efficient algorithms that balance local optimization quality with computational efficiency. This research introduces E2LS, a local search algorithm engineered to significantly reduce computational requirements by limiting the number of matrix multiplications. E2LS achieves this by leveraging 'free' edges in maximum weight perfect matching problems, allowing it to skip costly operations when updating candidate pools. This innovative approach enables E2LS to focus on more promising solutions, leading to either faster convergence to optimal solutions or higher solution quality within a given time frame. Empirical results demonstrate that E2LS consistently outperforms other local search algorithms, including column generation, in both solution quality and runtime. For SUKP, E2LS reaches a 0.0003% gap on large instances, while on BMCP, it achieves a 0.0005% gap, outperforming column generation by 1.5% in both cases. This improved local search algorithm serves as a building block for hybrid solution techniques, particularly when combined with column generation. On large SUKP instances, integrating E2LS yields a 2.0x speedup in total computation time, enabling column generation to achieve a 0.0002% gap, surpassing the 0.0003% gap achieved by E2LS alone. Similarly, on BMCP, the hybrid approach allows column generation to achieve a 0.0003% gap, surpassing E2LS's 0.0004% gap. These results indicate that E2LS makes SUKP more solvable under a sequential approach and significantly increases solution quality. This new local search algorithm further improves the hybrid algorithm's effectiveness on BMCP, achieving better results than on SUKP. Consequently, it is an excellent candidate for developing hybrid solution techniques aimed at expanding the practical applicability of these two machine learning problems. From a theoretical perspective, it is proposed that SUKP is more easily solvable than BMCP under computational complexity theory. This theoretical analysis is intended to be the subject of a forthcoming study. By leveraging a smart bike-sharing system, cyclists can inadvertently collect a substantial amount of data, including route information and times. Our proposed framework, "RouteMap," is designed to aggregate and analyze this data to generate detailed maps of urban cycling patterns. These maps, known as RouteMap, provide a visual representation of the frequency and efficiency of various routes in a city. Based on a multi-objective optimization framework, our approach generates trajectories that are optimal in terms of completion time and resistance to unexpected disturbances, while also taking into account safety constraints. Furthermore, our studies indicate that incorporating model uncertainty is crucial for creating reliable path plans, and that a straightforward extension of traditional path planners is insufficient for robust robotic control. We present and validate the mathematical formulation of our approach through a series of numerical experiments. Furthermore, we showcase its practical application in the autonomous navigation of a robotic arm on a diverse set of uncertain models. Policy replay, a technique that reduces this variance by computing the gradient of the expected action-value under a fixed distribution, known as experience replay, is an important technique in reinforcement learning. Recent advancements in reinforcement learning have introduced variance reduction based methods that improve the efficiency of these computations. This paper presents the variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework, which achieves replay in a way that is parallelizable and reduces the computational cost of computing gradients. By integrating this framework with online natural gradient methods, the VRER algorithm was shown to effectively converge to the optimal policy. Our experiments demonstrate that VRER is capable of reducing the computational cost of computing gradients and that integrating it with online natural gradient methods results in faster convergence. The VRER algorithm achieved state-of-the-art results in several continuous control tasks. By the same token, the VRER algorithm is capable of achieving state-of-the-art results in the challenging task of offline reinforcement learning. Our analysis of the VRER algorithm's performance reveals that its convergence rate is influenced by several key parameters. This analysis provides valuable insights into the relationship between these parameters and the rate at which VRER converges to the optimal policy. Our experiments validate the validity of our analytical findings and demonstrate that tuning these parameters in line with our analysis results in improved VRER performance. The proposed DCB achieved superior results on the Optical Flow Challenge 2021, ranking top in multiple categories, while being highly efficient, taking only 35.4 million operations and 0.81 megabytes of memory to implement. Notably, the DCB-based approach outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods in all relevant performance metrics. The source code for the DCB is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/ilya-shl/DCB. A detailed description of the DCB architecture and its performance can be found at https://iliashl.github.io/DCB-index.

A programming theory called Liquid Type Checking, when implemented, can almost completely eliminate memory safety errors and information-leaking vulnerabilities in programs written in low-level, imperative languages like C. This is because the theory combines with existing C type extenders to enforce memory usage rules, allowing for direct translation of high-level type warnings to strict type errors that cannot be easily worked around. A new implementation of Liquid C, called liquidhho, has been developed using a novel encoding of memory into the functional programming language Haskell, yielding better performance, greater expressiveness, and more robust error checking. This paper details the development of liquidhho and presents a series of performance and usability tests, including the verification of a highly concurrent data structure. This verification process uncovered a critical bug in the XZ utility used for data compression on Unix-like systems, which was previously unreported. liquidhho has been open-sourced and is available for public testing. As a fundamental unit of life, cells have long served as a foundational analysis for studying the intricate processes governing life. Given its numerous applications, cell identification and tracking have become a crucial aspect of image analysis. To develop a systematic approach to cell identification and tracking, we introduce a novel cell shape synthesis technique that aims to expand existing databases of cells. Our method utilizes deep generative models to create new cell shapes by learning the structural characteristics of cells, allowing us to successfully generate 10x more cell shapes than existing databases and accurately classify newly synthesized cells with a 96% accuracy rate. Notably, applying our synthesized cells to the problem of cell tracking demonstrates a significant improvement, with our approach increasing overall tracking performance by 5% and outperforming the state-of-the-art in cell tracking in 11 out of 14 benchmark datasets. Additionally, we release the first open-access, large-scale dataset of synthesized cell shapes to support the development of robust image analysis methods. The cell shape synthesis model and comprehensive dataset are publicly available at: https://github.com/CellShape/deep-cell-shapes. This study delves into BERT and XLNet, the leading NLP models of recent times, 
with a particular focus on the comparative analysis of their architectures and 
optimization techniques in the context of the pre-training and fine-tuning process. 
Key differences between these models and their innovative approaches are identified, 
such as BERT's multi-layer bi-directional self-attention mechanism and XLNet's 
multi-hop core reasoning architecture that utilizes max-out pooling. The work 
demonstrates that XLNet's performance surpasses BERT in several areas, including 
text classification and summarization, and attributes this advantage to a more 
efficient core reasoning strategy and optimized handling of the next sentence 
prediction task via the mask-token padding scheme. Furthermore, it proposes a 
modified version of XLNet, known as RoBERTa-XLNet, which integrates the core 
reasoning architecture of XLNet with the masked language modeling of BERT and 
exhibits enhanced performance in the context of natural language inference. 
Ultimately, the study highlights the importance of carefully designing the 
architecture of pre-trained language models in the pursuit of optimal performance.

Researchers used a controllable fluid dynamics model to study the swimming mechanics of the centipede species Loricales. They discovered that fluid force contributions significantly impact the creature's movement speed. In particular, alternating left and right drag created by the waves produced by its legs helps increase its speed by 15%, outperforming the speed increase that would result from equal and opposite inertia-based forces. This drag-based enhancement occurs because the alternating force component compensates for a loss of optimal thrust that would otherwise occur due to a delayed flap closure mechanism, a characteristic shared by many legged swimmers. Additionally, the study shows that fluid waves cause a speed increase of 11% when the centipede's legs move in unison, a phenomenon that doesn't happen under inertia-based forces. This research explains a natural phenomenon: the centipede's speed increases when its legs are damaged or not moving synchronously, a trait that has been observed in this species. The study also reveals that the force exerted by fluid waves helps create a consistent flow pattern behind the centipede's body, a feature that would be difficult to achieve through inertia-based forces. To model the centipede's leg movement accurately, the researchers used a complex movement pattern that incorporated the elasticity of its leg muscles and a delay in flap closure, a characteristic shared by many legged swimmers. This method effectively manages the intricate nature of coastal dynamics and its effects on a tsunami event, from the deep ocean to the point of land ingestion. We've demonstrated this adaptive strategy in an advanced numerical framework called Nxt, which is known for its open boundaries and multi-scale capabilities. We've utilized a refined coastal grid with diverse breakwater types and varied beach profiles, incorporating multiple scales and formats. Functional connectivity networks are generated by correlating blood oxygen levels across different brain locations and are often used in research, including studies of distinct individuals and groups.  One significant challenge in such research is determining the reliability of detected differences, including those observed in single subjects, group A versus group B, and group C comparisons.  Various studies have attempted to address this issue by calculating the reliability of network features derived from functional connectivity, but these efforts have focused primarily on inter-site effects in individual subjects or group-level comparisons.  To develop a reliable method, we introduced a multi-step approach to partition the brain into discrete regions with high inter-site effects, and we calculated the reliability of network features using a random partitioning process based on these regions.  Our results from resting-state fMRI data showed that the reliability of features was significantly higher for individual subjects (up to 87%), but also revealed that a significant proportion of group-level reliability originated from inter-site effects in group C comparisons.  These findings suggest that functional connectivity-based estimates are more reliable than previously thought, but also highlight the need to consider the impact of inter-site effects in statistical analyses, including those involving three-group comparisons.  One potential solution to mitigate this impact is to use datasets with a larger number of subjects, thereby increasing the statistical power to detect reliable features.  Our findings suggest that including sites with low inter-dependency on a few subjects does not significantly impact reliability, but including sites with low inter-dependency on a large number of subjects may significantly impact reliability.  In conclusion, our approach provides a systematic method to quantify the reliability of features derived from functional connectivity, including individual subjects, group-level differences, and the influence of inter-site effects, and highlights the need for larger datasets with high inter-dependency brain locations to ensure reliable research findings. This research is a starting point for developing an algorithm that can differentiate between guided design and exploratory material assembly and could potentially be applied to real-world robotic tasks. Artificial intelligence's capacity to address complex problems has grown significantly, yet its application in biologically inspired systems remains underutilized. A reinforcement learning approach can mimic the behavior of experimental manipulations that control plant growth and movement in response to environmental stimuli. Our study adapts this method of control in a computational model of the plant's behavioral mechanisms, allowing the model to mimic the effects of natural light exposure through internal signals and adjust its light sensitivity and signaling duration to achieve the desired outcomes. Furthermore, our model offers insights into how these internal controls coordinate to recreate the plant's phototrophic responses, which our experiments demonstrate are also essential for accurate reinforcement learning-driven plant simulation. These findings provide a framework for the development of AI systems inspired by the plant's abilities and could lead to the creation of more intelligent AI systems through the incorporation of biological insights. Existing machine learning methods, including those with deep structures, have difficulty solving problems with continuous targets, complex interactions, and nonlinear dynamics, which are typical characteristics of the plant's behavioral model. Our study demonstrates that addressing these challenges could yield significant advancements in AI development. A novel, open-source software framework based on Python has been designed to facilitate the integration of AI systems that mimic the plant's behavioral functions, which could also contribute to the development of AI systems that mimic human brain functions, as discussed in the article's discussion section. The research data, including source code, have been made available on an online platform.

Unfortunately, most current methods focus on isolating external influences and the pipeline's current performance, using fixed evaluation sets. This approach hinders the pipeline's potential for adaptation to novel, unseen tasks and external influences. To address this limitation, we introduce a new method for evaluating pre-processing pipelines called SUISEKI, an Japanese word meaning "to observe the flow". This method tracks changes in the pipeline's performance and its impact on downstream tasks through a continuous, adaptive framework. This method is represented as a graph where nodes correspond to specific pipeline operations like tokenization, decomposition, etc., and the edges have weights that indicate how much a given operation affects the pipeline's performance for a given task. By doing so, SUISEKI helps identify which pipeline components to improve and how to make the pipeline compatible with new tasks without the need for extensive re-training. SUISEKI's efficacy was demonstrated on various downstream tasks such as machine translation and question-answering, resulting in notable improvements by simply improving the pipeline's decomposition subsystem. This study explores the credibility of online headlines by introducing a set of artificially generated headlines and comparing them to genuine articles using a text-generation detection task. A comparison of four neural network models on this task revealed that the transformer model achieved the highest accuracy of 94%, surpassing the 90% accuracy of a recurrent neural network. Furthermore, the analysis found that the generated headlines had the least similarity to genuine articles in categories involving more complex language, such as technology and politics. A subsequent evaluation of a language model revealed a significant knowledge gap in three of the categories, but not in economics, which is often a target of information manipulation. A proposed method for identifying credible headlines utilizes a text-mining approach to weight headline words based on their relevance to search queries, resulting in improved accuracy for real vs. fake headlines. The generated headlines also enabled an examination of their evolution over time, showing a significant increase in convincingness after a dictionary expansion. The findings highlight the need for a combination of natural language generation and natural language understanding to combat online disinformation. By incorporating an autoencoding mechanism into the CGAN framework, ACGAN is developed to learn two types of portfolio management strategies. One strategy focuses on maximizing returns with minimal risk, similar to the traditional Markowitz framework. However, ACGAN also discovers alternative strategies that outperform the Markowitz model by utilizing a more comprehensive dataset of portfolios. Through numerous Monte Carlo simulations, ACGAN's portfolio allocation is compared to those generated by the Markowitz framework and evolutionary algorithms, such as the genetic algorithm. ACGAN's ability to discover robust portfolio strategies under various market conditions is a key benefit of this approach. Furthermore, the theoretical foundations of ACGAN-based portfolio allocation are explored, and the method is empirically validated using a dataset of weekly US stock market returns from 1962 to 2019. Interestingly, the top-performing portfolio strategies discovered by ACGAN typically involve high concentrations in a limited number of assets, known as the Nifty Fifty. However, these portfolios significantly deviate from the traditional Markowitz model and typical portfolio allocation methods by maintaining a diversified spread of investments. By utilizing deep learning to discover robust portfolio strategies, ACGAN is an advanced machine learning framework for portfolio allocation, particularly when compared to traditional methods. Further investigation into the alternative strategies discovered by ACGAN is warranted. Deep neural networks can effectively map complex input data, but their predictions often lack a clear explanation for their confidence levels. This issue is critical when working with limited and biased data, often required for security, medical, and environmental assessments. Bayesian neural networks offer an alternative by providing a distributional estimate of input and output states. Specifically, the authors propose BNN-CL, a classification framework based on a Bayesian neural network that uses a categorical likelihood function. They conduct a comprehensive comparison of various BNN categorical likelihoods, including standard and novel options. On five datasets with varying levels of complexity and sizes, BNN-CL outperforms non-Bayesian counterparts by significant margins, especially with the more effective likelihood functions. Furthermore, the study reveals that the conventional assumption of independent and identically distributed data is not necessary for accurate modeling, and includes a mathematical justification and empirical validation of this finding. Overall, the study highlights the importance of using a categorical likelihood function in BNNs for classification tasks. The authors plan to release the code used in this study, including the implementation of a likelihood function that uses a hierarchical Dirichlet prior to model the data distribution. This study revisits the concept of Church encodings for data structures in lambda-calculi, with a particular focus on their potential to expand the expressive capabilities of simply typed lambda-calculus. To that end, we establish a categorization theorem for certain typed lambda-calculi incorporating Church encodings, with data types restricted to recursive types with single recursive components. The theorem sets parameters for the conditions under which these lambda-calculi exhibit the same expressiveness as the untyped lambda-calculus. Subsequently, we investigate the methods of augmenting Church encodings to represent data structures that enable simply typed lambda-calculus to equal the expressiveness of the untyped lambda-calculus. Our work builds upon existing research, notably adapting Stewart's approach to incorporating inductive mutual recursion and extending previous findings on including booleans and ordered pairs. The major part of this research is divided into three cases: analyzing the extended Church encoding for recursive types with two recursive components, investigating methods of regularizing the data types via alternative presentations, and assessing the requirements for regular presentations to maintain equal expressiveness results. The methods of regular presentations comprise decomposing recursive fields, equational decompositions, and both types of mutual recursion. The analysis reveals a complex interplay among these methods, with certain combinations allowing the untyping of recursive fields, inductive mutual recursions, and a limited form of inductive self-referential recursion. Finally, we outline a method for deriving regular presentations from systems featuring regular data structures in their typing judgments, with an emphasis on its potential to facilitate the validation of program correctness. This research is the first to provide a comprehensive understanding of the full spectrum of data structure encodings expressible in lambda-calculi. The contributions of this work extend beyond lambda-calculi to encompass a broader class of typed systems with inductive-finite recursive types. The major outcomes of this study include the extension of previous results, the adaptation of Stewart's approach to inductive mutual recursion and extending previous findings on including booleans and ordered pairs. The work is further supplemented by a detailed examination of several crucial, long-standing open questions related to data structure encodings, with partial answers to the most prominent queries. The potential applications of this work extend beyond lambda-calculi to typed programming languages and system validation, with a major focus on its potential to facilitate the development of regular presentations through program correctness verification. This study introduces an enhanced collision avoidance approach for complex robotic groups moving at varying speeds. Unlike existing methods that rely on the positions of rogue robots, the proposed method considers the uncertainties of all participating robots, generating a more accurate representation of potential conflicts. Specifically, the new strategy utilizes the distribution of predicted interaction data, rather than mere proximity, to effect a smoother and more robust collision avoidance. By integrating the new method into existing collision avoidance frameworks, the simulation results reveal a notable reduction in collisions, with an average decrease of 42% for groups of robots and a 54% decrease in groups containing 'rogue' robots. Furthermore, the results show that the probability of successful avoidance increases by 50% to 70% compared to the original method. Moreover, the study demonstrates the potential of the new method to serve as a foundation for developing a robust training-through-reinforcement approach, thereby expanding the scope of collision avoidance research. The new method, known as the Distribution-based Collision Avoidance Method (DCAM), is presented in this work. Additionally, the study shows that the new method can be viewed as a special case of the Multi-Objective Distribution-based Collision Avoidance Method (MOD-CAM), where the new method is derived under the assumption of no uncertainty in the robotic group. The study presents a novel approach to training MOD-CAM, thereby offering a promising solution for real-world collision avoidance challenges. By incorporating the concept of successful avoidance into the reward function of the Multi-Objective Genetic Algorithm, the method evaluates various distribution-based collision avoidance strategies and selects the one with the highest probability of successful avoidance. By integrating the new method into the common collision avoidance framework, the study derives a new function for calculating the probability of successful avoidance, which in turn reveals a notable correlation between the distribution-based approach and collision-free rate. The study shows a substantial improvement in collision-free rate by a factor of 5.33 to 13.33, and an even higher factor of 27.33 to 54.67 for groups containing 'rogue' robots. The new method, DCAM, is shown to be an effective strategy to achieve a higher collision-free rate and train MOD-CAM, thereby offering a promising solution for real-world collision avoidance challenges. Dialogue State Tracking is a crucial component of Spoken Dialogue systems that tracks user inputs, output, and state changes. Current popular end-to end DST models have limitations in understanding dialogue contexts and individual turns. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a new approach that combines an attentional confusion network encoder with a flat graph attention mechanism to enhance dialogue state tracking performance. The proposed model achieves superior results with a state-of-the-art convergence speed on the DSTC7 dataset, significantly outperforming other advanced models in terms of accuracy and state tracking. Experiments demonstrate that incorporating an attentional confusion network encoder with flat graph attention yields a 6.18% absolute improvement in joint goal accuracy compared to the baseline model. Furthermore, detailed ablation studies confirm that the proposed model achieves 88.43% joint goal accuracy, surpassing previous state-of-the-art DST models by a notable margin. The proposed attentional confusion network encoder and associated code are now publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/HCST-Udacity/ACN_DST. A public demo of the model can be accessed at https://kc2d8c8b6b8c2.developerdemo.com/. A tutorial on this model can be found at https://analysis kc2d8c8b6b8c2.gitee.io/#/, with the associated paper submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computer, 2022. The primary contributions of this paper are a novel flat graph attention model with high efficiency and performance, and a proposed end-to-end DST model incorporating an ACN encoder as the graph attention model building block, yielding state-of-the-art results and outperforming previous models on the DSTC7 dataset in joint goal accuracy. The model achieves an absolute improvement of 6.18% in joint goal accuracy compared to the baseline model, and demonstrates high robustness and efficiency due to its use of a flat graph attention model. The paper also presents a new approach to DST model selection based on the flat score metric, and is the first to propose a novel ACN encoder with flat graph attention for DST applications. The open-source code enables other researchers to build similar models and conduct further experiments. The model has been deployed as a public demo, showcasing its ability to solve dialogue state tracking problems, and a tutorial is available for users to learn more about the technology. Quantum systems serve as the foundation for numerous cutting-edge technologies, but are also susceptible to decoherence, which hampers their performance. Investigating decoherence in entangled systems is crucial for understanding how to harness quantum technology effectively. This study focuses on comparing two common noise models for a two-qubit system, but approaches the analysis from a novel perspective. Rather than relying on specific models, we develop a general method to assess which model is most relevant given available data. By utilizing optimal estimators associated with different models, we introduce a metric that measures the distance between estimated parameters under one model and actual parameters under another. This metric enables direct comparisons of two models based on their past performance. However, our initial findings suggest that optimal estimators are inefficient, so we develop a simplified version of these estimators that are faster to compute and yield similar comparisons. The use of our estimators results in significant computational improvements. This study has broader implications, as the concepts explored here are not limited to the specific context of two-qubit systems and can be applied to various physical systems. Additionally, the software utilized in this research is publicly available at github.com/quantum-qrm/quantum-estimators. Several of the functions within this repository can be extended to other systems with little modification. A more detailed description of the software and its components can be found in the paper. Furthermore, the research presented here highlights key contributions, including the introduction of a novel method for comparing two different models, the development of faster estimators, the implementation of more optimal estimators that are faster than optimal estimators but still accurate, and the provision of publicly available software that can be easily adapted to other physical systems. Lastly, the research demonstrates that the use of our estimators results in substantial computational improvements, with the use of optimal estimators being 10-15 times slower than the use of simplified estimators and the use of sensitive estimators being 1000 times slower. A flowchart illustrating the order in which the different software components are called can be found in Figure 1 in the paper. Specifically, the research provides an example of how the use of optimal estimators can improve the assessment of different noise models for entangled two-bits when the actual model is either the amplitude-damping model or the phase-damping model. An algorithm called EDFA was employed to analyze the power spectral density and the time series data, allowing for the identification of distinct growth rates in both directions. An examination of the periodic components using the morphological decomposition method revealed the presence of discrete structures such as edge localized gaps and magnetic islands within a palm tree mode that emerged. The underlying physics behind this phenomenon is believed to stem from the destabilization of the computed mode, which is attributed to a computed source in the linear neoclassical instability theory. An effective region, characterized by a H-mode pedestal width of θy2 < 0.1, acts as a barrier that prevents the growth of these unstable modes, while their birth can be triggered by the collapse of this barrier and subsequent formation of magnetic islands and palm tree modes. The research findings demonstrate that the destabilization of these unstable modes is closely linked to the evolution of the computational physics and the structural changes in the plasma. The statistical analysis of the data reveals a significant positive correlation between the growth rate and period, as well as the period of the dominant instability. To investigate non-flow angular correlations between two particles, a new analytical framework has been created, which expresses angular distributions in terms of flow coefficients beyond the V0 collision plane. This approach extends previous studies of dipolar and quadrupolar correlations and introduces novel coefficients for higher-order analysis. The new methodology relies on a Fourier decomposition of charge azimuthal distributions, where each term corresponds to a specific flow coefficient. To illustrate this framework's feasibility, a V0-based measurement was performed using ATLAS detector data from 2.76 TeV Pb+Pb collisions, focusing on charged-particle transverse momentum between 1-20 GeV/c. Results are presented for dipolar, quadrupolar, and pentapolar correlations at various collision centrality levels. For the dipolar case, significant Correlation and anti-Correlation peaks are observed at approximately 0 and 0.5, respectively, while pentapolar results show enhanced Correlation at approximately 0.5. Furthermore, in both scenarios, an increase in correlation strength is seen with increasing centrality. Quadrupolar results show enhanced Correlation at approximately 0.22. These findings are in line with expectations from Monte Carlo predictions, which have been studied using various sources, including those incorporating both flow and jet-deflection simulations. This new analysis provides a complete understanding of the new coefficients' definitions and their underlying physical origins. Additionally, due to its sensitivity to a broader range of underlying flow coefficients, this method can potentially reveal the presence of unaccounted sources, such as jet-deflection correlation with itself or with another jet, which was previously suggested in a study using CMS detector data. In conclusion, this new framework offers a valuable tool for flow and jet physics analysis in high-energy collisions. Future studies will utilize this approach to investigate pentapolar correlation results in an even broader range of transverse momentum. References [25, 27] are cited in the original research paper. Healthcare institutions are increasingly adopting cloud-based data storage systems to access various healthcare documents, including patients' medical histories, prescriptions, and lab results, as a means of ensuring security and scalability. However, such systems make it necessary to handle sensitive data using external services, such as machine learning models, for processing and analysis. The problem arises in sharing accessed documents with third-party providers, such as healthcare facilities or research institutions, after having been processed by machine learning models. In this context, the risk of a data breach becomes a top priority, as any data leak could compromise the confidentiality of sensitive healthcare information. To mitigate this threat, we introduce a new approach, using an extended architecture, a deep learning model, and information theory-based methods, to minimize the risk of information leakage and protect cloud-based data from unauthorized disclosure. The proposed approach leverages a deep learning model, trained using data from the MNIST dataset, to apply image transformations to processed documents, while a second model, also trained on the MNIST dataset, is used to remove identifying information from images. Additionally, we recommend using mutual information to eliminate redundant information and an information-theoretic approach to quantize images while minimizing information loss, as measured by the residual entropy. The proposed approach was evaluated using a simulated environment and compared with a standard approach based on lossy compression, in terms of information leakage risk and document quality. The results demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces information leakage risk while delivering comparable document quality and a higher level of security than the standard approach. Through theoretical analysis and numerical assessments on various synthetic and real-world datasets, rCASPR is shown to surpass the linear sampling (LS) point-spread function and yield better image contrast, while also being simpler and more efficient to implement. Specifically, rCASPR is applied to the task of extended X-ray phase tomography, where it is used to reconstruct phase images using multiple data constraints, with a notable reduction in reconstruction errors and noise levels. Moreover, rCASPR is also used in a cross-validation study to demonstrate its ability to recover features from real-life paintings, such as Van Gogh's 'Zouave', with a notable improvement in its feature-based rating scores compared to the CSPI-based reconstruction. These experimental results collectively indicate that rCASPR is a highly effective and efficient linear sampling method, with numerous potential applications in various imaging fields. However, existing methods fail to fully leverage the teacher's knowledge due to incomplete channel reduction. Our findings indicate that DistPrune can effectively utilize teacher knowledge to efficiently configure student model weights, enhancing learning efficiency by 55.8% and reducing memory requirements. A significant issue in abstractive summarization is the prevalence of inaccuracies. We present a new approach, called SummChain, to generate summaries by linking entities into "chains". This method allows for the adjustment of entity relationships during summary generation, enabling the correction of errors and eliminating unnecessary entities. Building on the Transformer architecture, SummChain incorporates a novel object-relations loss to refine entity relationships. Experiments with the SummChain algorithm on two datasets have shown promising results, surpassing state-of-the-art models generated summaries in factual accuracy by 14.72% and outperforming them in summary length with a 2-fold decrease. Additionally, SummChain effectively rectified errors in reference summaries by correctly establishing relationships between entities and removing unessential entities. The code and model are available on GitHub. Furthermore, SummChain has successfully identified unessential entities previously present in reference summaries, thereby aiding human evaluators to assess its efficacy. This initiative aims to establish a new evaluation metric to assess generated summaries qualitatively. The research is accompanied by a new dataset compilation, called SummChain-50M, which contains an expanded collection of 1 million human-generated summary chains, providing a framework for the development of new summarization models. This work aims to pave the way for the design of summary generation algorithms that can guarantee the accuracy, coherence, and fluency of generated summaries. Entrainment, or the synchronization of vocal patterns, is a key indicator of conversational flow.
Recent research has increasingly used measurement tools to analyze and compare the conversational styles
of individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and neurotypical individuals.
However, the existing literature lacks a comprehensive, systematic measurement approach that unifies
the evaluation of different voice characteristics.
In response, we propose the ASD-Conversational Entrainment Measurement Framework (ACMF), a
structured method for measuring the degree to which individuals with ASD and ASD individuals match their
conversation partners synchronize their voices.
The framework comprises five sub-scales, each focused on a specific aspect of voice pattern synchronization:
matching pitch, pace, pause, pause duration, and pause frequency.
Each sub-scale is calculated from a fundamental frequency, speech rate, pause frequency, and
pause duration, respectively, and then summed to form the overall Entrainment Score.
In a study, we applied the ACMF to a dataset of 31 individuals with ASD and 31 matched controls, and
evaluated the sub-scales and Entrainment Score with both statistical and machine learning methods.
The results show that individuals with ASD, on average, have lower Entrainment Scores, and that certain
sub-scales are more sensitive to different types of autism.
Moreover, we found that certain sub-scales are more predictive of different autism types.
Our study indicates that the ACMF is a reliable tool for categorizing individuals with ASD based on their
conversational style.
Notably, we found that the sub-scales are more predictive of different autism types than traditional methods.
The ACMF is a versatile tool that can be used in a variety of applications, such as diagnosing and assessing
ASD, and developing personalized communication strategies. Moreover, it has the potential to be applied
in a broader context beyond autism spectrum disorder. Furthermore, we found that the sub-scales can be
used to develop a new classification system for ASD, and provide insights for estimating ASD subtypes. 
The research framework is generally applicable and can be used in any situation where vocal entrainment is measured to achieve a specific goal, and therefore, has a high potential for extension to other areas. 
In addition, we found that including a representation of each individual's Entrainment Score transformation can lead to better accuracy when classifying ASD subtypes. 
The combination of the sub-scales and representation learning method achieves a better accuracy rate (77%) compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods

A robotic swarm testbench known as SwarmLab was developed to analyze cooperative behavior in robotics.  This document outlines a novel extension to the SwarmLab framework called 'SwarmState', which enables estimating dynamic changes within simulated robotic environments with noise.  By integrating with SwarmLab, SwarmState allows for monitoring of cooperative behaviors, model validation, and educational purposes.  By leveraging either a basic or advanced Kalman filter, SwarmState can adapt to systems with increasing complexity to accurately predict system states even with noisy conditions.  This extension is implemented in C++ and accessible via a Python API for easy integration into user-defined robotic swarm models by facilitating state estimation based on sensor data.  This facilitates the observation of states that are not directly measurable in the system.  This contribution is presented in the form of a 15-minute conference talk, demonstrating its practical application with a robotic swarm example that requires measuring positions of the swarm's leader and follower to control the swarm's motion.  This experiment showcases the effectiveness of SwarmState with a 4-robot swarm, achieving an average estimation error of 0.07 meters for the leader's position and 0.11 meters for the follower's position. An efficient O(n^2/(log n)^3) runtime algorithm to compute Kendall's tau is presented for datasets of size n. The technique employed involves analyzing the matrix of pairings that underlies the traditional definition of Kendall's tau, and leveraging the concept of co-occurrence patterns within this matrix to identify monotonic relationships between observations. The novel approach yields a statistical test based on these co-occurrence patterns, allowing for the development of an equitable procedure to assess p-values. Furthermore, this method is shown to have asymptotic sensitivity equivalent to the Kolmogorov complexity of the relevant co-occurrence patterns, and empirical tests confirm its performance with actual sensitivity levels only modestly inferior to the optimal maximum possible sensitivity. The computational complexity of this algorithm is driven primarily by the need to execute a number of repetitions in the statistical test equal to O(n^(log n-1)). An alternative procedure is also presented that reduces the number of required repetitions to O(n^(log n-3)). The concept of equitable procedures was introduced to ensure that no individual's data could be used to gain an unfair advantage in a competitive statistical test, and alternative procedures exist that offer a runtime of O(n^(log n-2) to O(n^(log n-5)) respectively. The novel algorithm to compute Kendall's tau is shown to have runtime performance comparable to other existing procedures, such as O(n^2) for the standard definition and O(n^2.33) for Hájek and Šírová's definition, and superior to other known definitions with lower complexity. The theoretical and practical effectiveness of this approach have been confirmed through analysis of synthetic datasets and real-world data from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, and it has been demonstrated that the method yields results that are statistically significantly different from random noise in cases where the relationship is known. The algorithm's source code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/bradleym01/KendallTau. While maintaining the efficiency of those algorithms, the facet pivot method offers improved performance in both time and memory usage. This is achieved by leveraging a basis matrix that remains sparse during calculations. A pivot element is introduced at each iteration, eliminating the need for dense storage of the system matrix. A crucial step in this method involves checking for positive block entries in the basis matrix. If a suitable block is found, the algorithm proceeds without additional modifications. This strategy is proven to yield a feasible solution and track the dual objective function's evolution accurately. A small set of problem-specific strategies has been developed for scenarios where a suitable block cannot be identified. To further optimize performance, the facet pivot method incorporates a range finding procedure and provides an implementation-based time complexity analysis. This research focuses on developing effective anti-spoofing measures for facial recognition systems through transfer learning using pre-trained vision transformer models, with a goal of upgrading existing facial recognition technology for enhanced security and reliability. Building on the knowledge gained from large pre-training datasets, this study investigates the feasibility of using pre-trained vision transformers for anti-spoofing tasks and presents a method to fine-tune these models on various datasets. Furthermore, it evaluates the performance of different vision transformer architectures and the impact of batch normalization on anti-spoofing performance. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of transfer learning from pre-trained vision transformers for this application and suggest a range of options for model selection and optimization. Notably, this research reveals that using the Swin-B vision transformer architecture achieves a high accuracy of 97.88% using a relatively small ASVSPM dataset, with a model pre-trained on the large ImageNet dataset as the starting point. The findings also show that using the Swin-L vision transformer architecture achieves an accuracy of up to 99.13% on the CASIA-FASD dataset, which is one of the leading datasets for anti-spoofing research. Notably, this high accuracy achieved by Swin-L is 2.5% higher than the best reported result in the literature, as accessed in February 2021. The proposed method in this study has been successfully applied to two prominent vision transformer models, Res2Net and Swin-B, and has achieved impressive results on various datasets, including CASIA-FASD, ASVSPM, and UADEMY. The study's findings highlight the significant potential of using large vision transformer models for anti-spoofing applications and suggests that using a larger model with a smaller number of parameters can lead to improved accuracy. The research data and code are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashishgupta9/anti-spoofing-vision-transformer. The system's physical properties are largely influenced by the Ce 4f electronic state as observed through muon spin relaxation experiments, showing temperature and Rh content dependencies.  The temperature dependencies can be attributed to the development of magnetic clusters in the alloys, the freezing temperature of which increases with an increase in Rh content below approximately x = 0.6.  Below this temperature, the alloys exhibit slow magnetization fluctuations.  The analysis of the data indicates the existence of two types of magnetic clusters, one being small with a freezing temperature and the other larger with a freezing temperature shifted towards the system's low temperature region as the Rh content increases.  The increased cluster size results in the alloys exhibiting antiferromagnetic ordering behavior.  The analysis further reveals that the alloys' ground state is a heavy fermion antiferromagnet with a Curie-Weiss temperature shifting towards a low temperature region as the Rh content increases. Using approximately one billion collisions collected by the LHCb detector in 2011 and 2012, researchers investigated the difference between the CP-odd and CP-even oscillation states of B$_\mathrm{s}$ decays. To do this, they analyzed the J/π+π− final state, which arises from B$_\mathrm{s}$→J/ψK+π− or its CP-conjugate, and used a reconstruction technique sensitive to CP violation that utilized data from positively and negatively charged beams. This allowed them to construct parameters η and sin(2β) for the J/ψπ+π− final state, and to place tight constraints on CP violation in the B$_\mathrm{s}$→J/ψφ decay channel for the first time. While no CP violation was observed in either channel, the results are consistent with expectations and the margins of error are the tightest yet obtained for B$_\mathrm{s}$ decays. To put these findings into perspective, the researchers compared them with predictions based on the standard model of particle physics. In particular, any observed CP violation beyond a certain threshold would have far-reaching implications for our understanding of particle interactions. This analysis also serves as a crucial test of the idea that CP violation occurs at a level of about two thousandth in B$_\mathrm{s}$ decays. Furthermore, by comparing the CP violation observed in B$_\mathrm{s}$ decays to that of other channels, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of how these particles form and interact. This analysis provides valuable input into our knowledge of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa mixing matrix. And finally, by pushing the margins of error for CP violation as close to the detection margin as possible, researchers hope to push the detection power as far as possible. The goal of unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is to enhance the performance of an image classification model when training data does not accurately represent the target domain. This challenge is widespread in real-world applications, such as natural language processing and autonomous systems. One of the primary difficulties in UDA lies in the fact that contrastive learning techniques based on self-supervised learning are not easily modifiable for domain adaptation tasks. This paper presents CADA, a novel approach that combines multiple features to create a refined, contrastive framework tailored for UDA. First, we developed a domain-agnostic method for creating pairs of images without considering pose variations. Next, we integrated an augmented version of each image into the training loss function to further improve performance. This strategy allows for the creation of a feature space where the target domain is separated from the source domain. We tested CADA on multiple UDA datasets and found it to surpass state-of-the-art techniques in image classification performance. CADA's source code is available for public use at the URL https://github.com/asharari/CADA. CADA's results have been accepted for presentation at a conference and will be published in a forthcoming journal. CADA achieves a high performance of  $77.9\%$ on the ResNet-50 model on the VisDA2012 dataset, surpassing the performance of the best published method by $10.3\%$. CADA also achieves a high performance of $ $96.50\%$ (error rate of $3.50\%$) on the COUSU-Batch dataset, surpassing the performance of the best published method by $4.17\%$; the current best published method reports an error rate of $7.53\%$ corresponding to a correct classification rate of $92.47\%$. CADA also achieves a high performance of $ 83.36\%$ (error rate of $16.64\%$) on the Office-Home dataset; CADA outperforms the current best published method by $ 4.04\%$; the current best published method reports an error rate of $ $20.68\%$ in this dataset. Graph Neural Networks have achieved great success in working with complex graph data, but their complex models and outcomes make it challenging to understand their decisions. Therefore, explaining how these models work is essential to gaining their trust. Previous methods used backtracking and loss analysis, but these approaches have limitations, such as being impractical for large-scale datasets and sometimes providing inaccurate explanations. This paper introduces a new model explanation framework called PGExplainer that generates more accurate, relevant, and efficient explanations for GNN decisions by interpreting the primary graph patterns these models use to make predictions. By using a graph embedding method called link trail analysis, PGExplainer identifies significant graph patterns that serve as key evidence. In contrast to previous methods, PGExplainer focuses on explaining the graph structure itself rather than the model architecture. This allows it to bypass the complexity of the model and directly identify the important graph features the GNN models use to make predictions. The explanations generated by PGExplainer are easy to understand, which makes it an ideal tool for applications where explainability is crucial, such as healthcare and recommendation systems. Comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets from various domains have shown that PGExplainer outperforms existing explanation frameworks both quantitatively and qualitatively. For instance, it significantly improves explanation accuracy on datasets like Cora and PubMed-Diagnose by 19.0% and 14.6%, respectively. Moreover, it reduces explanation generation time by 85.9% on a dataset from the Kaggle EdNet challenge. This makes PGExplainer a practical and efficient solution for applications that require rapid-scale-auditing. The code for PGExplainer is available at https://github.com/AlibabaGroup/PGExplainer. This research also demonstrates that explaining decision support systems that rely on graph decision support systems is feasible without requiring the models or the underlying graph data, which makes it an ideal application for explainability tools. This is because such systems provide decision makers with relevant and easy-to-understand information about the cases they encounter. PGExplainer can generate explanations for these systems by identifying the significant graph patterns that serve as key evidence. A novel memory component called the Large Memory Unit (LMU) has been proposed, capable of efficiently allocating and utilizing multiple sizes of memory for deep neural network training. By overcoming existing memory limitations in data-parallel training on GPUs, the LMU allows for seamless access to large memory pools without undergoing frequent page swaps, thus reducing training times and boosting the efficiency of model compression. Moreover, the study reveals that incorporating compressed models and random loading of weights results in improved generalization over uncompressed models, while the emergence of unfaithful gradients introduces a new regularization mechanism that can be adjusted. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of the Large Memory Unit in unlocking deep learning potential on high-end GPUs with limited high-speed memory capacity. The LMU has been successfully integrated into the open-source DeepMeshNet library for meshnet model training. The source code and model weights are available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepMeshNet/LMU. A comprehensive tutorial can be accessed at https://github.com/DeepMeshNet/LMU/blob/main/docs/how-to-use-lmu-for-meshnet-training.md. The study also showcases the potential of training powerful visual correspondence models using cost volume and multi-scale classification at extremely large scales, thereby achieving state-of-the-art performance and advancing the field of meshnet models. These advanced models have been successfully deployed on the MeshnetDB database, a comprehensive 3D database of 100k+ point clouds. The database can be accessed at https://www.meshnetdb.com. Migration can significantly impact language development, yet a comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon is achievable only through integrating principles from social complexity and linguistic research. Achieving a general theory of how migration affects language is feasible, provided that key variables such as migration intensity, the number of languages and populations involved, and geographical conditions are taken into consideration. Consequently, any attempt to predict the impact of migration on language change should be grounded in a multi-disciplinary foundation encompassing elements from social anthropology, linguistics, theoretical physics, complex systems, and statistical mechanics. This integrative approach is exemplified in a case study focusing on the potential consequences of migration between two cities in close contact, which I will use to illustrate how migration influences language formation under various scenarios of migration and language exchange. This multi-disciplinary framework is presented as an innovative contribution to the field of linguistics, which has traditionally drawn upon insights from anthropology, sociology, and psychology, as well as comparative anatomy and physiology, historical comparison, historical philology, and historical philosophy. Furthermore, I provide an analysis of how an elementary model, which combines principles from systems research and statistical mechanics, can account for the complex effects of migration on language development. This model displays a wide range of language dynamics, which are largely consistent with historical records. An in-depth examination of the similarities between this linguistic model and systems research reveals an intriguing correspondence between linguistic processes and those in complex systems research, particularly in the context of migration. Conversely, I identify significant differences between the two fields, particularly in the context of exogenous events, feedback loops, and migratory flows. This integrative approach is seen as an attempt to revive the interest of linguists in the principles of systems research and the world of life, as well as to foster dialogue between the two fields. Despite improvements made to the PINN framework, the relationship between training methods and spectral bias remains poorly understood. By combining numerical sensitivity analysis, theoretical spectral analysis, and numerical experiments, we found that SGDM significantly decreases the spectral bias in PINNs by preventing overfitting and stabilizing the training process. Our work not only provides insights into the influence of training methods on spectral bias but also offers a practical approach for reducing bias in PINNs. Furthermore, we introduced the concept of spectral representability structure, which provides a theoretical understanding of the spectral behavior of PINNs trained using SGDM. Our study provides valuable guidance for PINN researchers and engineers. We also introduced a hyperparameter tuning framework based on Bayesian optimization, which demonstrated its effectiveness in achieving optimal bias-reduction results. By applying this framework, we successfully obtained a reduced relative spectral bias of at least two orders of magnitude. Our theoretical contributions focus on understanding the spectral behavior of PINNs, which are capable of approximating a wide range of spectral representations. Based on the principles of Fourier analysis and neural network spectral representation, we developed a theoretical framework for understanding the spectral representation of PINNs. By using the principles of neural network spectral representation, we determined the numerical approximation error in the spectral representation of PINNs. We derived the spectral representation of PINNs as a multidimensional Fourier series and provided a numerical approximation bound. We established a spectral representability structure for PINNs and identified the spectral representation as a solution to a minimization problem. Our numerical experiments involved training PINNs on a range of ordinary differential equations with various coefficients and nonlinearity. We used the SGDM method to investigate its effectiveness in reducing spectral bias. Our results showed that the SGDM method significantly decreases the spectral bias in PINNs by controlling the approximation error in the spectral representation. Our numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the hyperparameter tuning framework based on Bayesian optimization in achieving optimal bias-reduction results. Our framework successfully obtained a reduced relative spectral bias of at least two orders of magnitude. In contrast, manually developed symbolic rules enable better interpretability, but require a deeper level of human expertise. This study aims to bridge this gap by leveraging natural language transformations and introducing an objective function to improve the interpretability of learned policies through their similarity to symbolic rules. We achieve this with the RuleExplaner, a novel approach that uses reinforcement learning combined with rule-generating techniques to create more understandable policies for complex decision-making tasks. The RuleExplaner enhances existing reinforcement learning algorithms by introducing a novel objective function and a new method for explaining policies based on symbolic rules. Case studies have demonstrated that RuleExplaner can effectively improve the policy's interpretability in diverse scenarios while maintaining its effectiveness. Moreover, we evaluated the epistemic uncertainty of the learned policies using multiple testing frameworks and found that RuleExplaner's policies exhibit superior and more predictable performance compared to state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods. The RuleExplaner's source code is publicly available on GitHub. This research provides a framework for improving the interpretability of reinforcement learning methods, which is particularly important for high-stakes applications involving data privacy and security. By integrating symbolic reinforcement learning with reinforcement learning, our approach enhances the empirical performance and interpretability of learned policies simultaneously, which is a significant challenge in the field of reinforcement learning. The development of non-reciprocal optical devices of low size with consistent functionality is a vital objective that supports the creation of complex, directionally-based optical networks and photonic systems.  We present an approach that achieves all-optical diodes and quasi-circulators by incorporating chiral interresonator coupling into dual-cavity and multi-cavity systems.  The cavity-cavity coupling sets an asymmetrical boundary, resulting in diode-like characteristics with one-way excitation and bi-directional signal transmission.  Additionally, the multi-cavity system displays quasi-circulator characteristics with bi-directional signal transmission and isolation in selected paths.  The theory is supported by numerical simulations and potential applications in optical sensing and data processing are discussed.  This approach could be integrated into compact photonic systems built from low-VLSI microcavities to enable optical manipulation and processing of information.  Specifically, the diode and quasi-circulator structures could enhance the functionality of optical phase shifters, slow-light systems, and optical diode arrays by providing a simple and all-optical means of control.  We propose that these photonic circuits could be fabricated using photonic crystal, interferometric, or hybrid optical systems.
