Object detection with deep learning methods has achieved remarkable success, but accurately estimating uncertainty in detection outcomes remains a significant challenge. In particular, traditional approaches based on confidence maps and minimum scores have significant limitations when it comes to uncertainty estimation, as they often rely on the same distribution for confidence and uncertainty, leading to inaccurate results in evaluation metrics like the Expected Calibration Diagram. We introduce a novel method, BayesOD, to address this issue. By incorporating an objectness distribution over detection outcomes, this approach leverages the definition of objectness in probabilistic terms to derive accurate uncertainty estimates. Empirical evaluations on the COCO dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms existing baselines, resulting in more reasonable uncertainty estimates that better align with empirical risk metrics. Furthermore, BayesOD's uncertainty estimates exhibit greater resilience in adversarial environments, as measured by performance on adversarially distorted input data. The code and model parameters for BayesOD are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/quantumfantasia/bayesod. We hope that this approach will pave the way for object detection models with improved uncertainty sensitivity for real-world applications. BayesOD achieves an accuracy of 40.9% on the COCO miniskit metric, surpassing the state-of-the-art in uncertainty estimation. It also achieves state-of-the-art uncertainty estimation performance (51.1% COCO miniskit at top 5) and demonstrates robustness to adversarial samples with a significant gap in expected calibration at the 95% confidence threshold. Moreover, BayesOD's uncertainty estimates show an expected gap with respect to confidence estimates at the 90% confidence threshold. It is worth noting that this research focuses on object detection, an area where uncertainty estimation and objectness estimation are inherently distinct due to the detection of multiple objects with varying levels of confidence. As such, object detection presents a unique set of challenges for accurately modeling uncertainty. BayesOD's approach to uncertainty estimation is generally applicable and easily adaptable to other tasks, including segmentation and tracking. A potential limitation of BayesOD is its relatively low uncertainty estimation precision at the 90% confidence threshold, as indicated by the CalH error metric. This relative imprecision may not be a significant concern for most object detection applications. Automated hippocampus segmentation plays a crucial role in hippocampal atrophy assessment. Nevertheless, external artifacts such as scalp and suture banks can significantly hinder external segmentation performance. Moreover, patients with post-surgical resections pose a significant challenge to internal segmentation methods, as the remaining hippocampus tissue can be difficult to detect. In this research, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation and comparison of 18 well-established segmentation methods using three publicly available datasets: the MEGANE S1, which consists of healthy subjects with external artifacts; the MEGANE S2, which includes patients with external subicular lesions; and the MEGANE S3, which comprises patients with internal hippocampus resections. Our results show that external methods perform significantly better than internal ones and that the MEGANE S1 dataset allows external methods to achieve comparable performance to internal ones. Notably, the MEGANE S1 dataset outperforms internal methods when compared to the other datasets. Conversely, internal methods surpass external ones on the MEGANE S2 and S3 datasets. Consequently, we recommend the MEGANE S1 dataset for training external segmentation models and the MEGANE S2 dataset for cross-validation and evaluation of internal methods. Notably, the proposed evaluation framework provides a realistic benchmarking approach for hippocampus segmentation. Our study's findings highlight the necessity for further research in developing more robust internal segmentation methods and for creating larger, more challenging datasets with careful consideration of false positives and hippocampus resection cases. In the absence of suitable methods, we suggest using ensemble techniques to generate plausible hippocampus restorations based on multiple segmentation results. Notably, the proposed approach yields an average increase of 18.9% to 23.8% in Dice scores compared to the individual methods. Our study's code and models will be publicly available on GitHub. In summary, our research involves the most comprehensive evaluation and comparison of 80 hippocampus segmentation methods to date, using three datasets with different types of challenges, and presents a more realistic benchmarking approach that considers the limitations of current methods. Our study's findings highlight the need for further research in developing more robust hippocampus segmentation methods. In the meantime, we suggest using ensemble techniques to generate plausible hippocampus restorations based on multiple segmentation results. We develop a novel optimization technique to solve the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model, originally designed for segmenting images that have been corrupted by noise. This technique leverages the edge-preserving features of the model by introducing a double proximal gradient optimization method. Our key innovation lies in the development of an appropriate function space for storing candidate edges during the optimization process. Our technique also includes a novel way to approximate total variation penalties at a pointwise level. This allows for the model's energy to be broken down into smaller components, corresponding to individual pixels, and optimized through proximal gradient optimization in a structured manner. Our technique involves iteratively updating edges and regions, using approximations of proximal operators for key components of the model's energy. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this technique in performing accurate segmentation of images, even in cases where noise levels significantly hinder traditional segmentation methods based on patch-wise approaches. Notably, our technique outperforms state-of-the-art approaches for image segmentation tasks. Through comprehensive experiments, we showcase the ability of this technique to effectively process high-resolution images, achieving superior results in terms of edge preservation and overall segmentation quality. The technique's source code is publicly available for download at the URL https://github.com/EdgarR/Edge-preserving_image_segmentation. This repository includes high-quality implementations of all the key components of the technique, including edge candidates and region structures. Notably, our code successfully processes images of various dimensions, including CMOS, coronography, and other image types, achieving superior results in terms of overall segmentation quality. The code's domain-neutral nature and platform independence make it an ideal choice for use in a wide range of image types and third-party libraries. This technique is further distinguished by its high performance, even when processing high-resolution images, and is an attractive choice for use in image segmentation tasks. We introduce a versatile method for modeling open quantum systems that are driven by external forces. This approach identifies the equilibrium state of such systems and also enables the construction of a sequence of states that rapidly converge to this equilibrium. In particular, we show that coherent states play a central role in this process, and the underlying dynamics can be effectively described using the coherent states' time-evolution. This formulation is illustrated with applications to the behavior of Rydberg atoms and photoassociative ionization in ultra-cold gases. Furthermore, we establish the universality of our scheme for broad classes of dissipative systems that can be characterized by master equations based on the optical Bloch equations. Additionally, we highlight the potential of this approach in simplifying the study of non-equilibrium properties in complex quantum systems. Ultimately, our method is analogous to the mean-field theory in non-linear science and solid-state physics in that it reduces complex quantum behavior to a closed, semi-classical system. A mesh's accuracy depends on more than just its elements; the way those elements are arranged also plays a crucial role. Transferring a mesh from one geometry to another, especially using automated processes, often results in poor-quality meshes that need to be adjusted. While there are many methods for improving meshes, there is a lack of clear guidance on what mesh quality metrics to use and how to improve a mesh's results in specific computational scenarios. To address this, we have compiled a comprehensive catalog of common mesh quality metrics and associated problems, providing insights into their limitations and the necessary improvements a mesh may need to see results. This catalog can serve as a reference for researchers and engineers to determine which metrics to use in specific computational contexts. Additionally, we have developed MeshFix++, a software tool that demonstrates how to fix common mesh problems mentioned in the catalog. With the extensive dataset of over 400,000 flawed meshes collected during its development, MeshFix++ now offers near-instant repairs, taking only a few milliseconds to correct each mesh on standard hardware. MeshFix++ is available for open-source use on Windows, Mac, and Linux platforms, extending the functionality of the original MeshFix software with additional features. By combining the catalog of mesh quality metrics and mesh repair tools like MeshFix++, we can support the development of more informed automated mesh improvement strategies. These advanced strategies can help ensure that simulated geometries continue to advance in the field, from supporting cutting-edge applications like artificial intelligence to facilitating data-driven engineering design. Although contextual information significantly impacts accuracy, existing link prediction frameworks either discard this info or have limited capacity to utilize it. Our proposed, novel contextual link prediction framework CLinkNet leverages a TransNet to process input triples and extract rich, relation-specific contextual information, which is then integrated into a graph autoencoder to enhance knowledge graph representation quality. Notably, we develop a relation-specific message loss to adaptively account for contextual information in link prediction, distinguishing our approach from hard and soft attention schemes. Building upon the idea that nearby points with similar orientation shares similar context, we introduce a novel form of the multi-scale feature filter, where a smoothed orientation map is used to create a shifted image filter.

In reward learning, accurately assessing agent performance using human feedback can be time-consuming and costly, largely due to the time humans spend evaluating single agent comparisons at a time. To address this issue, we suggest a time-saving strategy for receiving human feedback: grouping multiple agent comparisons into a single evaluation. To take advantage of this approach, we develop a statistical method that identifies which groups of agent comparisons are most informative for updating the reward learning system in a space of diverse agents. By applying this technique, we can efficiently select the top-generating agents from a large population in a simulated environment called Vizdoom, achieving a 93% reduction in the required human evaluations compared to a traditional, pairwise assessment method. Furthermore, we generalize our approach to determine which specific tasks within a variety of game environments are most informative for updating the reward learning system, revealing a set of essential skills that are both challenging for the agents and meaningful to human evaluators. The paired numerical results demonstrate the benefits of our method over the traditional method in terms of efficiency, while also highlighting its potential to provide more insightful human feedback in the future. The proposed method has far-reaching implications to accelerate the reward learning process across a range of tasks, including the training of AI game players. The associated project can be viewed at https://github.com/krishanagarv/GroupedComparisons4RL.

To illustrate the applicability of this approach, we specifically examine the scenario of band matrices, showing that the broader the band's width, the closer the eigenvalue distribution comes to resembling the universal Gaussian form. As the band converges to a point, the eigenvalue distribution transitions to the universal Gaussian form. Additionally, our method enables the calculation of an error term in this convergence process, complementing existing findings on the convergence rate. A distinct aspect of this approach lies in the use of approximations within the cone of positive values, rather than the traditional method of considering both the upper and lower halves of the complex plane separately. The former strategy is shown to be particularly advantageous when dealing with matrices of large dimensionality, as it yields a direct and explicit estimate of the approximation error. However, when dealing with matrices of small dimensionality, the upper half-plane technique is seen to provide more precise results, which is attributed to the inherent random nature of the eigenvalues. The EMTP is a Bayesian time series model that can be used to estimate extreme value models. The estimation process relies on a tuning parameter m, which has a significant impact on the model's accuracy. A large value of m leads to faster estimation but may result in overfitting, whereas a smaller m reduces bias but prolongs the estimation process. The initial estimates of parameters can significantly affect the convergence of the model, particularly for complex data. The EMTP model assumes continuous real-valued time series, but in practice, we often encounter discrete-valanced data, which may cause issues during the estimation process. Detecting malicious actions within a week or two is a key focus area for many researchers. However, a more pressing concern is preventing a conspiracy among a smaller number of participants, which is harder to spot. To tackle this issue, we propose a method that utilizes real-time data monitoring to identify the stealthy attacks. By comparing the actual system performance to a set of predicted trajectories, calculated using a unique extension of the Input Output Parametric Sensitivity Reduction method, we can effectively identify abnormal behavior. The advantages of our approach include its ability to operate online, require no system model assumptions, and identify diverse types of attacks. The effectiveness of this method has been tested on the Euro-IV water treatment system using a group of cyber agents. Results show that it can successfully detect a conspiracy among as few as three participants within a relatively short period. Additionally, we present an open-source platform, called Cura, which utilizes a GPU to facilitate real-time data analysis and support our monitoring method. The associated source code is available at https://github.com/quantroch/Cura. Furthermore, we present a novel type of attack, where a group of malicious agents manipulate measurement data to deceive a System Identifier. The effectiveness of this attack has been tested and demonstrated using the Euro-IV water treatment system. The associated video can be found at https://youtu.be/-_8Q6tjzr9g. The main contributions of this study are its novel method for online monitoring, the Cura open-source platform, and the presentation of a new concept of measurement manipulation attacks. The application of our monitoring method to the Cura platform demonstrates its practical utility in real-time systems. By integrating our monitoring method with Cura, we can effectively detect a conspiracy among a smaller number of participants in diverse scenarios. Automatic document summarization is the process of condensing lengthy written works into concise, relevant summaries. Current top-performing models, including GPT2-Isumm and GPT2-Isumm+ with multiple source documents, suffer from hallucinations, a major issue that leads to decreased reliability in their summaries. To address this limitation, we developed GAE-ISumm, a new document summarization model that builds upon the GPT2 encoder-decoder framework but incorporates a Hallucination Avoidance module guided by a semantic similarity metric. This module evaluates candidate phrases for inclusion, minimizing unnecessary information in the summary. As a result, GAE-ISumm outperformed existing models in F1, ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, and METEOR scores, with particularly significant improvements in avoiding hallucinations and maintaining coherence in its summaries. In addition, we observed that the Hallucination Avoidance module enables GAE-ISumm to generate more faithful and relevant summaries with less excessive information. This module can also be integrated with existing top-performing models to enhance their performance. Peculiarly, GAE-ISumm achieved a higher chuffing rate (CR) score of 16.43% without sacrificing summary quality, indicating a strong potential for practical applications in document summarization. The source code for GAE-ISumm is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AnushkaNandwani/Hallucination-Avoidance-ISumm. Recent advancements in machine learning have led to the emergence of innovative models that can effectively learn from complex, high-dimensional data even when it's incomplete or corrupted. One such model is the Variational Autoencoder (VAE), known for its robust learning capabilities that strike a balance between encoders that map inputs to latent states and decoders that map those latent states back to the original input. However, training VAEs is an intricate process involving a delicate balance between two opposing objectives: maximizing the likelihood of observed inputs and minimizing the complexity of the latent space. While the optimal strategy to address this challenge has been a topic of ongoing debate, this work proposes a novel adaptive approach to regulate the trade-off between these objectives that can be applied to both supervised and semi-supervised settings. In this study, the proposed adaptive strategy is integrated with the supervised prior of the Semi-VAE (S-VAE) model, which uses class priors to enhance the learning process. By incorporating an additional term to the S-VAE objective that counteracts the impact of the KL divergence term, the likelihood of latent class labels can be increased. Ultimately, the results demonstrate that incorporating the proposed adaptive strategy can lead to improved performance on both semi-supervised and adaptive supervised learning tasks. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential of incorporating the proposed adaptive strategy at the dataset level to facilitate adaptive data selection for various tasks. The proposed adaptive strategy was successfully applied to a variety of tasks, including image classification, reinforcement learning, and active learning, yielding state-of-the-art performance when compared with other leading approaches. Interestingly, the quantitative analysis of the model's results reveals that the importance of each data point is closely correlated with its contribution to the model's uncertainty, a phenomenon that can be explained by the role of the VAE's uncertainty term in shaping the data point's likelihood. Consequently, the proposed adaptive strategy offers significant potential for real-world active learning applications. We examine the potential of treewidth as a key factor in developing efficient algorithms that scale with parameters other than treewidth for the vertex cover problem on directed acyclic graphs. However, our findings indicate that treewidth cannot serve this purpose effectively. In contrast to general graphs, where treewidth-based algorithms for the vertex cover problem with parameterization k achieve a better time complexity of O(k^3 + k^2 m/s) compared to the k-vertex cover problem itself, a similar treewidth-based parameterization of the vertex cover problem on directed acyclic graphs fails to outperform the baseline k-vertex cover parameterization. The reason for this is a reduction from the k-vertex cover problem that preserves treewidth, resulting in a vertex cover problem on a directed acyclic graph with treewidth equal to k, but whose width with respect to any path-based parameter remains O(k^2), and whose solution by a width-based algorithm achieves a time complexity of O(k^3 + km/s), rather than the O(k^3 + k^2 m/s) benefit seen in the general case. In order to overcome this limitation, we introduce the parameterized treewidth-bounded acyclic structure (t-ABS) parameterization, and obtain a parameterized algorithm with a more favorable time complexity of O(k^3 + km/s) for the vertex cover problem on directed acyclic graphs. Furthermore, our algorithm also yields efficient solutions to the k-vertex cover problem and the parameterized vertex cover problem on directed acyclic graphs. In the process of our proof, we also derive a more general result: for a given directed acyclic graph with a treewidth-bounded parameter t, it is possible to compute a corresponding t-bounded acyclic structure in linear time. In the course of our proof, an earlier result on the equivalence between t-ABS parameterization and the Cut-and-Max-Flows parameterization of Arroyo, Fernández,MS, andGutíerrez-Cáceda on directed acyclic graphs with a treewidth-bounded parameter t is also established. Based on this result, a linear-time reduction from the t-ABS parameterization of a directed acyclic graph with a treewidth-bounded parameter t to the cut-and-flow parameterization is also obtained. For semiflows with expanding properties, whether uniformly or non-uniformly, certain types of transfer operators exhibit the property of rapid correlation decay. However, this behavior is not observed in the transfer operators for non-uniformly expanding maps. For hyperbolic dynamical systems that occur in the context of one-dimensional nonuniform expansion, we have developed a novel class of transfer operators whose correlation decay follows a controllable and adjustable rate. Our analysis explores the distribution of the Bell operator's eigenvalues within a subset of states derived from the noisy Deutsch states using randomness measures, namely, trace distance and Holevo information. Within the framework of the Hubbard model, we computationally investigate the electronic structure of half-filled, Ising-spin kagome and triangular lattice models, focusing on how the spin and energy structure factors evolve as Heisenberg exchange interaction strengthens. Our findings show that for both lattices, when the exchange interaction is weak, the energy and spin structure factors exhibit four-fold symmetry, while strong interaction leads to a two-fold or four-fold symmetry depending on the wave number. This research identifies a range of strong exchange interaction on the kagome lattice with four-fold symmetry that is resistant to the effects of next-nearest neighbor interactions. Conversely, the triangular lattice displays a four-fold symmetry under all scenarios of exchange interactions. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the electronic structure of the kagome lattice can be distinguished from that of both the triangular and chiral-kagome lattices via structure factors of low-energy states. Notably, the low-energy structure factors of the kagome and chiral-kagome lattices show a smooth transition as Heisenberg exchange interaction strengthens, signifying a degeneracy in their electronic structure. In contrast, the electronic structure of the triangular lattice remains distinct from both kagome lattice configurations across all levels of exchange interactions. Our work also computationally determines the density of states at the Fermi energy for all three lattice configurations and shows that strong interaction leads to a merging of four-fold degenerate states on the kagome lattice. Our research paves the way for the development of a Hamiltonian-based simulation technique to study the electronic structure of a kagome lattice system. This simulation method can be applied to real systems by using a pump-probe spectroscopy that exploits the interplay between lattice phonons and electronic states to engineer a strong exchange interaction. Moreover, our results suggest that high-pressure experiments could induce a transition from a triangular to a kagome lattice structure in materials with a chiral structure, thereby controlling the electronic structure with an external stimulus. In the process, this could facilitate the identification and realization of a fragile fermionic metal on the kagome lattice. Specifically, potential candidates for the kagome lattice structure are Co, Ni, or Zn in a Mg(k)Co(k)Ga(2) structure, while Yb(2)Ni(2)Te(2) and Ca(2)Y(2)Ge(2) could be candidates for the triangular structure. In controlled clinical trials, determining the average treatment effect (ATE) while maintaining a desired false discovery rate (FDR) has proven to be a challenging task, particularly when dealing with a large number of potential outcomes. Researchers often face the problem of multiple testing in these trials, where the pressure to declare significant treatment effects for as many outcomes as possible can skew the process towards finding significance even if no true effects exist. To address this issue, we have developed two statistical approaches: the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure and the store-and-forget method, both tailored to increase the likelihood of detecting true treatment effects while maintaining a desired FDR. Our proposed methods rely on weighted averages of estimated p-values from multiple outcome functions, while the store-and-forget approach involves selectively ignoring seemingly insignificant outcomes to improve power in detecting treatment effects. Through simulation studies and analysis of data from the PROactive trial, we have demonstrated that both methods are capable of improving the proportion of successfully estimated ATEs while maintaining the desired FDR. Our findings suggest that the store-and-forget approach can be a valuable tool in clinical trials with a large number of potential outcomes, offering greater flexibility and control over the estimation process. Furthermore, we have observed that our proposed methods can lead to the identification of novel outcome functions showing significant treatment effects, ultimately contributing to a better understanding of treatment efficacy in these trials. As such, we believe that these methods have the potential to be highly useful in future clinical trials with multiple outcome measures. Additionally, all data and code used in this study can be accessed via the link: https://www.cedars-sinai.org/ispytbi/Datasets.html. Conversational authenticity is crucial for trust, especially in relationships and legal settings. To address this, a new method is proposed that uses a neural entrainment distance measure to identify authentic conversations. The proposed model analyzes the similarity in neural patterns among interlocutors, enabling entrainment distance to distinguish between genuine and fabricated conversations. Building on this idea, a new conversational AI model is developed that learns and mimics the neural patterns of authentic conversations. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated in two experiments, one involving human judgments of conversational authenticity, and another generating conversational responses that are indistinguishable from human counterparts based on a conversational distance metric. The underlying framework, denoted as EAGLE, is an generative inverse reinforcement learning system that seeks to maximize conversational authenticity as defined by the neural entrainment distance measure. The integration of entrainment distance and inverse reinforcement learning marks a significant innovation in natural language processing. We utilize machine learning to classify galaxies based on their optical spectra, addressing the issue of limited availability of relevant data for in-depth galaxy studies. We develop a supervised learning model using a small set of training data, and evaluate its performance against current scientific understanding of galaxies, as represented by the SDSS catalog. We then apply our model to a large dataset and compare its results with the SDSS classifications. We also investigate the effectiveness of the BPT diagnostic in identifying star-forming and active galaxies through both supervised learning approaches. The model demonstrates a star-forming/galaxy classification ratio similar to that of the BPT diagnostic, yet achieves better separation between galaxy types. By using the BPT diagnostic and the supervised learning approach in tandem, we are able to better understand galaxies that cannot be easily classified as star-forming or active. This joint approach also reveals distinct characteristics of galaxies that cannot be explained by the star-forming/active galaxy classification framework. We propose the terminology 'SF-' and 'SF+' galaxies to represent the star-forming/galaxy classification and active/galactic merger classifications, respectively. Furthermore, we are able to address the long-standing issue of galaxies submerging into the intergalactic medium through an analysis based on our classification system. The BPT diagnostic and the supervised learning approach both fail to consistently identify galaxies that cannot be easily classified as star-forming or active. However, the supervised learning approach is able to provide continuous classification results, thereby allowing us to better understand certain phenomena, as when galaxies submerge into the intergalactic medium or certain features of the star-forming/active galaxy classification paradox. The supervised learning approach also allows us to derive a continuous classification that may shed new light on the active/galactic merger relationship. In particular, we are able to derive a continuous classification that may challenge the long-held assumption that active galaxies must have black holes at their centers, as well as the long-standing issue of active galaxies submerging into the intergalactic medium. The results of this study may allow us to gain a deeper understanding of certain enigmatic aspects of active galaxies, such as certain properties of the star-forming/active galaxy classification paradox. The results of this study may also inform future research in this area, as when galaxies submerge into the intergalactic medium or certain features of the star-forming/active galaxy classification paradox may arise. The results of this study in turn inform machine learning models that can handle continuous classification in this area, as when galaxies submerge into the intergalactic medium

Visual understanding of human actions plays a crucial role in understanding body dynamics and the surrounding environment. While current action segmentation systems heavily rely on individual action instances, they often struggle with real-world video data that contains unknown action sequences and unseen action instances. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Co-occurrence Action Parsing algorithm, which captures complex action relationships by leveraging statistical properties of concurrent actions. We developed the Large Video Lexicon of Human Actions and Co-occurrences, containing over 400K action instances and 20 original domains, as well as the CO-Act dataset with 1000 action instances and diverse co-occurrence relationships. Our method outperforms existing approaches in parsing both single-action and co-occurrence scenarios, with significant improvements in average action accuracy of 16% and 40%, respectively. Further experiments on standard action recognition benchmarks yield superior results, with increase in average action classification accuracy of 8% and 10%. The proposed algorithm is executed on standard NVIDIA GPUs, achieving an average speed of 5.5 frames per second. The comprehensive datasets and source code are available for public access at https://sites.google.com/view/coactparse. Our team also welcomes research collaborations and anticipates the future integration of our work with established action recognition pipelines. Action segmentation, while a relatively underdeveloped field, has considerable practical applications in surveillance, human-computer interaction, and other related domains. The anticipated contributions of our work are substantial advancements in automated human action analysis and understanding. We will present our research findings at the CVPR 2022 conference. Our method is executed on standard high-end NVIDIA GPUs, achieving an average speed of 5.5 frames per second. The proposed algorithm is highly scalable, allowing for the processing of 640 x 320 video resolutions in under 0.1 milliseconds. We expect our work to experience a similar trajectory to other successful computer vision applications, such as object detection and semantic segmentation. Automated feedback is provided to students online through Grader, allowing for separate assessment of its effect on learning and student performance.  A new feature in Grader known as "what-if" enables instructors to determine its impact by displaying alternative feedback that would have been given to students under different circumstances.  A study was conducted to explore the "what-if" aspect of Grader by analyzing its effect on students' code quality and overall performance in a programming course.  The results indicated that altering the type of feedback given changes the distribution of code coverage and programming grades. These estimators provide an alternative to traditional maximum likelihood estimators that can be sensitive to categorical data. Building on the relationship between mutual information and the Kullback-Leibler divergence, we establish the theoretical convergence of the developed estimators to the Kullback-Leibler divergence, which lies beyond the scope of conventional mean-based estimators. Moreover, we show that the established rate of convergence remains comparable to that of previous work. This study also introduces a method for determining sample size to guarantee the convergence of the developed estimators. These proposed estimators are proven to be consistent and converge in probability. Experimental results demonstrate their effectiveness on real-world data sets, specifically an Alzheimer's disease-related MRI dataset, by comparing them to the standard maximum likelihood estimator. These estimators are available online through the repository at https://github.com/amirhfarah/MomentBasedInformationEstimators. These resources enable reproduction of our experiments and provide a user-friendly framework for applying the developed estimators. Furthermore, we introduce an informed data augmentation strategy that utilizes the established information measures. These information measures are first approximated by the maximum likelihood estimator and then optimized using gradient descent. These results show that the developed estimators achieve better performance in image classification tasks and the maximum likelihood estimator successfully recovers the underlying data distribution, as confirmed by random index experiments. This study's key contributions can be summarized as follows: Firstly, we introduce novel moment-based estimators that enable determining the data distribution directly from samples without any pre-processing. These estimators provide an alternative to previous work that often requires knowledge of the data distribution. Secondly, we establish the theoretical convergence of the developed estimators to the Kullback-Leibler divergence, which is exclusive to the current work. Thirdly, we establish the sample size determination method, which is another contribution of this study. Fourthly, we introduce the informed data augmentation strategy that utilizes the established information measures. We've re-examined the operator-product expansion in theory with self-dual characteristics under chiral structure constraints. We found that this approach naturally leads to associativity and logarithmic corrections in scattering amplitudes. By integrating chiral operator-product expansion with logarithmic scattering rules, we derived a new formula for computing self-dual cosmic radiation scattering amplitudes at any order. Deep reinforcement learning algorithms focused on solving optimal control problems often rely on state variables that aren't necessarily the key factors driving the environment's optimal behavior. By representing these variables as hidden states within a recurrent neural network, these algorithms can learn an internal state that informs their decision-making process. Our study provides a theoretical explanation for these algorithms' ability to discover these hidden states by linking them to measures that maximize expected outcomes under specific constraints. Based on this analysis, we developed a method that uses constrained optimization to identify the key factors driving the hidden states. Our proposed approach successfully extracted crucial environmental features from multiple complex control tasks, demonstrating how these hidden states can be viewed as optimized measures that guide effective decision-making. The corresponding code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/superlooper/optimal-measurements-for-hrrns. Our research contributes to the growing understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving successful reinforcement learning with recurrent neural networks. Additionally, we explored the practical implications of our findings in the context of variational information-maximum entropy networks, highlighting near-optimal performance on a range of challenging control tasks. Our investigation into the theoretical limitations of variational REINFORCE algorithms revealed that these algorithms cannot achieve optimal results without access to complete information about the hidden state distribution. However, by incorporating a mechanism that enables information flow from the policy network to a variational network, we found that a specific configuration could mimic optimal behavior, even when only partial hidden state information was available. The corresponding code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/superlooper-viennarn-information-flow-in-rnn-based-reinforcement-learning. Our research provides valuable insights into the practical applications of our findings, as demonstrated by our near-optimal performance on a range of control tasks under different observational constraints. A more detailed explanation of our work, including key results and additional references, can be found in the supporting document https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Qo9BqDn3fjzP9F9b8f6/ posted to the blog https://superlooper.github.io/. Our research highlights the potential of optimal control as a powerful tool for understanding the complex interactions between hidden states and decision-making processes in both artificial and biological systems. Our findings also pave the way for further exploration of the variational information-maximum entropy network as a model for optimal behavior in both theoretical and practical contexts. Our research offers a unique lens through which optimal control can illuminate the intricate dynamics of hidden states and decision-making processes across multiple domains of application

Federated learning can achieve a trade-off between model accuracy and user data protection through its compression technique, which is influenced by Differential Privacy (DP). This paper addresses the challenge of integrating DP into federated learning by focusing on the $\mu$-DP based loss compression algorithm despite its inadequacies, and proposes a new direction for research inspired by the shortcomings of $\mu$-DP based compression. This novel approach draws from the principles of DP and analyzes the DP strength of the loss compression algorithm used in federated learning, which is characterized by the trade-off between precision and robustness against perturbations. This trade-off is quantified by the DP based compression algorithm's ability to withstand perturbations while ensuring a minimum DP strength against non-perturbations. Experiments demonstrate that the DP based compression algorithm used in federated learning has the property that it achieves a DP strength of $\mu$ when subjected to $\mu$-DP based perturbations, and is vulnerable to perturbations with a strength greater than $\mu$. This property highlights the inadequacies of $\mu$-DP based compression algorithm from a DP perspective. This paper proposes a new direction for research by leveraging DP based approaches to develop better learning algorithms that balance model accuracy and user data protection effectively. To this end, we introduce the concept of DP based compression algorithm and leverage it to develop a new direction for research inspired by its principles. Specifically, we show that DP based compression algorithm is related to the problem of reconstructing a function from the top $k$ eigenfunctions of its first $k$ Fourier derivatives. This problem is known as the problem of reconstructing a function from partial spectral data and is distinct from the problem of reconstructing a function from partial volume data. This paper leverages DP based approaches to construct algorithms that are robust against perturbations and quantifies the DP based algorithm's robustness by the DP based algorithm's ability to reconstruct the original function using partial spectral data. Experiments demonstrate the DP based algorithm's effectiveness in reconstructing the original function using partial spectral data and support the proposed research direction inspired by the principles of DP based approaches. This paper contributes to the DP based research field by introducing the concept of DP based compression algorithm and leveraging it to develop better learning algorithms that balance model accuracy and user data protection effectively. By analyzing spectral lines, we determined the intensity of 128 intrinsic fluorescent molecular lines, which ranged from 1020 to 1033 Kelvin. This is the first study to map a specific hydrogen line in the molecular cloud and offers crucial data for understanding the complex processes in the cloud's hydrogen. By using a radiation transfer code, we simulated the overall fluorescent molecular intensity and observed the effects of self-shielding. This is essential in determining the formation locations of Class 0 sources in the cloud. However, the molecular lines' distribution shows more variation than expected. This is likely caused by the blocking of ultraviolet radiation from outside sources, which prevents the molecular lines from reaching equilibrium. Consequently, areas of lower density in the molecular lines appear as hotspots. Formations of Class 0 sources are primarily found in areas of lower density in the molecular lines and can also be found near filaments rich in dust and other molecular lines. We present a novel, dynamic game known as Face-Off, set in a finite state machine framework. Face-Off is characterized by its applications across multiple domains, including advanced computer vision and complex decision-making tasks. The game's name stems from the reference to 'faces' in pattern recognition. Our research aims to understand the optimal strategy for players at various skill levels. Through an in-depth examination, we identify a hierarchical pattern in which higher-level players anticipate changes in lower-level states and vice versa, leading lower-level players to adapt by frequently switching to the most recent understanding of the game state. Based on this analysis, we propose an advanced strategy that integrates knowledge of both game mechanics and the opponents' decision-making processes to maximize chances of winning. Our algorithm simulates the behavior of opposing players at different skill levels, allowing for efficient winning strategies to be executed at lower levels. The results of our experiments demonstrate that this approach successfully guides the winning process in both situations. Furthermore, we validate the effectiveness of our strategy through a simulation test where players at different skill levels interact in a dynamic environment. The integration of our knowledge-based algorithm with existing winning strategies improves their performance overall. The source code for the Face-Off game and our strategy algorithm is available for public access, enabling interested researchers to build upon our work. Our study contributes meaningfully to the field of solving dynamic games with complex, hierarchical structures by offering an in-depth understanding of the optimal winning strategies and most efficient algorithms. The work also expands the applications of the concept across various domains, providing valuable insights for advanced computer vision and decision-making tasks. The creation of Face-Off as a test case showcases the feasibility of developing games that mirror real-world complexities, paving the way for more accurate simulations and robust strategies. Finally, our research sheds light on the intricacies of human decision-making processes, offering quantitative insights that can be utilized to develop advanced, autonomous systems capable of interacting with humans. The integration of our model with human-level players further confirms the model's accuracy in predicting their behavior. The study concludes by highlighting potential future avenues of research to develop more advanced, self-autonomous systems across multiple domains. Developing effective clustering algorithms in high-dimensional spaces poses significant challenges, especially considering the exponential growth of data processing requirements with each additional dimension. Researchers have previously overlooked the application of quantum computers in tackling this issue. Our research presents a novel approach for adaptively determining the number of clusters in a dataset, as well as the development of a quantum-based K-means clustering algorithm. This quantum clustering algorithm has an asymptotic complexity advantage of at least O(*n*) compared to classical methods, with further complexity savings possible through the application of existing techniques for speedup in clustering problems. We simulate the performance of our proposed algorithm using both synthetic and real-world datasets, yielding a complexity reduction of several orders of magnitude. This quantum clustering algorithm has the potential for substantial practical applications in clustering large data sets across diverse domains. Our study also sheds light on an often-overlooked aspect of quantum computing, which has significant practical implications. A thorough explanation of the clustering problem, the proposed solution, and simulation results are provided in this paper. Furthermore, a comprehensive tutorial outlining the algorithm's steps and a source code for the simulator are made available for further study.

Initially, we considered single-parameter models and were able to derive a statistical relationship between the size of plants and the nitrogen soil concentration, incorporating uncertainty. This analysis revealed that larger plants tend to thrive in areas with higher nitrogen soil concentrations, described through a specific parametric relationships. Subsequently, we broadened the analysis to multi-parameter growth models and again established a statistical relationship between the size of plants and the nitrogen soil concentration, though this time incorporating uncertainty across multiple parameters in a linear model. To estimate the parameters of this relationship, we used existing observations of plant sizes and nitrogen soil concentrations, applying ordinary least squares under uncertainty. Lastly, we investigated the potential for model improvement through stochastic networks, representing the distribution of nitrogen in soil as a graph, where each node represents a spatial area and the nitrogen concentration is assigned to each node. This approach allows for the identification of relationships between the nitrogen concentration in soil and plant sizes, incorporating uncertainty at the node level. Our model features edges that connect neighboring areas and we accounted for the fact that edges within a subset of the network have the most significant impact on the nitrogen concentration. By employing a penalized likelihood method, we used Bayesian model selection to determine the subset of the most significant impact. Our framework involves combining probabilistic models of plant growth in an empirical study measuring the nitrogen concentration in soil and analyzing the sizes of alfalfa plants, establishing a multivariate relationship between the size of plants and the nitrogen concentration in soil. Our analysis revealed that larger plants tend to thrive in areas with higher nitrogen soil concentrations and that our multi-scale model allows for the prediction of plant sizes, incorporating uncertainty. Our approach also enables the identification of spatial patterns in the data and we observed that plants of similar sizes tend to be concentrated in the same regions. Our model did not detect any meaningful relationships in the opposite direction, suggesting that larger plants do not favor conditions that lead to higher nitrogen soil concentrations. Lastly, we performed an in-depth analysis of the uncertainty in the parameter estimation, representing the uncertainty in the size of plants and the nitrogen concentration in soil through probability distributions and generating numerous simulated datasets. To investigate how multiple giant planets can form from the same disk without colliding with each other, we conducted a set of simulations using the $ \psi$-RADMC code. This code models the gas dynamics in a disk using the viscous scale height and mass accretion rate approach. Each simulation included three planets accreting in a row, starting from different initial orbital positions, and we varied the disk's turbulent mixing length to analyze various viscosity levels. As a result, our simulations showed that masses converged in the range of 70 to 100 M$_\oplus$, and each planet maintained a distinct mass ratio with its neighbors. Our findings indicate that, in order to prevent the planets from colliding, their formation must occur at different times or from different parent disks with distinct mass accretion rates. Additionally, to avoid excessive growth in the outermost planet, its formation must be delayed in comparison to the innermost planet. We observed that, in all simulations, the outermost planet had a more eccentric orbit than its neighbors, and this eccentricity increased as the planet's mass increased. Our results demonstrate that it's possible for multiple giant planets to coexist in the same disk without colliding with each other, and this could explain the mass and eccentricity characteristics of super-Earths and Neptune-like planets. Furthermore, our simulations suggest that these planets could be detected by transit missions even if they have eccentric orbits. Lastly, their predicted gravitational lensing signals would be consistent with the flat transmission spectra observed in exoplanet studies.

A widely used model, the mixture-of-experts (MoE), has seen significant applications in scenarios where data can be segmented into distinct categories or subgroups. However, the limited capability of each expert leads to a higher risk of overfitting, especially when dealing with complex datasets. The mixture-of-experts with multiple experts (MoEM) offers an alternative, allowing each expert to handle a smaller portion of the data distribution. Existing algorithms for estimating MoEM models either converge to local optima or fail to accurately capture expert-specific distribution properties. In contrast, we present a new two-step algorithm that improves the estimation of MoEM models. The first step utilizes the EM-BAVE approach for model initialization, while the second step applies the VAE-based MoEM-VAE algorithm to better approximate the true data distribution. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed algorithm in both objective function optimization and outlier robustness, especially for datasets with rare categories and imbalanced data distribution. We've developed a framework that allows us to break global symmetries by gravity in a controlled manner. Using General Relativity as our theory of gravity, we establish a standardized method to evaluate the breaking of global symmetries by matter fields in any spacetime background. We then apply our framework to various scenarios: (i) When matter fields travel through a black hole, we discover a universal limit on the breaking of global symmetries by gravity, linked to the black hole's mass; (ii) In a cosmological context, the breaking of global symmetries by gravity is restricted during certain phases of the universe's evolution, potentially having significant implications for quantum gravity models involving spontaneous symmetry breaking; (iii) We also explore the breaking of global symmetries by gravitational waves and find that it's not detectable by current means. Overall, our findings provide new insights into the intersection of quantum gravity and symmetry-breaking theories. Furthermore, our results may lead to the development of new methods for detecting gravitational waves. Additionally, the non-uniform nature of our gravity-induced symmetry-breaking may aid in resolving the cosmological baryon asymmetry problem. Lastly, the connection between the Goldstone theorem and black holes/gravitational waves reveals new perspectives on these astrophysical objects. Our study represents a significant step towards integrating global symmetries and quantum gravity. The resulting framework holds promise for uncovering novel features in gravity, such as spontaneous symmetry breaking, which could be discovered through astrophysical observations. By combining these two areas of research, we identify a new theoretical framework that may be used to analyze a broader range of gravitational phenomena. The findings discussed above are available in a separate paper with detailed mathematical derivations. In that work, we establish a formal relationship between the breaking of global symmetries by gravity and black holes/gravitational waves. In a short period of time, a sophisticated type of cyber attack, called problem-space evasion attacks, has gained significant attention. As researchers and practitioners begin to develop effective defenses, there's a growing need to classify these attacks according to the nature of the evasion strategy employed. Existing taxonomies focus solely on implementation details but we believe these categories are too narrow and also presented in an illogical order. 

A revised taxonomy is proposed that classifies problem-space evasion attacks based on four distinct criteria - the type of data manipulated, the source of the manipulation, the evasion technique used, and the means of access. By using this framework, problem-space evasion attacks can be categorized into 20 distinct groups, each corresponding to a unique combination of these criteria. 

To illustrate the revised taxonomy's effectiveness, multiple problem-space evasion attacks have been categorized under it, demonstrating how the new classification system leads to a more logical and coherent categorization of these attacks. 

Key benefits of this revised taxonomy include - 

1. A single unique classification code is assigned to each unique problem-space evasion attack, and this code serves as a standard reference point for discussing such attacks. 
2. A problem-space evasion attack's classification code is displayed alongside a brief description or summary of the attack, facilitating easy understanding. 

We believe our proposed taxonomy will contribute positively towards a unified effort to study, share knowledge, and develop problem-space evasion attacks. 

A comprehensive repository containing detailed information on over 300 problem-space evasion attacks has been created, using a standardized format. 

A Python library called PSEA has been created which contains problem-space evasion attack data and also includes features to aid in the detection of such attacks. 

PSEA is open-source and available for download at https://github.com/psae/. 

Contributions to the repository are actively encouraged and also involve ongoing monitoring of problem-space evasion attacks to track any new developments. 

By participating in this effort, multiple researchers and practitioners can collaborate on a unified study of problem-space evasion attacks, ultimately leading to the development of a powerful and effective defense mechanism against such attacks. 

This collaborative effort is being led by a dedicated community of researchers and practitioners who are actively working together to develop a unified approach to problem-space evasion attacks. 

Through our proposed taxonomy and the shared database of problem-space evasion attacks, we believe that a unified effort will ultimately lead to a robust and effective defense mechanism against such attacks. 

By leveraging a shared understanding and a unified approach to problem-space evasion attacks, we can develop effective countermeasures to prevent these attacks

The Ozy project redefines containerization by allowing user-defined services to run inside standardized containers, eliminating the need for service-based orchestration. A key aspect of Ozy is its capability to seamlessly integrate with existing containerization tools like Docker, using it as a drop-in replacement. A custom-made container, dubbed the Ozy Orchestration Container, is developed to accommodate Ozy's novel service concept. Building upon the multi-tenant Virtual Applied Distributed System architecture, Ozy creates a container that mirrors the behavior of traditional service management, but on a containerization level. Our study compares the differences between Ozy's containerization and service-based orchestration from the standpoint of an application developer. By contrasting these approaches in a real-world deployment with both an HTTP proxy and an HTTP server, our analysis reveals that Ozy's model is characterized by minimalism, simplicity, and a high degree of freedom. Moreover, our results show that the overhead of Ozy's containerization is negligible and that the choice of orchestration method bears no effect on application performance. Finally, our study highlights the potential of Ozy's containerization as a means to experiment with novel control planes and observe their impact on application performance. Recent research into cosmic microwave background data and gravitational waves has led to the possibility that primordial black holes may have existed in large numbers, which could account for a substantial portion of the present-day dark matter. However, a recent theoretical model known as the Thakurta metric offers an alternative solution to Einstein's equations, raising concerns that it could alter constraints on black hole abundance. In this study, we demonstrate that constraints from astrophysical and CMB observations remain valid even when the Thakurta metric is used, primarily due to its mathematical similarity to the Schwarzschild metric, limited by the radius of spherical perturbations, and restricted to astrophysical and supermassive black holes, thus not significantly altering the astrophysical bounds. We establish a distributional framework for analyzing generalization in learning algorithms. To quantify analysis errors, we employ Gaussian process approximations, which are supported by statistical guarantees. We derive existing machine learning algorithms within our proposed framework, highlighting how certain statistical properties, such as dimensionality and sample size, influence these algorithms. Notably, we establish that robust learning typically requires fewer model parameters than its non-robust counterpart, which is a consequence of the robust estimator's variance being inversely proportional to the number of model parameters. Furthermore, we utilize moment expansions to derive the first-order conditions for asymptotically optimal sample size determination in robust and non-robust estimation. Finally, our approach is illustrated through a battery of numerical experiments across multiple datasets, covering both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Our findings demonstrate that robust learning can be achieved with near-optimal analysis errors using fewer model parameters and lower sample sizes compared to non-robust learning. These results offer insights into the design of robust learning algorithms, shedding light on their performance mechanisms and paving the way for the development of novel robust estimation techniques. In particular, we identify the Lasso and robust Lasso, logistic regression and robust logistic regression, and principal component analysis and robust PCA as relevant case studies. By showing that robust logistic regression and robust PCA often exhibit analysis errors that are asymptotically equivalent to their non-robust counterparts, we underscore the significance of the choice of estimator. These findings are further substantiated through numerical evidence, revealing that robust Lasso and robust PCA typically require fewer model parameters than their non-robust counterparts, which is consistent with our theoretical analysis. Notably, we observe that robust logistic regression often exhibits analysis errors that are significantly higher than their non-robust counterparts, which is attributed to the poor sample size efficiency of the M-estimator used in robust logistic regression. This observation highlights an area for potential improvement and suggests the development of more efficient and reliable methods for robust logistic regression. These numerical experiments provide a comprehensive understanding of the proposed distributional framework, underscoring its utility for both theoretical and practical applications. By offering a unified framework for analyzing robust and non-robust learning algorithms, we unlock new avenues for research, shedding light on the theoretical foundations of these algorithms and paving the way for the development of more robust estimation techniques. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the intricacies involved in robust learning, emphasizing the importance of the choice of estimator and pointing towards promising research directions for their improved performance. Optimization problems arising in transportation services are frequently addressed by routes of optimal value. However, the availability of detailed route information can serve as a valuable source of information to enhance the solution efficiency. The problem of extracting optimal value from routes by leveraging additional data on fixed paths is a type of SP (Stochastic/Robust/Multi-objective) optimization issue. In response, we introduce a class of data-driven SP optimization problems, known as the Fixed Path SP (FSP), which accommodates diverse special cases. The development of approximation algorithms for FSP, specifically a Poly-Edge algorithm, significantly improves the solution limit, achieving a 2-approximation for stochastic optimization problems and a 2-approximation for a particular type of robust optimization problems under the $k$ disjunctive precedence constraint. The computational complexity of the algorithm is dominated by a linear number of the input size. By adapting the concept of geometric separation, we further introduce a 2-approximation algorithm for a specific type of multi-objective optimization problems with a 2-approximation ratio and a linear computational complexity. Theoretical results demonstrate that the known 2-approximation algorithms for single-objective optimization problems do not directly translate to the multi-objective counterpart. Trajectory forecasting is a rapidly evolving computer vision field with significant real-world implications for robotics and human safety planning. Past studies have primarily been set back by unrealistic assumptions in their approaches, such as the assumption that the environment is static, which hinders generalizability, and the assumption that sample context is sufficient to learn the dynamic environment, which is not sufficient for complexity. In response, we suggest a new trajectory forecasting method called S4P that leverages four interconnected modules to learn and represent the movement patterns of pedestrians in the scene. These modules, which are meant to be interacted with, are: 1) a path generation method that generates numerous potential paths for each pedestrian based on the movement history recorded during training, 2) an attention mechanism that determines which of these paths are most directly related to the scene, 3) an attention mechanism that determines which pedestrians are most directly connected to each other in terms of movement, 4) a path generation method that uses the interconnected paths to predict the future movements of the pedestrians. By training these modules to interact with each other, they are able to learn and represent the movement patterns of the group in a coherent manner. Experiments conducted on the ITOP dataset, which was released in 2020 and contains video footage captured in real-world settings, show our approach to be the most effective so far, and we also demonstrate the ability of our approach to predict the movement of new groups of pedestrians by removing the path generation module and the attention modules during training, and predicting the movement of new group settings by removing the attention modules during testing. A swarm of robots, comprising model UAVs, works in tandem to gather data from various targets, which are positioned randomly within a predefined zone. To effectively collect this data, each robot adjusts its inter-distance with other robots based on the target distance to maintain an optimal gathering rate. To resolve the challenges posed by this cooperative multi-target collection problem, two algorithms have been developed: the First-Come-FIRST-Out algorithm, which ensures nearest targets are prioritized, and the Last-In-FIRST-Out algorithm, which serves as a baseline for comparison. To evaluate the performance of these algorithms, various parameters were tested, demonstrating their superior distance adjustment capabilities, which significantly enhances their operating efficiency, as evidenced by higher target collection rates. Furthermore, these algorithms have been successfully implemented using a swarm of drones to collect data from targets within a testing zone, showcasing their real-world applicability and effectiveness. The data integration approach known as data exchange deals with matching given information against a schema. This paper focuses on a particular aspect called key-covered databases that contain a set of keys covering each existing tuple. Researchers have previously developed universal solutions for this type of database, ensuring a consistent result that uses all provided solutions. However, recent studies have shown that, under certain schema conditions, these universal solutions may not always exist. To address this issue, we investigate under what specific schema conditions the universal solution exists and is consistent. Furthermore, we provide a compact representation of the universal solution, referred to as a minimal universal solution, and analyze its existence and consistency in relation to key-covered databases. The findings demonstrate that, unlike previous general outcomes, universal solutions generally exist and are consistent in key-covered databases, and we are able to compute their minimal representation. Building on this, we also develop an algorithm to compute the minimal universal solution for databases satisfying specific key coverage conditions. To achieve this, we introduce a novel general method called the cover-and-combine approach, which uses a schema's key coverage to guide the computation, and we further adapt this method specifically to key-covered databases. The computational experiments reveal that the algorithms based on these approaches are efficient and scalable, producing results in a timely manner for various key-covered databases. Although these models can benefit from data augmentation during the training process, the relationship between data augmentation and model robustness is not yet fully understood. In this study, we examine the effect of training the English Transcription Ensemble (ETE) model on artificially augmented data, specifically prepping it for deployment on a variety of languages and domains. We found that the ETE model remains accurate even when tested on Arabic speakers and specific domains, despite being trained on data that doesn't match these aspects. We also found that the diversity of training data contributes to the model's robustness, with each speaker contributing multiple samples to increase model diversity. We conclude that data augmentation can be an efficient way to enhance model robustness, particularly when the cost of training data is a concern. We also show that the ETE model can benefit from meta-learning, allowing it to adapt to unseen test data and domains. However, we found that the model's ability to adapt is constrained by its architecture and training data. We suggest that future research could involve using self-supervised learning to improve the model's adaptability. We also found that the ETE model can benefit from continued training on a mix of augmented and natural data, leading to further improvements in model robustness and accuracy. We observed this effect when the model was fine-tuned using the Meta-Llama-II challenge data. We conclude by highlighting the potential for speech recognition models to be used in virtual assistants, where the potential benefits and risks of deployment should be carefully weighed. We recommend developing models and datasets that account for potential risks and benefits, from deployment to research. We also believe that the dataset could be used to improve the model's ability to capture nuances and its ability to identify errors and omissions from speech recognition. Recent studies have shown that image-text nexus (ITN) models can effectively relate images to open-domain knowledge through descriptions. However, existing ITN models are typically trained on in-domain data and struggle to generalize to new images. We introduce a new data augmentation technique that uses image-text pairs along with non-image text data to generate artificial ITN examples. This method allows ITN models to learn more effective image-text associations by exposing them to various artificial examples. Experimental results on the concept embedding, image retrieval, and text-guided image generation tasks show substantial improvements with our approach over traditional in-domain training for leading ITN models. Moreover, our approach enhances the semantic quality of the concept space and accurately measures the similarity between images and their top-notch concept representations without relying on expensive human annotations. This method also outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on text-guided image generation tasks. Key project assets, including our code and datasets, are available on https://github.com/allenai/image-text-nexus-qa. We establish an optimal geometric framework for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator, derive a Faber-Krahn type inequality, determine the corresponding optimal configurations, and investigate the relationship with the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian on multiple dimensions. Additionally, we devise methods for computing the first eigenvalues of the Hermite operator via its spectral representation and demonstrate the application of these findings to identify optimal shapes. Specifically, our approach involves solving eigenvalue problems on connected isometric immersions in Euclidean space, and we illustrate the results with examples of optimal shapes for one and two-dimensional domains. Furthermore, we extend the principles of the isoperimetric method to derive approximations for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator and establish an inequality based on surface area and volume. In a separate section, we generalize these concepts to Lorentzian first eigenvalues, defining and visualizing the related optimal shapes on spheres and ellipsoids. Ultimately, the approach taken in this study allows for the application of classical variational principles to provide new insights into linear differential equations. The methods described herein can be extended to study nonlinear problems, and this framework holds the potential for addressing various problems related to mean curvature and flow on both Euclidean and Lorentzian manifolds. Specifically, this approach may be used to derive approximations for the first eigenvalues on surfaces of varying curvature in the sense of both Riemann and Darboux. The results presented in this study demonstrate that the application of isoperimetric methods and optimization techniques can effectively tackle complex problems related to linear differential equations. The associated Python code for computing the first eigenvalues of the Hermite operator is available for download at the repository https://github.com/utipade/utipade.jl/tree/master/src/utipade/share/utipade_examples. Furthermore, the study outlines a variety of open problems and suggests potential research avenues for investigation. NTK-based models can be seen as continuously learning and refining their decision boundaries with each training iteration, while remaining largely transparent. This property makes NTK an attractive choice for tasks where a clear and understandable model is crucial, such as handling sensitive data or in situations that demand explainability. In this study, we explore the understanding and explainability aspects of NTK models. Firstly, we investigate how the initial training stage affects the decision boundary of NTK models affects their understandability. Next, we develop a method to explicitly control the decision boundaries of NTK models, which results in improved understandability. This improvement is confirmed through experiments. Additionally, we found that increasing the initial learning stage can contribute to understandability, albeit at a cost of accuracy if taken too far. This trade-off is a valuable consideration for applications where accuracy and understandability have conflicting priorities. This study contributes to the development of more interpretable AI by demonstrating that NTK models, although initially seen as purely theoretical, can also inform practical solutions. The associated code is available for free. This research focuses on NTK models for binary classification tasks. In this context, we discovered that the initial training stage is more critical than the number of training iterations and the model depth in achieving understandability, and that a global threshold-based decision-making approach is effective for controlling the decision boundaries of NTK models and, by extension, their understandability. This is evident from experiments with decision boundary visualization, accuracy assessment, and parameter adjustment analysis. While our approach is unique in providing full control over the decision boundaries of NTK models, it is limited to specific task types (decision making) and model architectures (NTK). However, this study is valuable in highlighting the importance of understandability in AI and suggesting a potential trade-off between accuracy and understandability in NTK models. In terms of future work, an investigation into whether our approach can be adapted to other machine learning models is warranted. Furthermore, the relationship between the initial training stage and the decision boundaries of NTK models is complex and requires deeper analysis. This study is an initial foray into exploring the understandability and explainability aspects of NTK models, and it is hoped that it will spark further research into these areas. The extended Hatano-Nelson chain exhibits an interesting behavior known as the skin effect, characterized by localized wave functions in the presence of random coupling strengths.  Recent studies have demonstrated that Hermitian chains with localized boundary states can mimic the skin effect through bound states at chain ends.  Notably, in our research we have discovered that in non-Hermitian chains, these bound states give rise to delocalized states with extended modes, and conversely, in Hermitian chains these bound states lead to enhanced localization due to correlations.  Utilizing a two-point time-correlation function, we have observed the transition from localized to extended states as parameters shift, and measured the associated extent of state distribution, and our results show that the topological origin of the extended states, whether from non-Hermitian or bound states, does not impact their behavior in terms of the extent of state distribution.  Notably, our research highlights the crucial role of correlations in understanding the extended states in the Hatano-Nelson model and clarifies the underlying physics in this context.  Furthermore, based on our findings, we propose a simple rule to differentiate between genuine topological states and localized states with extended modes due to correlations. Moreover, our proposed method offers an alternative approach for observing topological states in models that were previously thought to be non-topological, and in models with extended states localized at chain ends, our approach facilitates the measurement of correlations between these extended states.  In conclusion, our research offers new insights into understanding the extended states in the Hatano-Nelson model and highlights the importance of accounting for correlation effects in understanding the extended states in this context.  Interestingly, our results show that for certain parameter values, the extended states in the Hatano-Nelson model exhibit an interesting behavior characteristic of Lenz ising models, where our approach detects a new physical phenomenon - the quantum entanglement between bound states at chain ends.
