Research into electronic speech generation and human perception suggests that the perceived quality of such speech is influenced by factors such as naturalness, which cannot be directly addressed through current techniques. An adaptive learning method using human feedback has been developed, enabling the generation of more appealing speech. We tested this approach with sentences of varying emotional intensity, adjusting the emotional quality of female-synthesized speech using convex combinations of vocal features. The outcome showed that altering a limited set of features (average pitch, energy, and spectral slope) can result in more natural-sounding speech. Furthermore, we found that the perceived competence of female speech is linked to the average pitch and energy, while perceived emotional appeal is associated with spectral slope. This finding aligns with previous studies on human speech. We also developed an algorithm that uses this information to create more engaging synthesized speech over time. By combining the potential benefits of varying emotional expressions, this approach successfully produces more appealing speech that surpasses the naturalness of a state-of-the-art emotional speech dataset. Crucially, the quality of the generated speech improves gradually with each iteration, thanks to the adaptive learning strategy. Interestingly, the synthesized speech also tends to be easier to understand, with the average sentence's intelligibility increasing by around 10%. We make available the data collected for this study, which includes human ratings of emotional appeal and competence in a large dataset of female speech, as well as an implementation of the adaptive learning algorithm. This work has significant implications for the development of more natural-sounding electronic speech, enabling applications in areas like human-robot interaction. In the future, we aim to expand our findings to include a broader range of voices and emotions. Additionally, we suggest conducting more in-depth analyses of human perception to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying features involved. Ultimately, this research has the potential to produce more appealing and emotionally expressive electronic speech that interacts more smoothly with humans. To promote the creation of more human-like electronic speech, the data and code for this study are being made available, along with an open call for participation in further research. The data can be accessed at: https://osf.io/du6fj/, while the code can be found at: https://osf.io/x4as5.,.  Please note that the code and data are currently only available in Spanish but will be translated into English soon.

The addition of a heavy scalar field, coupled to the dark matter through a Yukawa interaction, acts as a mediator to facilitate the interaction between dark matter particles. A significant aspect of this interaction arises from the scalar field's fluctuations, which provide the dark matter stability without resorting to symmetries like gauge or discrete. While the dark matter interaction is relatively weak at low temperatures, it becomes sufficiently strong at high temperatures, leading to rapid dark matter particle production during the early universe. The proposed model offers a potential solution to the dark matter problem by offering an understanding of its origin and properties. Our model construction process is designed to be methodical and systematic, starting with a version of the model that has the minimum number of required fields, which in this case is two. A thorough examination of the model's implications, including its effects on the universe's thermal history and the creation of dark matter, is also conducted. The model's viability is further assessed by analyzing its influence on the dark matter density and the recombination history of the universe using a combination of big bang nucleosynthesis, cosmic microwave background, and galactic structure observations. Ultimately, model parameters that meet all constraints are identified, which in turn allows for accurate predictions to be made about the universe's thermal history and the properties of dark matter. A detailed analysis of the model's implications for direct and indirect dark matter detection experiments is also conducted. By systematically deriving a version of the model with multiple fields, including fermions and bosons, the scalar mediator's role in the model's physics can be fully understood. Consequently, a more in-depth and comprehensive investigation of the model's properties is required. The model's equivalence to an $SU(6)$ gauge theory, in which the dark matter stability arises from an accidental symmetry, is also demonstrated. By systematically examining the model's properties, it becomes evident that the dark matter stability in this scenario is a consequence of the accidental symmetry, which in turn results in the desired dark matter properties. In this study, we investigated how the energy spectrum of the $\_{}^{19}_{11}S$S nucleus changes when considering a constant Minimal Length (D) in a solvable model. The $\_{}^{19}_{11}S$S nucleus has a triaxile shape and is thus classified as a deformed, rotational-nuclear system with a $X(5)$ symmetry. The Hamiltonian of this system was derived from the combination of three deformed Hamiltonians, including those for $\mathcal{I}_x$, $\mathcal{I}_y$, and $\mathcal{I}_z$. By using the $\kappa$-$\beta$ approximation, we calculated the energy levels of this system, taking into account the Minimal Length parameter. The results showed that each energy level was shifted compared to its counterpart without the Minimal Length parameter. Notably, in the Minimal Length parameter, the degeneracy between the rotational and the non-rotational energy levels was removed. The energy-level spectrum as a function of the Multi-Pole Vibrational Quantum Number ($\beta$) increased, and that as a function of the Projection of the Seniority-$\lambda$ Pairing Quantum Number ($\kappa$) increased with the addition of the Minimal Length parameter. The effect of the Minimal Length parameter on the energy levels of the triaxile nuclei was found to be in agreement with the Energy-level rule. The Minimal Length parameter made the energy-level spectrum as a function of $\beta$ softer, thus allowing lower energy levels to be realized. The effect of the Minimal Length parameter on the energy levels of triaxile nuclei contrasts with that in the case of the well-known Quasi-Symmetric Scheme. The results of this study can be applied to other Low-Lying Triaxile Nuclei, such as $\_{}^{110}_{47}Ag$, providing a basis for understanding their nuclear behavior. Change detection in multi-temporal satellite images is a critical process in various data analysis and decision-making applications, encompassing multiple fields like disaster response, urban planning, and land use assessment. The traditional supervised approach, which necessitates numerous training data, may not always be feasible or practical due to the labor and time required for manual labeling. In contrast, unsupervised change detection offers a more viable alternative, albeit often resulting in fewer accurate detections. To strike a balance between the need for minimal training data and improved change detection performance, a novel unsupervised approach focused on saliency region detection in satellite image pairs is developed and tested. This approach leverages user-provided region of interest data and automatically identifies changes within an image pair, detecting salient regions and temporo-spatial changes simultaneously. To evaluate its effectiveness, SalientChangeDect was tested using two distinct datasets, and the results demonstrate its ability to significantly improve change detection accuracy with only a small reduction in detection precision compared to a supervised alternative. Moreover, our experiments show that SalientChangeDect outperforms existing unsupervised change detection methods, including existing deep learning-based architectures, in terms of accuracy and precision. By combining change detection with saliency theory, SalientChangeDect is able to effectively balance user data requirements and overall performance. To facilitate further research, the method's source code and pre-trained models have been made publicly available. SalientChangeDect shows considerable promise as a valuable tool for performing change detection tasks on satellite data, particularly those with limited labeling resources. By leveraging user-provided region of interest data, SalientChangeDect is able to accurately detect changes within an image pair, yielding high F1 and accuracy scores of 0.873 and 0.879, respectively. The ever-growing complexity and capability of neural networks significantly affects the space required in memory, the computational resources needed, and the time taken to execute them. As a result, this may lead to issues with devices that have limited resources, such as smart speakers and wearable devices. A critical problem in addressing these limitations is selecting which layers to keep and which to remove from the network in order to optimize the remaining model's performance. We present a new approach called AxonRem, which utilizes the structural properties of neural networks to efficiently remove layers. This method treats the network as a graph where each layer is an node, and we employ a greedy algorithm that keeps the nodes with the most connections to significantly reduce the resources required. Our experiments, which were conducted on 11 benchmark datasets and various neural network architectures, demonstrate that AxonRem can achieve a substantial decrease in model size, computational requirements, and timing. Moreover, we evaluated and assessed the performance of multiple pruning techniques and found AxonRem to result in only a minor loss in accuracy while delivering a more substantial improvement in our main objective, which is to minimize the resources required. AxonRem outperformed the existing state-of-the-art layer pruning techniques by achieving a greater reduction in model size and faster execution speed while experiencing a relatively minor loss in accuracy. The code used in this study is available at the following link: https://github.com/ashishgupta16/AxonRem. As a result, we derive two formulations for the dimer partition function, both confirming prior results from Paquette and Cohn-Kost. One function is expressed as a sum of weighted, distorted trees, while the other is written as a determinant of a specific matrix arrangement. We present a novel method that utilizes a smartphone-equipped IMU to accurately capture and assemble panoramic scenes in challenging environments, characterized by moving cameras. By leveraging IMU data, we accurately determine the position of the camera at the moment of each image capture, and subsequently corrects any distortions and aligns the images. Notably, our approach is entirely based on the smartphone itself, thereby avoiding increased costs associated with external accessories. Comprehensive experiments conducted indoors and outdoors showcase the effectiveness of our approach in both static and dynamic settings. Furthermore, we evaluate our method against state-of-the-art panoramic stitching techniques using single-image position estimates derived from deep learning models. Interestingly, our results reveal that the IMU-based image positions generally coincide with those derived from deep learning models, and often yield superior stitching outcomes. A demonstration video highlighting the stitching results of our approach can be found at https://www.columbia.edu/~ae3648/projection_video.mp4. The source code and IMU data of our work are publicly available at https://github.com/AE3648/IMU_panorama. A new approach to tunneling time, rooted in the average number of tunneling events required to extract a particle from a tunneling configuration, is developed and demonstrated. This revised time measure, distinct from Gamow's tunneling time, is unaffected by the tunneling Hamiltonian's complex inner product properties with states and is applicable to a broad range of tunneling processes. As such, it offers a more neutral and versatile method for determining tunneling times. A critical aspect of this approach is its capacity to reveal spin fluctuations in tunneling events. As a practical example, we apply this technique to examine tunneling in hydrogenic atoms transitioning between states, both within the same energy level and across different levels. Our findings indicate a significant disparity between this new tunneling time average and the Gamow time, with the latter exhibiting marked fluctuations in magnitude and direction that are heavily influenced by the tunneling Hamiltonian's inner product properties. In contrast, the proposed tunneling time average demonstrates a more consistent and moderate magnitude, with absolute values ranging from 10^-21 to 10^-19 seconds, with notable exceptions of near-zero or positive times occurring at specific energy conditions. This novel approach to tunneling time is also discussed in relation to recent experimental findings on tunneling in quantum systems. Additionally, we have determined that the proposed tunneling time is capable of revealing spin fluctuations in tunneling events. Spin fluctuations in hydrogenic atomic atom tunneling, for instance, may manifest as virtual spin transmutations, with frequencies of up to 1040 Hz and an average duration of microseconds, resulting in a 100% likelihood of returning to the original spin state after tunneling within a microsecond window. Similarly, tunneling between states of opposite spins may result in significant spin fluctuations, with some tunneling events potentially changing spin orientation by 180 degrees. These spin fluctuations may potentially be observed through the polarization of recoil photons emitted during tunneling. Importantly, the proposed tunneling time is applicable not just to tunneling times but also to related quantities, such as tunneling widths, Gamow states, and tunneling matrices. As such, it offers a more general and versatile method for revealing fluctuations in tunneling characteristics. Furthermore, we have determined that the proposed tunneling time is a semi-classical average that emerges from the quantum averaging of tunneling events spanning a range of tunneling lengths. The existing methods for visually identifying intestinal parasites, such as manual examination by a doctor or images analyzed by a deep learning network, are considered prone to inaccuracies. This study investigates whether an unconventional approach - incorporating an individual's name on the image - can enhance the accuracy of visual diagnosis. The study compares not only the effectiveness of human visual examination with that of a deep learning network, but also the impact of adding the person's name to the image before visual inspection. Our findings reveal that human visual examination is surpassed by the deep learning network in accuracy, but including the person's name leads to improved performance, with the added benefit of fewer false positives for the easily identifiable species. Our research has significant implications for the implementation of visual diagnosis and deep learning network systems, as well as the understanding of human visual intelligence. This work may hold potential for the development of novel visual diagnosis aids in the future. This paper introduces an advanced state feedback controller for a quadcopter, combining a Nonlinear H-infinity approach with a Genetic Filter. The Genetic Filter method employs Genetic Algorithm-based techniques to derive a constant gain that minimizes the quadcopter's trajectory tracking error in the presence of disturbances. The proposed approach uses the Quadcopter Dynamics Model, formulated as a set of Ordinary Differential Equations, and evaluates the tracking error based on a Quadratic Cost Function. Experimental results demonstrate that the Genetic Filter-enhanced controller outperforms a conventional Adaptive Linear Quadratic Regulator-based approach, showcasing improved tracking accuracy and robustness under various external disturbances. Furthermore, the genetic genetic approach outperforms traditional Genetic Algorithm-based methods, confirming its utility as a robust and efficient control tool. Heterogeneous simulations were conducted using MATLAB/Simulink, supported by a C++ High-Speed Implementation for real-time applications. The study includes a comprehensive analysis of its computational complexity, making the genetic genetic approach a high-speed and efficient control solution. Theseresults showcase the potential of this controller in real-time applications, including autonomous quadcopter systems. The pion-nucleon sigma term is an essential concept in modern nuclear physics and has also been a focus point of study at Bonn and Jefferson Lab experiments. Our results demonstrate that the PCVC and PCAC relations hold at non-vanishing lattice lattice lattice spacings with a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, using unitarity and consistency equations, the mass counterterm and the pion-nucleon sigma term are determined at three lattice spacings and two pion masses. This study aims to examine the influence of active galactic nuclei (AGN) on their host galaxies across various redshift ranges. To achieve this, we used the XMM-UDS field, which offers high-resolution X-ray and optical-cum-submillimeter data, covering a substantial area of the UKIDSS Ultra-Deep Survey. This dataset contains 105 AGN with 0.5<z<2.5 and 10^43<L(2-10 keV)<10^44 erg/s. By using our accurate photometric redshifts, we generated AGN-galaxy subsamples at multiple redshift intervals and utilized our galaxy classification method to study the AGN-galaxy population. Our results indicate that the AGN-galaxy sample exhibits rapid evolution as AGN activity tends to increase from spiral to early-type galaxies. This phenomenon is most pronounced in the z=1.6-2.5 interval, where the classification precision is highest. Furthermore, we found that the AGN-galaxy sample shows diverse behavior based on galaxy classification. However, we did not detect the AGN-galaxy sample exhibiting significant star formation or strong radio emission. This contrasts with the host galaxies of radio galaxies, which show prominent star formation and radio emission at certain redshift intervals. Our study suggests that the primary factor driving the evolution of AGN activity is likely the interaction between the AGN and surrounding starburst or early-type galactic material. This may result in the observed variable AGN-galaxy population. Additionally, we propose that the late-stage quasar life occurs around z=1.6, coinciding with the peak quasar abundance at redshift 4 and supporting the 'quiescent star formation' model for supermassive black holes. Finally, we found that early-type galaxies hosting AGN with Mr=-18 contain a massive 10^10 M_sun stellar mass component, based on spectral energy distribution analysis. This finding aligns with the 'quiescent star formation' model for supermassive black holes. However, we estimate that less than 1% of early-type galaxies hosting AGN with Mr=-18 in the z=1.6-2.5 interval possess an AGN. This implies that AGN activity is unlikely to be the primary driver of galactic quiescence. Similarly, we found that AGN activity in early-type galaxies does not significantly impact their mass. This study employs a density functional based approach to investigate the density modification caused by short-range correlations in nuclear models, focusing particularly on the associated length scales. By incorporating this correlation information into nucleon structure densities, this work aims to resolve the existing discrepancy with experimental findings. Furthermore, this study explores how the density modification caused by short-range correlations affects the neutron skin thickness in various atomic nuclei. Additionally, this work uses ab-initio calculated neutron distribution profiles as a reference to investigate the sensitivity of predicted neutron skin thickness in isotopes of calcium and magnesium to different theoretical parameters. Finally, this study demonstrates how the consideration of short-range correlations and isovector Giant Resonance effects impacts predictions of the neutron skin thickness in asymmetric nuclei. These studies employ chiral effective field theory based propagators to establish a systematic approach to short-range correlations in nuclear models. By building upon this framework, this study derives an approximate length scale for short-range correlations, which is then incorporated into nuclear models to obtain an estimated order of magnitude. By integrating this approximate correlation information into nuclear models, this work shows that it can largely account for the existing discrepancy with experimental findings of the proton structure radius obtained from deep-inelastic scattering experiments. Conversely, this study discovers that while the consideration of short-range correlations significantly impacts predictions of the neutron skin thickness in atomic nuclei, this effect is less pronounced than that observed in experimental findings of the predicted quantity. We suggest representing images in complex RGB format to facilitate the efficient transformation of complex-valued data, which allows us to build scalable represenations of various dimensions. This approach provides a natural way to handle image rotation by employing complex-valued scaling, which results in improved handling of hue shifts and correlation between color channels. Based on this idea, we have developed two complex-domain networks, one for low-level operations and the other for high-level, that work together to predict image rotation. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy when predicting rotation angles. We also show that incorporating multiple scales in the network is similar to employing a convolutional layer, which aids in the prediction of image rotation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the HTSD dataset and performs comparably to existing techniques on the PASCAL-11 and ImageNet-22 datasets. Additionally, we have created a new dataset called ImageNet-22, consisting of 1 million images, to facilitate the prediction of large-scale rotation. This dataset can be utilized for a variety of tasks, such as image manipulation and generation. We have also provided a demonstration of our method's ability to generate surreal, yet realistic, images by using the GAN network. The code for our method is available online at this URL https://github.com/kuo-yc/complex-image-rotation. The concept of geometrical scaling, initially discovered in deep inelastic scattering, now applies across a range of different reactions, thanks to the universal nature of the JIMWY solution in the diffractive scattering mechanism. Recent studies have found evidence of geometrical scaling in electron-lead collisions at the electron-ion collider. We examine the geometrical scaling in the context of the saturation model, taking into account a critical threshold in the number of participants and how it affects the geometrical scaling factor. Calculations based on the saturation model reveal that geometrical scaling holds for a wide range of rapidity ranges, from small (RPS) to large (PS) rapidity, with the factor R_G being directly proportional to the threshold k_F/T. To validate the geometrical scaling model, we compare calculated gluon distribution functions at various rapidity ranges to those measured in deep inelastic scattering and electron-lead collisions. Gluon distribution at rapidity ranges of RPS and PS exhibit similar behavior, with GLx in the former and GL2 in the latter, with the factor GLx being directly proportional to 1/T and 1/T^2 respectively, with both distributions converging at high T. Moreover, calculations based on the saturation model reveal that geometrical scaling in the saturation model holds up to high values of k_F/T=6.8. This is particularly significant given that such values of k_F/T are indeed relevant in the context of electron-lead collisions at an electron energy of 18.6 GeV. Importantly, these findings suggest that geometrical scaling in the saturation model can be easily tested at the electron-ion collider. Such a test would be highly significant, given that such a scaling has important implications for our understanding of the diffractive scattering mechanism and the nature of the saturation threshold. Moreover, achieving a deeper understanding of geometrical scaling in the saturation model would open up new avenues of research, particularly in the context of the electron-ion collider, by allowing researchers to directly extract critical information about the critical threshold in the number of participants. Using the $\sim 10^5$ stellar counterparts of the Rennan Street yet Another Code (RUNACE) simulation, we study the influence of core-collapse supernovae (CCSN) progenitors on the chemical makeup of their host galaxies at an early stage. By sampling these progenitors stochastically according to a distribution derived from RUNACE's single-star evolutionary model, we account for variations in mass loss throughout their life cycles. This approach mirrors how stars form and evolve in the cosmos. Following the formation of RUNACE's first 10^5 stars, we track the run of metal content (up to Fe) across various mass ranges, finding that our deterministic model significantly overestimates metal enrichment for stars in the mass range of M_star = 0.1 - 0.4 times solar mass within the first 10 million years. In contrast, our stochastic model delivers results in line with RUNACE's predictions. These findings highlight the importance of stochastic sampling when core-collapse supernovae progenitor mass distributions are unknown. This approach enables accurate calculations of metal enrichment for galaxies in the early universe. The corresponding data package can be accessed at https://doi.org/10/4854. Our novel method InvariantSyn is introduced for creating synthetic samples based on existing instances from imbalanced datasets. Synthetic data generation through InvariantSyn allows retained instances and newly created samples to maintain balance across the dataset, a first of its kind property. Moreover, our theoretical analysis proves the predictive stability of models incorporating our method, signifying that our model performance will consistently improve as more synthetic examples are added. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate significant advantages of InvariantSyn over the current state-of-the-art approaches in addressing imbalanced data. A key benefit of our method over traditional oversampling techniques is the ability to significantly enhance diversity within the synthetic data, a crucial aspect of classifying complex datasets. Additionally, our method's ability to maintain predictive stability while expanding the training set with increased data highlights its advantages over existing research. Further insights into the effects of varying data, algorithmic parameters on the performance of our approach are provided through exploratory data analysis. Variational quantum models, with their ability to combine quantum and classical computing, offer an innovative approach for optimizing quantum circuits. A key aspect of these models is selecting the output measure, as different choices can yield distinct models with varying capacities for learning. In this paper, we explore the potential benefits of using the output state instead of eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian in a variational quantum model. By fixing the Hamiltonian, we demonstrate that a state output leads to a convex optimization problem, whereas an eigenstate output corresponds to a comb optimization problem. We compare the performance of these output choices on two well-known problems: quantum state reconstruction and Hamiltonian learning, utilizing the H2X2 molecule on up to 16 qubits. Results indicate that using the state output produces equivalent or better results, and in some cases, it reduces the quantum noise threshold for successful Hamiltonian learning by approximately 5%. Since state output-based optimization is immune to local minima and has a convex optimization landscape, it offers improved scalability for complex problems. However, it comes with a cost: a significant increase in computational cost due to the need to compute the density matrix. In conclusion, we recommend using the state output for its capacity to enhance scalability, particularly for complex problems on large-scale near-term devices. However, to minimize computational costs, eigenvalues can be used as an effective approximation for a short exploratory search. In practice, this means using the state output for global optimization and switching to eigenvalue-based optimization for fine-tuning. By combining these strategies, variational quantum model scalability improves. Additionally, we found that using the state output for quantum state reconstruction enables a new approach by minimizing the overlap between reconstructed states and genuine states. This method can detect when states are indistinguishable and identify the symmetry group governing such indistinguishability. In the future, this approach could contribute to the discovery of symmetry in many-body quantum systems. Due to the limitations of current quantum computers, accurate state output generation requires sophisticated post-processing techniques to counteract noise effects. Nevertheless, we believe that leveraging the state output offers a new perspective for variational quantum model optimization and quantum machine learning. This study proposes a novel approach to enhance the sensitivity of existing neutron scattering experiments to detect and analyze the interaction of coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, specifically using the known CEvNS event rate to estimate the neutrino cross section and the nervous potential. By employing established measurements from the BBN process, the limits can be set on the maximum neutrino flux emitted by nearby point sources within the solar system. In a broader range of objectives, the research aims to achieve two main goals. Firstly, it seeks to utilize existing neutron scattering experiments to establish an operational upper limit on the CEvNS event rate, thereby preventing the uncontrolled detection of the neutrino flux. Secondly, it aims to explore the feasibility of leveraging established measurements to establish a reliable upper limit on the maximum neutrino cross section, exemplified by the CEvNS event rate measured by the BBN process, and demonstrate its utility in constraining beyond-standard-model interactions mediated by the $U$ and $D$ lepton generations. This study's findings suggest that the BBN process has effectively prevented the uncontrolled detection of the neutrino flux, while the same approach could be adopted to achieve a comparable upper limit on the SCANS and the PS-NCX experiments. quantum systems based on a small number of observations.

Individuals with weakened immune systems are more susceptible to a serious infection known as listeriosis, which can be triggered by the consumption of contaminated food items. The use of gastric acid inhibitors has been linked to an increased risk of developing listeriosis, prompting researchers to examine the relationship between these chemicals and the onset of the disease through a mathematical model. By assuming that the use of gastric acid inhibitors accelerates listeriosis to occur earlier in the infection timeframe, a simulation study found that the disease would likely start sooner but the same or fewer people would be affected. The study highlights that the timing of listeriosis onset can be impacted by factors other than the bacteria's growth rate, such as the individual's immune response and food quality. By refining the mathematical model, researchers gained a deeper understanding of how the use of gastric acid inhibitors affects the onset and duration of listeriosis. The study's results suggest that the use of gastric acid inhibitors could contribute to the earlier occurrence of listeriosis, which would typically manifest 2-3 days earlier in the infection process. By adjusting for lost organisms that escape the host's immune system, the model found that the use of gastric acid inhibitors would result in listeriosis occurring 1-2 days earlier in the infection process. The study's findings provide valuable insights for healthcare professionals and food safety experts to better understand the relationship between gastric acid inhibitors and the development of listeriosis. By mathematically simulating scenarios with fewer infected individuals, the study demonstrated that an efficient case-finding strategy could potentially identify up to 90% of all listeriosis cases if an additional 1-2% of suspected cases are reported to authorities. The study's results highlight the importance of factoring in human behavior when designing public health policies to combat listeriosis. By assuming that a limited portion of the population becomes aware of the disease through media announcements and that an additional limited portion of affected individuals report their symptoms, the study found that an awareness campaign could reduce the average number of listeriosis cases by 0.03-0.06% if 50-80% of affected individuals report their symptoms and by 0.01-0.02% if  the campaign's impact on detection occurs after the critical timeframe when the bacteria reach their maximum size. The study's findings indicate that an efficient case-finding strategy, combined with a large percentage of affected individuals reporting their symptoms and occurring in a population with a high level of awareness, can significantly reduce the average number of listeriosis cases.

This research investigates the challenges posed by hardware impairments in a secure multiuser communication system that incorporates reconfigurable intelligent surfaces. To accurately analyze this problem, we use a comprehensive model that accounts for the combined impact of hardware impairments and phase shifts. By utilizing this accurate system model, we develop two practical strategies for maximizing the overall throughput in such a system: one that iteratively optimizes each user's transmission rate and another that simultaneously optimizes the overall sum rate. Interestingly, we find that the second strategy yields approximately five times better performance than the first strategy after each iteration. Furthermore, we simplify the computationally intensive second strategy into a more manageable and efficient problem whose solution can be easily obtained using standard methods. Our simulation results confirm that these novel approaches significantly outperform existing benchmarks by reducing maximum hardware impairments and increasing system throughput. A key learning technique from animal studies, hindsight summarization, involves revising past experiences to focus on cause-effect relationships, thus enhancing understanding. This paper explores the applicability of hindsight summmarization in the context of deep reinforcement learning, an area where little research has been conducted. The study demonstrates that incorporating hindsight optimization can significantly boost the accuracy of policy networks in reinforcement learning, specifically during training. By reevaluating outcomes of partially completed episodes in a game-like environment, HRO allows the agent to identify key variables and their interactions, ultimately leading to lower prediction errors. The experimental outcomes confirm that the use of hindsight optimization in deep reinforcement learning yields improved predictive accuracy, lower training loss, and higher episode rewards, providing a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners to gain deeper insights into their agent's decision-making processes, especially during the training process. The research also offers a flexible framework for the application of hindsight optimization in other machine learning domains. The solar wind's energy distribution changes dramatically between 1 AU and closer to the sun, particularly at 0.1 AU. To understand how this phenomenon affects small spacecraft, we analyzed the trajectories of 32 tiny units deployed by the Juno spacecraft near the end of its mission. Most of these units had heliocentric orbits starting at 0.101 AU with varying initial velocities. However, the ones that survived have heliocentric orbits beginning at around 0.085 AU. This implies that to overcome solar gravity at close range, energy distributions must be significantly higher than those observed at 1 AU. Furthermore, we propose a theoretical model based on the idea that small particles in space follow a universal energy pattern when lost, which we can express using the binary unperturbed entropy. This entropy concept offers a reliable measure of the space in a system's phase space and can be applied to various scenarios, including loss of small particles in space. By taking into account the presence of a massive object, such as a binary star system, we can calculate the entropy required for a small particle to escape and move to infinity. Using the Juno spacecraft's data, we calculated the binary entropy of the spacecraft at different heliocentric distances and derived an energy threshold below which small particles would be trapped in the solar system. Our model has broad implications and can be applied to various observational datasets, as well as scenarios involving the loss of small particles in binary star systems. Such a model could also be used to estimate the velocity of small particles intercepted by large spacecraft in simulated crossers. Such an algorithm is already in use for the Europa Clipper mission. Our model's formula and algorithm are available online at the https://github.com/sdssastro/junentropy/tree/main/junentropy/junentropy code-sharing platform.

Recent studies on the Emptiness Index and R-negative weight have led to a new understanding, revealing a fundamental link between R-negative states and light-emitting (scissors) modes. Notably, R-negative states were found to have significantly lower transition strengths to positive parity states, compared to their R-positive counterparts. Through this connection, researchers have discovered that the Emptiness Index can serve as an indicator for the scissors degree of freedom, enabling the characterization of R-negative states and their association with light-emitting (scissors) modes. Moreover, this framework offers a unified picture that encompasses nuclear light-emitting phenomena across various regions of nuclear models, ranging from the Pir Su 100 region to the neutron-deficient region. Researchers have also proposed that the R-negative weight may lose its significance in regions where the scissors degree of freedom becomes increasingly dominated by collective effects, as seen in deformed heavy radon isotopes. To explore this further, Emptiness Index calculations were conducted for a Radon isotopic chain to investigate the onset of collective effects. The results show that the Emptiness Index exhibits regional regularities and irregularities, mirroring R-negative weight characteristics, and highlights the emergence of collective effects in deformed Radon isotopes. Consequently, this framework offers a promising approach for classifying light-emitting phenomena in regions of nuclear models that were previously unaccounted for by traditional R-branching rules. Furthermore, this unified framework has the potential to uncover novel regions of nuclear light-emitting regularities that are currently unknown. In conclusion, the underlying physics behind the Emptiness Index and its connection to the scissors degree of freedom has been thoroughly dissected, underscoring how this concept has significantly broadened our understanding of nuclear light-emitting phenomena. Additionally, Emptiness Index calculations have become an indispensable tool for predicting the emergence of light-emitting collective effects in exotic nuclei. As a result, this framework offers an unparalleled opportunity for in-depth explorations of the Emptiness Index role in the near future, particularly regarding the observation of static and dynamic properties of the scissors mode. By combining theoretical analyses with experimental observations, the Emptiness Index has the potential to uncover novel regularities and phenomena that are still unknown today. Therefore, this framework serves as a foundational gateway to the Emptiness Index, highlighting its far-reaching significance across a wide range of exotic in macroscopically observable light-emitting phenomena. In this study, we present a groundbreaking approach in the Arabic domain. First, we create a comprehensive dataset of news articles from all major Arab countries, annotating it with the help of trained arbiters to ensure exceptional quality. In a previous study, we developed a joint model of syntax and semantics called SemCog, where we analyzed English texts to identify common semantic patterns in both syntax and vocabulary. This model discovered that, in English, certain word patterns that convey meaning are closely associated with specific structural arrangements. This research suggested that, in English, semantic patterns are largely determined by the context in which they are used. To take our findings to the next level, we have now extended our model to analyze a broader range of languages, including Arabic, Chinese, French, and Russian. Despite our expectations, we found that the types of semantic patterns identified in English are not unique to that language. Rather, our model discovered similar patterns in the other languages we studied, with some notable differences, however. For example, it appears that short, simple word patterns are more prevalent in languages that are easily written and understood. Additionally, our model discovered that, in languages where the order of words is not fixed, semantic patterns are more closely linked to specific word positions than in languages where the order of words is more consistent. These results confirm that the concept of semantic patterns is not exclusive to English or any other single language, but rather reflects a broader, universal aspect of human language. To validate our findings, we have now conducted a series of studies with native speakers of Arabic, Chinese, and French, who were asked to analyze and categorize the word patterns identified by our model. Interestingly, our results show that, while the types of word patterns identified by our model are the same for each language, the way in which they are categorized is highly variable. This research highlights the benefits of collaborating across languages to gain a deeper understanding of the complex and multifaceted nature of human language. We believe that the insights gained through this research have significant implications for the development of language processing technologies. Furthermore, our findings offer valuable lessons for linguists, cognitive scientists, and the broader academic community. We analyzed the prevalence of tidal features in early-type galaxies using data from the GHOSTS survey, incorporating deep $u^*g^*r^*i^*z^*$ images and central kinematics. By visual inspection, we identified 229 tidal features out of 789 early-type galaxies, and we calculated the fraction of these features in reference to their parent galaxies' masses. We observed a significant trend where the proportion of tidal features increases with galaxy mass. We explored the properties of these tidal features, noting that they tend to have low velocity dispersions and minor axes that are about 0.7 times that of their host galaxies. We calculated the ratio of their dynamical masses to their host galaxies' masses and found it to be roughly 0.1-0.2. We attempted to explain the origin of these tidal features through interactions with smaller companion galaxies or major mergers, but the exact nature and characteristics of these events remain uncertain. The implications of these findings, particularly regarding tidal features' potential impact on galaxy assembly histories, will be further investigated in future research. Furthermore, we suggest the use of tidal features as markers in early-type galaxy assembly histories. By developing a quantitative method to detect tidal features, this feature will be revealed and its statistical properties established. As a result, this approach will enable a more systematic and accurate measurement of tidal features' occurrence and characteristics across various galaxy masses and assembly histories. Using this technique, differences in tidal features' occurrence will be identified among galaxies of different masses and star formation levels. The potential of using tidal features as markers in galaxies of different cosmic masses and environments will be explored. The results will be presented in a follow-up study.

This theory presents a novel approach to resolving the radiation problem by harnessing massive objects' gravitational power to convert rest mass into energy. Similarly to Einstein's General Relativity, it allows for the preservation of principles such as energy-momentum conservation and angular momentum conservation. This conservation approach differs from General Relativity in that it conserves the energy-momentum tensor instead of the stress tensor, thereby avoiding the loss of energy and momentum by massive objects. This conservation approach is also supported by a mathematical theorem. The theory proposes that massive objects can emit gravitational radiation in the form of a pure monopole, thereby converting rest mass into energy. This process is illustrated using a mathematical example based on the Schwarzschild metric. The theory also reveals the relationship between the absence of dark matter and the absence of radiation, thereby providing an alternative to the hierarchical galaxy-formation model. Additionally, it is shown that stellar oscillations are suppressed in the Newtonian framework, while they are predicted to occur within the framework of ASTG. These systems have become widespread in applications like precision spectroscopy, elastic light scattering measurements, and laser surgery, where near-infrared pulses are used to generate or manipulate sub-femtosecond, attosecond or even zeptosecond pulses. To address this challenge, we present a software package, EP, which provides an efficient and accurate solution to the one-way propagation of nonlinear pulses through independent nonlinear media, utilizing the frozen-polarization approximation and an advanced nonlinear spectrum propagation model. This EP software is built upon a Python framework with SciPy libraries and offers easy access to its methods through a user-friendly interface. Moreover, the software generates independent simulation results, which are free from the influence of previous users. The accuracy and performance of EP are validated by comparing it with other numerical methods, which are available in the public domain. In this article, we provide a comprehensive introduction to the theoretical foundation and numerical implementation of the EP software, which is available under a free open-source license at https://github.com/frozenpolarization/EP. These demonstration examples showcase the theoretical and software developments presented in this work. Lastly, the EP software is presented as a contribution to the scientific community, which may benefit from its usage in the modeling of laser pulses and nonlinear processes. Further development of the EP software, which is considered as an underactive project, is proposed along with the suggestion of potential new features that could be incorporated into the software. For most machine translation tasks, it is crucial to ensure that the text generated is relevant both visually and semantically, in relation to a specific image. However, existing text generation frameworks often produce noisy or uncoherent results, which do not align with the context of the image. To address this issue, we have developed a new framework called MAGIC that produces text and video scripts with improved coherence and context relevance. This is achieved by modifying the text encoder in a two-finger typing system, where one finger generates raw samples and the other filters them based on a target sequence representing the context. The raw samples are represented as continuous vectors, which are processed by a discrete word embedding layer to produce noise-filled samples with the same distribution as the target words. A cross-attention module then selects the most relevant words and displaces the noise through repeated iterations of the cross-attention module and a noise-removed sampling module. The raw samples are finally processed by a discrete token embedding layer, which is conditioned on the context through multiple layers of the bidirectional transformer encoder. The context in the top layer is generated by computing the token-wise attention unrolling from the input tokens to the rich semantic representation in the bottom layer. The context is used to displace the noise in the feature map using the mean absolute error, resulting in a noise-free feature map that represents the context. The raw samples are then processed by a discrete token embedding layer, which is conditioned on the context, producing the final text generation results with improved coherence and context relevance. This is demonstrated through both qualitative and quantitative experiments on text and video scripts, which show that the proposed framework produces text and video scripts with improved coherence and context relevance. The code and data are available online. Furthermore, we have observed that modifying the text encoder in a two-finger typing system has a more significant impact than modifying the token embedding layer, suggesting that the former approach produces more robust text generation results. Additionally, we have proposed a new adaptation method called MAGIC-AD that adapts the context from images to other modalities, such as speech, by modifying the cross-attention module in the feature map, which produces the final text generation results with improved coherence and context relevance. To overcome this limitation, a new approach called the Index-Based Continual Learning Table (IBLT-CL) is proposed, allowing these models to learn from experience without gradual memory loss. By leveraging an index system, IBLT-CL can efficiently store and update complex multi-dimensional data, demonstrating the ability to accurately recall past events with high precision >99%. By applying IBLT-CL, a novel history-dependent plasticity model based on machine learning is developed, which can effectively model past events with no memory loss and accurately predict material hardening. Furthermore, applying IBLT-CL to a constitutive model results in a significant reduction in computational memory usage, a minimal increase in computational time, and memory savings of up to 3 orders of magnitude without the need for specialized hardware. The approach also enables seamless integration with multi-step time-integration methods, while preserving numerical stability and efficiency. The developed machine learning-based plasticity model matches the behavior of a constitutive model based on classical mechanics, and predicting its response using such a model results in accurate and numerically stable outcomes. The approach also enables seamless prediction of damage in materials as well as the modeling of complex multi-stage material hardening. The feasibility and effectiveness of the IBLT-CL approach are validated through numerical simulations of finite element analyses. The resulting model shows promising applications in the numerical analysis of material processes involving multiple stages. In recent years, quantization has become a widely accepted technique for deploying neural networks on devices that require efficient processing and storage. However, the traditional approach to quantization often lacks a clear overall objective, resulting in conflicting goals between accuracy and computational overhead. This paper presents a new optimization technique called AskewSGD, which integrates a log-sigmoid approximation to optimize the overall objective of quantization. AskewSGD achieves this by approximating the objective function with a differentiable pattern similar to a Gaussian distribution, and through its use, we make the objective function amenable to gradient-based optimization. Our experiments show that AskewSGD consistently outperforms existing methods, and when combined with other optimization techniques such as channel pruning, it leads to significant improvements in output quality and computational reductions. This technique has been successfully implemented as an open-source library called AsQNet. AskewSGD is integrated into Pytorch, allowing for easy quantization of neural networks. It provides users with a range of customization options, including the ability to specify the number of quantization bits, a memory-optimized quantization pattern, and an online quantization scheme. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the quantization techniques and their applications. Our approach is validated through a series of experiments that demonstrate its effectiveness on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet. AskewSGD has been successfully applied to a range of vision tasks, including classification, regession, detection and segmentation. This paper presents a case study of its application to a real-world autonomous driving system. To facilitate easy replication of our results, we provide an accompanying codebase that includes the AskewSGD implementation and a set of example benchmarks. This paper appears in the Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, 2021.

Breaking down complex statements into simpler phrases using elementary knowledge helps models avoid overcomplication and misunderstandings. We introduce a model-agnostic technique that dynamically restructures the sentence by identifying critical words signifying change in truth value, thereby organizing the input for better comprehension. This method, demonstrated with the TREC CADRE dataset containing nuanced assertions, leads to an enhanced retrieval of clarifying phrases which in turn improves the model's overall accuracy of correct evaluations. The technique, named LogiCUT, achieves a notable 11.9% increase in F1 score compared to the existing best approach, and when combined with existing retrieval methods, yields an average improvement of 14.1% F1 score. To achieve this, we've numerically modeled how magnetized thermal filaments deform when subjected to pressure gradients. Our results indicate that there are two possible mechanisms for the creation of radio filaments: (a) a single thread collapsing due to instabilities that form within a coil that's wrapped too tightly around a magnetic field line, and (b) a split thread reforming itself through the merging of two separate filaments that have diverged. Both scenarios are consistent with observations of filament fragmentation and reformation. As the stability of the coils relies on the balance between external pressure and magnetic field line curvature, we've calculated the range of scales for the curvature that maintains the coils' stability. The task of text-generation in dialogue demands producing coherent, relevant text given the conversation context and optimal conversation progression. Current approaches typically rely on pre-trained language models that correct and refine user inputs, but often fall short by generating inadequate responses due to limited memory capacity and poorly coordinated strategy. To address these limitations, a novel framework is introduced, utilizing a combination of memory augmented neural networks and self-supervised learning to create a more effective text-generator. By employing a neural network with memory capabilities, this framework enables a more efficient text-generator by directly optimizing the conversation's coherence and relevance. Furthermore, the introduction of a self-supervised learning mechanism allows the generator to coordinate its strategy effectively, even without a pre-defined set of rules. Additionally, this framework has successfully produced highly accurate results on the CMU Movie Database dataset, surpassing the database's accuracy by nearly 90%. Notably, the framework's generated responses have achieved 92.1% or higher coherence, relevance, and fluency scores, thereby meeting the dialogue system's requirements for accuracy. Consequently, this framework has great potential to create highly realist and interactive dialogue systems that can effectively engage users. This study introduces a sophisticated driving scenario analysis method that utilizes sensor data from cameras and radar. A probabilistic data association algorithm is employed to track multiple targets. An intersection kernel used in the algorithm allows for the modeling of a vehicle's shape, enabling the estimation of its state given observations from various angles. A joint association method is applied to link measurements to target states. Estimates of driving situation parameters, including time-to-collision and lateral offset, are obtained by modeling the motion of identified objects. Validation using data from driving scenarios and camera/radar sensors showcases the effectiveness of this approach in accurately estimating key driving scenario parameters. Moreover, it suggests potential applications in driver assistance systems. Our method outperforms simpler time-to-collision estimation methods, achieving a mean absolute error of 1.32 seconds and 0.88 meters on a specific dataset. Furthermore, it demonstrates a notable improvement when compared to a learning-based approach that encounters issues in certain scenario situations. Our proposed algorithm can be utilized in a variety of driving assistance systems, such as collision avoidance and advanced driver attention modules. It represents a crucial step towards the development of highly accurate and robust driver assistance technologies. This study highlights the importance of accounting for the size and shape of vehicles and measurement noise in the estimation of time-to-collision when analyzing driving scenarios. It also emphasizes the need for accurate tracking of target states and joint association methods in the analysis of multiple target scenarios. A comprehensive description of our method's architecture and code is provided through the inclusion of additional files. Our proposed algorithm is trained using data from a variety of driving scenarios and camera/radar sensors, achieving generalizability. It passes a rigorous set of evaluation tests, including adversarial attacks and rigorous performance assessments. Our method outperforms existing solutions in a dataset consisting of naturalistic driving scenarios and achieves state-of-the-art performance. A detailed list of potential applications and research directions is presented in the conclusion section. The increased adoption of orthogonal time-frequency space (OTFS) technology has highlighted its susceptibility to channel estimation inaccuracies due to hardware impairments and insufficient cyclic prefix (CP). To address these issues, we have developed an advanced deep learning-based channel estimation approach using enhanced extreme learning machine (ELM). By incorporating a novel weight calculation method in ELM, our proposed model can effectively learn the complex time-domain channel responses and compensate for CP shortcomings. To achieve this, we have designed a novel OTFS-ELM architecture, which leverages a complex-valued activation function and a separate imaginary channel for accurate representation of time-domain channels. Experimental results have shown that the proposed OTFS-ELM technology significantly outperforms existing methods in various scenarios, with notable enhancements in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and relative BER. Notably, our OTFS-ELM technology exhibits superior robustness in scenarios with hardware impairments and CP deficiencies. To further highlight its practical applications, we have used the proposed model to simulate a OTFS-based uplink system with multi-user diversity and spatial multiplexing, which demonstrates the potential of OTFS-ELM technology in large-scale systems. Projective measurement is a fundamental process in quantum mechanics that treats the state of a quantum system as a probability distribution over multiple possible outcomes. The theory of non-projective measurement offers various alternative methods that remain unexplored in practical applications. This paper examines multiple scenarios in which non-projective measurement can lead to equivalent results to projective measurement, including scenarios where measurement outcomes do not depend on the quantum system's state, the number of measurement outcomes exceeds that of the system's dimensions, and the non-projective measurement's outcome probability distribution does not align with the system's quantum state's probability distribution. The paper also presents a non-projective measurement method with properties analogous to von Neumann projection. Furthermore, we discuss the principles underlying non-projective measurement and illustrate how it relates to entanglement and quantum nonlocality. Finally, we propose a multi-party non-projective measurement scheme based on quantum circuit technology, which may be essential for its practical implementation. This study contributes new ideas to the development of projective and non-projective measurement methods and sheds light on the critical distinction between entanglement and nonlocality. Additionally, our research paves the way for the practical application of nonlocal entanglement in multi-party quantum systems. This study further highlights the importance of entanglement in addressing foundational questions of quantum mechanics. The COVID-19 global outbreak prompted a widespread response in contact tracing technologies, leading to both novel non-centralized contact tracing apps and the expansion of existing surveillance systems. While contact tracing technologies aim to halt disease transmission, they have also raised significant concerns over government control and privacy losses. This study provides an overview of the contact tracing technology landscape, including an analysis of the technical aspects of centralization and de-centralization, the impact on government control, and individual privacy. Furthermore, it discusses the trade-offs between these factors and potential consequences, such as reduced efficiency and mass surveillance, to provide insights for selecting suitable solutions tailored to local conditions. Based on our findings, we suggest developing private, distributed, and private sector-driven contact tracing solutions. This study is part of a broader research effort that aims to investigate the technical and societal implications of COVID-19. Two quantum subsystems with pre-existing correlations, controlled by a central regulator, are considered in the context of decoherence and relaxation within a larger environment. Measuring decoherence and relaxation in this scenario is challenging due to the subsystems' limited accessibility individually, however increased accessibility is provided when the subsystems are in a high entanglement state. Focusing on a specific protocol - projective measurements on one subsystem - it is discovered that decoherence and relaxation significantly speed up when in an entanglement state, as opposed to when not entangled. Moreover, it is demonstrated that measurements on highly entangled subsystems provide valuable insights into their respective densities and interactions. Subsequently, it is proposed that, under the influence of rapid decoherence, the time frame for relaxing and measuring correlations is effectively narrowed down to brief 'windows of lucidity'. These brief periods, influenced by entanglement, grant limited access to relaxing subsystems. As a result, the rate at which non-Markovian behavior changes, influenced by the entanglement energy spectrum, plays a crucial role in these brief lucidity periods. Consequently, the limited accessibility of relaxing subsystems, coupled with the entanglement spectrum, provides a new understanding for explaining the emergence of thermodynamic behavior from quantum mechanics. Crucially, it is demonstrated that entanglement itself gives rise to the non-equilibrium richness of this quantum-to-classical transition. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that 'entanglement for lucidity' might be a general principle underlying the transition from quantum to classical behavior in complex systems. Lucidity windows may vary in duration and shape depending on the system in question - however, the principle remains applicable to a wide range of scenarios. This research aims to evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms on a real-world scenario of single vehicle travel time prediction. Diverging from the focus on flow-level travel times, our study centers on a more efficient and detailed prediction of individual vehicle travel times. To accomplish this, we introduce a novel dataset derived from a large GPS dataset collected from 95,000 vehicles covering 472 million kilometers over a period of five years. This dataset enables travel time prediction on various routes in multiple cities, allowing us to compare the effectiveness of multiple models in terms of accuracy, complexity, and processing speed. Notably, our analysis reveals that traditional machine learning algorithms, specifically gradient boosting decision tree models, outperform graph neural networks like the GNN-TT model. Moreover, we identify multiple model capabilities that are comparable or superior to previously proposed models, such as the LST-TT, ORN, and FCK models, which often employ complicated and unstable mechanisms like attention and reinforcement learning or employ a flow-based approach to predict individual vehicle travel times. Ultimately, our study proposes a versatile framework that is compatible with diverse machine learning algorithms, allowing us to evaluate the performance of various baselines and advanced models, ultimately concluding that gradient boosting decision tree models and multilayer perceptrons are the top choices for accurate and efficient single vehicle travel time prediction. This research is available online at https://github.com/traffic4d/single_vehicle_ttt. A demo of the model's performance can be accessed at https://demo.traffic4d.com/svtt. We hope that our study and associated resources can aid in the development of more accurate real-time travel time prediction and forecasting systems. The existence of a primordial magnetic field (PMF) is a topic of ongoing debate, with potential evidence suggested by the dispersion measure of fast radio bursts and gamma-ray anomalies. We investigate how such a field would interact with the universe during inflation and gravitational wave production, and find that it can significantly influence the waves' motion. The PMF would act as a brake on gravitational waves, slowing them down and making them more detectable at lower frequencies. The resulting deceleration could enhance their signal power at frequencies below about 100 MHz, increasing detection prospects at low frequencies. The LIGO/Virgo detectors are unable to directly measure PMF-induced effects on gravitational waves, but their strain data shows oscillations at around 100 Hz that could be interpreted as gravitational wave modulation by a PMF. We found that existing gravitational wave events are insufficient to conclusively prove PMF existence. The potential impact of PMF on gravitational waves and future detection methods are also discussed. Our study shows that by taking into account PMF-induced effects, the sensitivity of LIGO/Virgo and DECIGO gravitational wave detectors can be maximized to detect PMF, specifically up to a frequency of 100 MHz. The potential of next-generation 350 MHz instruments like the Square Kilometer Array also exists to directly detect PMF, assuming it exists at a strength of J = 10^-9 Mpc^-2. The future detection of PMF is feasible by directly observing it with instruments like the SKA or by indirectly inferring it from gravitational wave data. The former is more sensitive to PMF strength, while the latter is more sensitive to PMF duration. The potential impact of PMF on gravitational waves and future detection methods are also discussed. Light field photography requires the capture and representation of multiple perspective images, resulting in large data sizes that pose significant compression challenges. Recent research introduced the disparity-aided light field model to enhance compression efficiency by accounting for the relationships among light field pixels and their spatial positions. Building upon this concept, a proposed paper introduces the Disparity-Aided Image-based Light Field (DA-ILF) model, which leverages the disparity-aided model and introduces an image-based representation to capture both color and geometric information across light field pixels. By integrating this model into a joint source-channel coding scheme, the DA-ILF model achieves significant compression gains over state-of-the-art light field coding methods in both rate--distortion and rendering performance. Furthermore, the proposed scheme exhibits improved scalability and robustness in encoding and decoding processes. Experimental results confirm that the proposed DA-ILF model outperforms the existing light field coding approaches while approaching the performance of state-of-the-art single-image compression methods. Notably, the proposed scheme's improved image-based representation and joint encoding scheme result in scale-invariant compression properties. This scale invariance is a rare capability among existing light field image compression schemes. A fundamental analysis of the proposed DA-ILF model highlights the critical importance of image-based representation in light field compression, as well as the need for joint encoding schemes to achieve optimal compression results. A scale-invariant compression coder based on the DA-ILF model has been proposed and demonstrated to achieve compression efficiency comparable to state-of-the-art single-image coders. This study presents an innovative, semi-interactive cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) approach that enhances query translation by integrating user feedback and sibling context information, aiming to surpass the limitations of traditional pre-trained and fully interactive translation-based methods. A novel, semi-interactive mechanism is devised to iteratively update the query through sibling context and user feedback, resulting in improved retrieval accuracy and diversity. Experimental evaluations on three datasets and multiple languages/databases indicate a significant 5% F-measure enhancement compared to the most effective translation-based method. Moreover, we demonstrate that our approach achieves a diversity of sibling results equivalent to or better than existing methods, with the user often selecting top results. The proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and baselines plus with various levels of interaction, showcasing its effectiveness and efficiency. Finally, user studies demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing methods in user satisfaction, with results from even a single interaction yielding a 20% improvement. The proposed approach and associated resources are available for research and development at https://github.com/ouyangq/semi-interactive-clir. To better grasp intricate patterns in demographic data, we require models that can naturally account for variations at a fine-scale. We have therefore developed a Poisson-Dirichlet mixture model, consisting of multiple Poisson-Dirichlet process mixtures, each representing a distinct demographic segment. Initially, we identify demographic sections with non-overlapping age ranges using PDMMs, and then integrate an Ito process model to smooth out discrete age boundaries. This combined model, known as PDIDP, enables the representation of demographic trends across continuous and discrete domains, and is validated through applications to Sardinian genetics and UK census data. The model is implemented in the scalpath package. This research forms the foundation for understanding the complex demographic history of populations with non-overlapping age brackets. In particular, we apply the model to analyze the distinct demographic sections observed in Sardinian genetics, specifically the 'Isolotto' effect, and identify potential applications in exploring changes in UK population growth rates over time. The model, available on GitHub, has been complemented by the development of the scalpath package, which provides efficient computational scaling. Furthermore, the research data package 'demographics' has been created to facilitate replicability and collaboration. The model, data package, and implementation of the scalpath R package can be accessed at the specified URLs. A shorter version of this research has been previously published in 'Proceedings of Machine Learning Research'.

We found that when the disk is thin and structurally sound, its turbulence behaves differently in the middle layer compared to the upper layers, whereas in a thicker disk, the middle layer and upper layers exhibit similar turbulence patterns. However, these disk structures' implications on planet formation and particle trapping show that turbulence remains a complex and poorly understood phenomenon. Utilizing a simplified model, we simulated the magnetic field's behavior and how it generates a spiral structure that can be influenced by the disk's viscosity. Although the simulation results confirm that a magnetorotational instability can develop in a disk's boundary layer, it also highlights that the magnetorotational turbulence is significantly reduced when compared to a purely hydrodynamic simulation in a disk's middle region. This suggests that the magnetically influenced turbulence in a disk is largely confined to the disk's boundary layers, implying that the mid-plane of the disk may remain relatively calm and less prone to strong turbulence. Consequently, small dust particles may accumulate more easily in the disk's middle layer due to reduced turbulence, making them more susceptible to being eaten by gas density fluctuations in the disk's boundary layers. Ultimately, the simulation results indicate that the level of magnetic field strength in a disk and its associated turbulence in the disk's boundary layers must be taken into consideration when modeling planetary formation and particle accumulation. The application of atmospheric dispersion compensators in telescopes requires precise modeling of the atmospheric dispersion pattern (ADP) to effectively correct for dispersion. Despite the abundance of atmospheric dispersion models, the question remains as to which model offers the most accurate representation of the ADP with sufficient precision for observational purposes. In our study, we have collected and compared the ADPs from eight different models, with the goal of identifying the model that matches observed ADPs the closest. Our comparison shows that the K1 filter-based model developed by the China Miring Telescope, specifically designed for 1.5 meters telescopes, closely aligns with observed ADPs across various wavelengths, exhibiting a difference of less than 0.05 arcseconds in the blue spectrum. In contrast, the ADC designs generated using seven other models fail to match observed ADPs as well as the K1 design does. As such, we highly recommend this K1 model over the other ADC designs for better performance, particularly in the blue spectrum of the spectrum. Furthermore, we plan to release the K1 model, along with an ADC design software, to the public via our website, in the hopes of benefiting the community with this useful tool. We highly recommend using the Bayesian neural network with Horseshoe prior (H-BNN) on correlated variables. This method effectively treats the network as a non-parametric function and learns the distribution of variables using the Horseshoe prior. In the process, it identifies distinct groups of variables and learns their respective distributions. This technique, however, assumes that all groups share a correlation structure, an assumption that might lead to inaccurate results in cases of highly variable dependencies. In such scenarios, additional priors like the shrinkage prior (S-BNN) can provide better accuracy. By comparing the performance of these methods on synthetic and real-world data, we observed a substantial improvement in modeling and variable selection using the H-BNN and S-BNN approaches, respectively. Furthermore, we observed a substantial decrease in the effective dimensionality of the S-BNN approach. Additionally, we evaluated the S-BNN approach on both regression and classification tasks, and found it to be on par with non-bayesian approaches. This method provides an attractive trade-off between modeling complexity and variable selection. This method has been implemented in the pyhbn library, available on PyPI.
