Unraveling the effects of neural network layer removal on image classification errors has become a significant pursuit in understanding neural network behavior. Current methods, however, primarily focus on using network weights as a proxy for the architecture's complexity, and they fail to capture the intricate relationship between image features and classification mistakes. In this work, we introduce a novel, iterative image-based magnitude pruning technique for CNNs, which enables us to directly assess how much an image's visual details influence a specific network layer's accuracy. By applying our method to multiple datasets, such as CIFAR and Tiny-ImageNet, as well as diverse network architectures, including ResNet, we find that the importance of each layer varies greatly, with some contributing much more to network performance than others. Our results consistently indicate that the initial few layers of a CNN are responsible for the majority of its accuracy. Based on these findings, we suggest a hybrid network approach, where the most critical, visually-informed layers are prioritized, and less important layers are pruned, while retaining vertically stacked architectures to leverage their potential synergies. In line with our findings, we experimentally demonstrate that the generalization capability of the visually-informed group of layers lies largely untapped on large image datasets, such as ImageNet. Moreover, we find that combining the predictions from individual network segments significantly enhances the overall prediction accuracy, with the difference being more pronounced on more complex image benchmarks. By pushing the boundaries of pruning-based network architecture exploration, we believe that our approach will serve as a valuable tool for the community. The robustness of quantum classifiers against malicious modifications has yet to be thoroughly investigated. We treat quantum classifiers as being used in critical applications where reliability is paramount. In this context, the accuracy of quantum classifiers is assessed against a range of deliberate errors introduced into quantum data sets. This is the first study to examine the impact of adverse examples on a variety of quantum classifiers, including both fully connected and knapsack networks. To investigate the severity of these adverse examples, the performance of quantum classifiers is compared under conditions of increasing data corruption. Our analysis reveals the vulnerability of quantum classifiers to even minor data corruption and the significant impact this has on their classification accuracy. Furthermore, the advantages and disadvantages of different quantum classifier architectures are discussed in terms of their resilience to data corruption. Our findings are an important step towards understanding the reliability of quantum classifiers and their practical implementation in critical applications. They also prompt several avenues for future research, including the development of quantum classifier architectures that can withstand deliberate errors and the exploration of methods to counteract adverse examples. Additionally, the significant performance disparity between the best quantum classifiers and various traditional classifiers serves as a motivation for future research in quantum machine learning. This research could potentially bridge the current performance gap between these two fields and shed new light on the unique advantages and disadvantages of quantum machine learning. Accurate radio propagation modeling is crucial for communication systems planning, and recent advancements in geographic information systems have improved models' accuracy. Similarly, deep convolutional neural networks have demonstrated high predictive accuracy in various fields, prompting their application in radio propagation modeling. By treating input data as 2D spatial images, deep networks can learn implicit relationships between modeling inputs, comparable to the systemic understanding gained from traditional modeling approaches. We introduce a novel deep network-based modeling approach, leveraging a spatial attention mechanism to adapt to diverse modeling scenarios. To assess its efficacy, we compared our method with established modeling techniques on real-world datasets, finding it yields significantly better results. Furthermore, we analyzed the learned weight matrices to gain insights into the mapping between modeling inputs and outputs. Our analysis revealed the network prioritizes spatial details within individual input data, indicating it focuses on local patterns like signal attenuation due to obstacles. We found the network also incorporates interdependence between inputs, implying it recognizes patterns like the human body's impact on overall propagation. These findings show a deep network-based modeling approach can be both highly predictive and shed new light on the complex relationships within modeling inputs. As a result, it may serve as a powerful supplement or potential replacement for traditional modeling methods. By using neural networks to reverse-engineer these models, we can better understand the underlying system and improve the accuracy of geographic information systems. To further establish the reliability of deep networks in this context, we performed an extensive examination of the robustness and reliability of our method using a diverse set of datasets and modeling configurations. Our method passed these rigorous tests, demonstrating its superior performance and system safety in this domain. Importantly, this research highlights the importance of systematic evaluation for deep networks in real-world applications, as well as the need to adapt established modeling practices to the unique characteristics of spatial data. Looking ahead, the integration of our method could significantly enhance the accuracy and efficiency of communication systems planning, geographic information systems, and other areas involving spatial data analysis. As a result, it may have far-reaching implications for various applications, such as big data analysis. Furthermore, the insights gained from this research could inform the development of Explainable AI methods, which aim to shed light on the complex decision-making processes within neural networks, particularly in the spatial domain. To facilitate future research in this area, we have made our code and data available for public access, enabling researchers to build upon our findings and improve the accuracy of neural network-based modeling approaches. One of the key challenges of the energy transition is efficiently optimizing power system development and operation to minimize costs. To this end, medium-term planning models with detailed generation capacities are applied, but these models are only partially effective in optimizing costs, as they do not take into account specific generation technologies or temporal frameworks. To address this limitation, we investigated the importance of incorporating a high-resolution time frame into these models by comparing the costs of annual vs quarterly time splits. Our study used a detailed model of the German electricity grid, which incorporates specific generation technologies, to analyze the costs of annual and quarterly time splits. The results show that incorporating a high-resolution time frame reduces costs associated with misallocating generation capacities by 10-15%, primarily by allowing for more precise modeling of renewable generation variability. To verify these findings, we employed three different modeling approaches, namely an investment model with a spatial double dividend, a hybrid model with variable temporal properties, and a day-ahead market model with precise temporal resolution. Our study shows that the cost savings associated with high-resolution time frames are largely consistent across these models, suggesting that our findings are robust. However, incorporating a high-resolution time frame comes at the cost of significantly increased computational complexity and costs, rendering it impractical for annual planning sessions. Consequently, we propose a simplified approach to incorporating a high-resolution time frame into planning models, which is computationally efficient and results in cost savings of 5-10%. This approach can be integrated into existing planning models as a module and is suitable for annual planning sessions. To validate this module, we conducted a case study on German power system development under the European Union's National Emission Reduction Plans and compared the results with those of quarterly time splits. Our study shows that incorporating this module yields system-level costs 2.4% lower than those of quarterly time splits. Furthermore, we identified specific measures to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions and power outages through power system development and operation. Our study reveals that power system development and operation under the EU's National Emissions Reduction Plans would result in significantly higher costs and more outages than continuing with the existing policy if based on quarterly time splits. However, incorporating our module which simplifies high-resolution time framing in planning models can significantly mitigate these costs and outages. The main contributions of this study are the demonstration of the importance of incorporating a high-resolution time frame into planning models, the proposal of a module to simplify high-resolution time framing in these models, and the identification of critical measures to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions and power outages through power system development

This is an undergraduate project that showcases the mathematical induction method for proving the Collatz conjecture, as outlined in associated textbook materials. The project was written under the guidance of Dr. Karlo Chan. 

The project begins by defining the function $C(x)$, which performs the Collatz transformation on any given integer $x$, and subsequently retrieves a set $S$ of numbers that will help establish the induction step of the conjecture. 

The first step of the induction proof assumes the conjecture is true for all integers from 1 to some number $k$, and then uses these assumptions to show the conjecture is true for $k+1$. 

The project then sets up two separate cases for its induction step, which analyzes the Collatz transformation when given an even number or an odd number, respectively. 

Case 1 uses the function $C(2n)=C(n)$, combined with the assumption that the conjecture is true for $2n$, to show the conjecture is true for $n$. 

Case 2 uses the function $C(2n-1)=C \cdot (2n-1)$, combined with the assumption that the conjecture is true for $2n-1$, to show the conjecture is true for $2n-1$. 

The project concludes by noting that since the conjecture is true for all odd numbers by the nature of its base assumptions, and the same can be done for even numbers, this proves the conjecture is true for all integers. 

It's worth noting that this project does not actually prove the conjecture as it was already given as true, as per the textbook's nature. The project serves as a demonstration of how to utilize mathematical induction for this particular conjecture. The actual proof of the conjecture remains unresolved. The project's findings were discussed in a meeting with the supervisor on 2/3/2021. 

I would like to express my gratitude to my supervisor, Dr. Karlo Chan, for his guidance and support throughout this project. I would also like to acknowledge the constant discussions we had, as well as the initial meeting to discuss this project, which took place on 2/3/2021. 

I hope that sharing my project will inspire others to work on solving the Collatz conjecture, which has been unresolved since 1937.

As machine learning becomes more entrenched in our daily lives, its decisions often seem perplexing despite their underlying simplicity when explained. Consequently, legitimizing these models within various fields is essential. Sensitive information found in documents, for example, requires reliable classification to ensure accurate handling. In this study, we investigate how to incorporate explainable AI into the binarization process of BERT, making its document classification decisions more understandable. Through computational experiments, we compared the accuracy and speed of X-BERT (the base model), BERT with LIME-based explanations, and BERT with Deep LIME-based explanations. Interestingly, our results demonstrate that adding explanations remarkably enhanced the model's accuracy without compromising speed, outperforming X-BERT. Furthermore, we discovered that explaining the model did not always improve the model's binarization process accuracy, but when combined with BERT, it significantly improved the binarization process accuracy. Our findings highlight the promise of explainable AI in making AI decision-making more transparent, especially in critical fields like document classification. They also suggest the potential for further research on how explaining AI impacts decision-making across various domains. Importantly, our study contributes to the document classification field by incorporating the crucial aspect of machine understanding into the binarization process. Based on our findings, we developed a hybrid system by integrating the Deep LIME-based explanations with the BERT model, resulting in the highest accuracy among all models tested. Our code is available on the GitHub platform. Ultimately, our study serves as a foundation for future research on the transparency of machine learning, especially in the document classification field. Automated evaluation metrics (AEMs) play a vital role in assessing text summarization models. However, existing AEMs are deficient in evaluating summary diversity and relatability to human judgments. This research introduces SummScore, a novel AEM designed to address these shortcomings. SummScore assesses a summary by measuring the overlap in sentences and ideas to account for diversity, utilizing a unique neural model that generates guidance with pre-trained BERT. Performance tests on six diverse summarization datasets indicate that SummScore outperforms existing metrics in terms of diversity and alignment with human evaluations. SummScore's performance is even more pronounced when compared to leading AEMs in conjunction with human-based evaluation metrics. Additionally, SummScore's results suggest that current summariation models tend to replicate existing information rather than generating original ideas. The proposed metric is complemented by a diverse set of reference summaries created through a crowdsourced effort, mirroring the type of summaries generated by state-of-the-art summarization models. The evaluation toolkit, datasets, and source code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Chaubay/SummScore. This research is supported by the National Science Foundation grant RII-1931848. In many scientific research areas, cross-modal data is widely available and heavily used. Cross-modal recovery from noisy and incomplete data has become an essential task in both academia and industry. This study focuses on recovering a common vector from multiple correlated datasets using low-rank matrix factorization. The study introduces a new framework called CCR, which utilizes cross-correlation properties to decompose cross-modal data into rank-one unitary matrices. The CCR framework leverages these properties through an optimization procedure that incorporates an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm. Theoretical analyses demonstrate that the proposed CCR framework can effectively recover a common vector from sparse samples, with the number of required samples increasing linearly with the sparsity level and the square of the number of modalities. The CCR framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in several challenging cross-modal datasets, including material recognition in microscopy images and speech recognition in video. The methods and source code are publicly available. This study also reveals an interesting phenomenon - the more sparse level we can recover, the more cross-correlated data we need to achieve the same recovery error barrier. This discovery sheds new light on the cross-correlation properties in cross-modal recovery and provides a solid theoretical foundation for future research in this area. This study presents an empirical analysis of cross-modal recovery and provides several practical recommendations for real-world applications. Our research proposes the BEVFusion framework, a novel neural approach that streamlines the object detection process by directly projecting 3D LiDAR data onto a 3D bounding prism representation.  BeVFusion significantly outperforms existing methods, which rely on more complicated 3D LiDAR-based models, such as point cloud-based ones, by an impressive 650% in terms of detection accuracy on the KITTI object detection task.  Notably, our approach exhibits robust performance under real-world LiDAR failures, with a remarkably low influence from individual 2D beam sweeps, thus enhancing overall results by 13% and 21% respectively on iCAR and KITTI datasets.  Comprehensive experiments confirm that our BEVFusion framework consistently outperforms industry standards, including KITTI CAR, AVOD 2.1, HDv2, ATG, ATSS, and F-PSN, under various real-world LiDAR failures conditions.  Extensive ablation studies demonstrate the critical role of our BEVFusion framework's key components, including geometric priors, overlap loss, and point loss, which collectively result in a notable 21% improvement in object detection performance.  Furthermore, our BEVFusion framework achieves exceptional results on KITTI and iCAR datasets with an impressive IoU of 72.85% and 64.04%, respectively.  The proposed BEVFusion framework is now available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/AdityaKrGupta/BEVFusion.  Our approach's notable achievements are further highlighted by superior time efficiency, requiring only 0.04 seconds to predict 3D objects.  This remarkable speed and performance combination makes the BEVFusion framework an industry-leading approach to 3D object detection.  Notably, our approach's novel 3D object representation, known as the bounding prism, significantly outperforms traditional methods, including IoU-based ones, by an impressive 21% and 13% respectively on KITTI and iCAR datasets.  The BEVFusion framework's geometric prior model, comprised of a prism, consists of five distinct components, including center of gravity, size, orientation, height, and the center of the bottom plate.  The geometric prior model's notable components, such as the center of gravity and size, significantly outperform existing methods, by an impressive 21% and 13% respectively on KITTI and iCAR datasets. Recent advancements in mining significant design changes from large databases using deep learning have shown promising results. Nevertheless, the practical application of this method is hindered by two limitations: the variability of conclusions and the lack of cross-project relevance. This study examines the effect of two solution strategies for these limitations in design mining using an electronic circuit design dataset. The first strategy involves using ensemble methods to enhance conclusion stability by comparing multiple algorithms and reducing the impact of hyperparameter tuning. The second strategy involves leveraging knowledge transfer, which utilizes pre-trained networks trained on diverse tasks to extract relevant information from the target database. The results indicate that the application of ensemble methods to a state-of-the-art algorithm yields better conclusion stability, whereas the incorporation of knowledge transfer methods yields more relevant conclusions. Furthermore, the integration of these techniques yields greater insight into the significance of design change. As such, the outcome of this study is the development of two enhanced design mining algorithms that surpass the existing state of the art in conclusion stability and cross-project relevance. Experimental evaluations confirm the effectiveness of these methods. The accompanying code and pre-trained models are available for download on the GitHub repository 10.5281/eben@5.533.

The application of tensor completion in streaming data has been a subject of ongoing research. Artificial intelligence networks excel at detecting and verifying objects within images, but humans may interpret distorted images differently due to factors like texture, lighting, and camera angle. We conducted an experiment to compare the accuracy of AI and humans in object recognition, presenting the latter with severely distorted images in a manner that individual features cannot be reliably identified. For both AI and humans, the task involved classifying objects in images into one of 50 categories. We found that AI models, despite achieving an average accuracy of 39% on severely distorted images, still posed a significant threat to human security against sophisticated machine-based attacks. We further investigated the human performance in this task and observed that people struggled to recognize objects that were not frequently encountered, and those with less experience in object categorization were severely impaired in object recognition tasks with severely distorted images. We discuss the implications of this study and explore potential applications of this study in full. We make available the complete dataset used in this study to promote future research in object recognition across various domains. We propose an open challenge to enhance object recognition robustness against image manipulations by AI and humans. We conclude that people's ability to recognize objects is more resilient to image manipulations than AI, but AI's role should not be underestimated as it holds the future of object recognition technology. We show that people's reliance on AI in object recognition should not be seen as a threat but rather as an opportunity for collaboration between humans and machines. This assessment involved employing 5 distinct GPT-2 models with differing parameter counts, ranging from 68 million to 154 billion parameters, on a range of tasks from semantic retrieval to abstract reasoning. This analysis examines the spectrum of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) with a first-order phase transition in the context of recent Large Hadron Collider results. By maximizing the energy released in the phase transition into dark matter particles, and considering various experimental constraints, we identify the areas of the NMSSM's parameter space that remain viable in the face of experiments at the Large Hadron Collider. Our findings indicate that many areas of the NMSSM's parameter space, which previously favored a strong phase transition and now appear incompatible with experiments, can be eliminated through a more accurate assessment of how the Higgs boson's decay rate changes during a first-order phase transition. This results in a strong lower limit on the masses of particles in the NMSSM's multiplet. However, when these findings are combined with data from the Direct Detection of Dark Matter experiments, it becomes apparent that a more complex first-order phase transition in the NMSSM leads to a mass range for the Lightest Supersymmetric Particle (LSP) that is largely incompatible with experiments. This in turn, raises the possibility that a more realistic model of a strong first-order phase transition in the NMSSM leading to LSPs with masses largely beyond the reach of current experiments, may be necessary to explain the observed phenomena of the Higgs boson if it undergoes a first-order phase transition in the context of the NMSSM.

The results demonstrate both the fundamental characteristics of topological defects and the explicit breaking of $Z_3$ symmetry. Explicit symmetry breaking is increased with the number of lattice sites in the temporal direction. The model's vertices are modified to include a high-order term, facilitating a smooth transition to the standard Klein-Gordon theory, while the topological defect's core energy remains independent of this transformation. Furthermore, the study investigates the relationship between the core energy and the model's parameters, providing a basis for understanding the properties of topological defects in both the low- and high-limits of the model. We found that the star formation rates calculated from near-infrared and submillimeter data were consistently 10 to 100 times higher than those estimated from CO and H30α emissions. The primary goal of this research is to introduce and analyze novel kernel-based techniques for solving non-linear eigenvalue problems centered on Lert-type operators with Volterra kernel type. These methods leverage kernel-based techniques and are an extension of existing parametric projection methods, such as Galerkin approaches, which converge rapidly but may require large dim $T$ due to a slow decay of the spectral values. The introduced methods involve a parametric collocation technique, which yields a discrete eigenvalue problem by equating the kernel-based approximations of the Lert-type operator with corresponding eigenfunctions. This approach leads to a finite dimensional problem with a simpler structure than the Galerkin approach, and is shown to converge rapidly in theory, with empirical results confirming its efficiency and demonstrating its potential for handling problems that were previously intractable. These methods also facilitate the development of a fully discrete scheme with nearly optimal computational complexity, which is achieved by combining the kernel-based technique with a finite difference method in the spatial variable. Moreover, numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the methods' effectiveness, particularly for problems with singular eigenvalues and index jump. These methods have additional value as a theoretical tool for evaluating the approximation error of kernel-based techniques. These methods are currently being applied in a forthcoming paper to derive sharp bounds for the approximation error of fundamental solutions to non-homogeneous Dirichlet problems with singular or degenerate diffusion coefficients. 

The accompanying MATLAB code is available for download at: https://github.com/AdolfoBarreiro/KernelBasedMethods4NEVP/tree/main/code. 

A more in-depth exploration of the related non-linear eigenvalue problems is provided in the book "Kernel-based methods for nonlinear eigenvalue problems" edited by Adriana Sauter and Stefano P. Becker, which is currently under review at SIAM.

GdInO3 is a cubic crystalline compound, classified as an intrinsic p-type semiconductor with the fluorite structure, and its electronic properties are attributed to the presence of Gd3+ ions in a cubic lattice. Through the combination of first-principles calculations and experimental techniques, researchers investigated the electronic, vibrational, and magnetic properties of GdInO3, including the existence of several stable polymorphs. Calculations indicated that GdInO3 polymorphs exhibit varying levels of stability, and their differences can be characterized by the distortion of InO62 octahedra and the resulting changes in spin states among Gd3+ ions. Experimentally, several stable polymorphs were synthesized and characterized using X-ray diffraction, X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, and magnetization measurements. The results confirmed that the synthesized compounds match the calculated phase equilibrium temperatures, and GdInO3 polymorphs can be classified into two groups, stabilized by either tetragonal or orthorhombic distortions. Moreover, the presence of these distortions leads to the variation of electronic, vibrational, and magnetic properties among the compounds, and this distortion-induced phenomenon can be utilized for the development of multifunctional materials and devices. Ultimately, the research on GdInO3 polymorphs has significant implications for the understanding of intrinsic p-type semiconductors and the creation of functional materials for optoelectronic, spintronics, and thermoelectric applications. Additionally, the research provides a new perspective on the design of multifunctional materials, showcasing a successful case of functional modulation through atomic substitution in oxide systems. Finally, the research opens up a new avenue for the exploration of rare-earth metal monoxide semiconductors, and the results can be extended to other systems with similar properties and applications. In conclusion, the study on GdInO3, a widely known but still evolving material, has contributed to the advancement of research in functional materials and devices. The development of multifunctional devices based on GdInO3 could be achieved by combining techniques like electron beam irradiation, electrostatic force microscopy, and localized heating, and this research could be applied to the development of devices for local electrical, magnetic, and optoelectronic properties. Furthermore, the methods used in this study can be employed for the local manipulation of GdInO3 polymorphs and the exploration of novel functional materials at the nanoscale.

In recent years, there has been a surge in interest in developing machine learning models capable of processing sparse networks, which are ubiquitous in various fields. This paper presents a novel approach centered around the Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM), yielding the SNHAM embedding method. By analyzing the inherent characteristics of sparse networks, we demonstrate that a low-rank approximation of SNHAM leads to an accurate estimation of the network's adjacency matrix. To address computational efficiency, we introduce a randomized sampling-based technique, reducing computational complexity and enhancing runtime performance. Our approach also enables the incorporation of diverse network attributes through a flexible weighting scheme. We evaluate the effectiveness of SNHAM embeddings on multiple real-world network datasets, highlighting its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in node classification tasks and network visualization. Notably, SNHAM embeddings contribute to a more sparse and informative representation of nodes, which can be leveraged for node prediction tasks. Specifically, we show that these embeddings enable the development of a highly accurate classifier for unknown nodes in sparse networks. Furthermore, we propose a novel visualization method, Node Selection and Embedding Representation (NSRR), that utilizes SNHAM embeddings to identify key nodes in a network. By iteratively replacing a subset of nodes in the network with unseen nodes, NSRR efficiently generates a concise subset of critical nodes explaining the majority of the network's variance. had a significant economic impact, leading many individuals to question their
effectiveness. Lockdowns work by restricting the movement of people, particularly
in regions where a large portion of the population is at risk. However, locking down
an entire nation may not be an ideal solution, as it's a broad generalization that
doesn't account for regional variations in population density and vulnerability to
the virus. To address these concerns, researchers have explored alternative
strategies. They developed a mathematical model that simulates different
hypotheses regarding the actions of hospitals and health care facilities to
help control the spread of the virus. By simulating various scenarios, including
the implementation of non-pharmaceutical interventions such as the closure of
hospitals and health care facilities, the delivery of home care, and the
implementation of strict isolation and contact tracing measures, the model
evaluates their effectiveness in controlling the spread of the virus. The model's
predictions reveal that the actions of hospitals and health care facilities play a
significant role in containing the spread of the virus. In scenarios where the
population's initial susceptibility to the virus is high, the implementation of
strict isolation and contact tracing measures result in a limited reduction in the
peak number of active cases. Conversely, the model's predictions are reversed when
the population's initial susceptibility to the virus is low. Furthermore, the
model's analysis suggests that the implementation of a targeted strategy, such as
the strict isolation and contact tracing of high-susceptibility populations,
may be a more effective approach than a broad lockdown measure. The model's
predictions are validated by the analysis of real-world data from the United
States. The model's results provide valuable insights to policymakers, offering
practical advice and guidance. The model's source code and data are publicly
accessible through an open-source repository. https://github.com/AbhishekAnandGh0st/COVID-19/tree/main/MathematicalModel. This research investigates how principal component analysis handles weighted data in recovering a low-rank matrix. Specifically, we analyze what happens when a single principal component is chosen based on a weighted combination of the matrix's singular values. Our study reveals that this approach is highly dependent on the weights and can be vulnerable to poor choices. Surprisingly, even when using optimal weights derived from matrix recovery conditions, a low-rank matrix is not necessarily well-represented within the nearest neighbor set in feature space. However, when the top singular values adhere to the matrix recovery conditions, a matrix is well-represented through PCA-based feature mapping. Additionally, we provide a new set of matrix recovery conditions centered around PCA. Our experiments verify that our recommended weights outperform traditional PCA, leading to a significant improvement in matrix recovery. Furthermore, PCA-based feature mapping with the optimal weights is shown to be robust against adversarial attacks in the context of multi-class classification, outperforming other feature mapping methods like linear discriminant analysis and random feature mapping. This research highlights the importance of using weighted PCA for low-rank matrix recovery and related tasks. A Python package called scPca is also introduced, which incorporates several matrix recovery and feature mapping methods and applies them to different tasks. This package is available on PyPI at https://pypi.org/project/scPca/0.0.1/. A comprehensive collection of code is also shared at https://github.com/Chen-Keim-Keen/weighted-PCA. Detailed explanations and additional experiments can be found in the supplementary materials section. Lastly, the research is accompanied by two different sets of matrices, which are available at https://github.com/Chen-Keim-Keen/weighted-PCA. One set is utilized for matrix recovery and the other set is utilized for classification purposes. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework, known as LASSIE, for semantic segmentation in lumbar spine surgery. It combines a U-Net style network, called V-Net, with a knowledge distillation system utilizing a spinal discectomy mask. Additionally, the framework incorporates a classification module that predicts whether a given lumbar spine image is normal or affected by trauma, using a binary classifier trained on the Balanced Accuracy dataset. The results demonstrate that the framework achieves balanced accuracy of 0.83 on the validation dataset and 0.81 on the test dataset. Furthermore, the framework's ability to generate meaningful segmentation masks is reinforced by high average Jaccard indices of 0.85 (J) for both the validation and test datasets. Notably, the framework's performance surpasses that of human radiologists, who achieved an average balanced accuracy of 0.69 (+/- 0.04) for a small test dataset. The framework's code is publicly available on the GitHub platform at the URL https://github.com/education4ai/LASSIE. A video showcasing the framework's performance can be accessed on the https://4ai.ai/lassevid.html website. Notably, the framework has the potential to greatly reduce the reliance of radiologists on human eyes during the analysis process, ultimately leading to a significant reduction in the time required for diagnosis. This, in turn, could enable the use of deep learning-based automated lumbar spine image segmentation for clinical applications due to its high reliability. Furthermore, the framework's performance on scenarios involving multiple anatomical structures and functions is a crucial step towards the development of a fully automated diagnosis system. This, in turn, could lead to the creation of a decision support tool based on deep learning that can aid radiologists in their work and potentially replace them for certain tasks on the back-end. A potential next step for the framework involves the use of more advanced techniques, such as attention-based models, for the identification of specific regions of interest within the images. Furthermore, the framework's performance on scenarios involving more complex image corruptions and conditional distributions may be crucial for its practical application in real-world clinical settings. A comprehensive evaluation of the framework using more realistic image scenarios and clinical data is necessary for its practical use in centralised or federated learning environments. In statistical analysis, assumptions regarding complete data are frequently compromised by the common problem of data missingness. Consequently, data analysis often requires addressing missing data issues. Although various techniques have been developed to handle missing data, such as multiple imputation and inverse probability weighting, there is a lack of understanding about how these methods affect confidence intervals. Causal inference models, particularly those involving instrumental variables, are particularly challenging in this regard. This study introduces a new approach to evaluating the robustness of conclusions drawn from causal models involving missing data. This approach, based on the E-value, enables the analysis of how the uncertainty associated with imputation or weighting methods affects the reliability of causal conclusions. Using IV analysis as a case study, we illustrate how the E-value can be employed to quantify the uncertainty associated with both multiple imputation and IPCW estimators of the IPW estimators. Simulation results and real-world data analysis further demonstrate the utility of this framework for evaluating the robustness of causal estimates and intervals. This study's general methodology enables the extension of this framework to other estimators and models, thereby providing a unified framework for assessing the reliability of causal estimates and intervals. Furthermore, this study's introduction of the E-value concept and its application to causal inference in the presence of missing data significantly broadens the scope of previous work in this field. This study's findings suggest that while the E-value does not yield a definitive lower bound in all scenarios, it is a more conservative estimator than traditional standard errors. Consequently, the E-value may yield higher estimates that surpass the confidence interval limits. Nevertheless, the E-value offers valuable insights into the reliability of causal conclusions drawn from models with missing data. To explore how library choice influences code security, we examined how developers
use three prominent cryptographic libraries - Python's cryptography, Java's
commons-codec, and C's openSSL - across five vulnerable projects, collecting over
3000 functions from these libraries. Our analysis indicates that the higher risk of
information disclosure comes not from the libraries themselves, but from how these
functions are used, with the repeated misuse of hash functions standing out in
particular. Additionally, we found that the risk of information disclosure varies
considerably depending on the library and function in question, with developers
exposing sensitive information more often when using Python's cryptography than
Java's commons-codec or C's openSSL. Our research shows the importance of how a
library is designed and used, highlighting the need for libraries to facilitate
secure coding practices that minimize the risk of information disclosure. Furthermore,
our findings suggest that libraries that make errors easy to commit also make it
easier to avoid these errors in the first place. This behavior is particularly
notable in the context of hash functions, where the risk of information disclosure
is typically eliminated when the function is used correctly. Therefore, library
designers and developers should prioritize practices that minimize the likelihood
of errors occurring in the first place, rather than simply reducing their impact. 
Lastly, our study offers suggestions for improving the design of cryptographic
libraries to reduce the likelihood of information disclosure, such as eliminating
functions with high misuse risk like hash functions. 
A final discussion on potential future research avenues is presented. 
These ideas could contribute to reducing the likelihood of information
disclosure in the codebases of vulnerable projects. 
Our research is accessible at https://info-disclosurgy.github.io. 
Key words: info-disclosurgy, library design, library misuse, 
cryptographic libraries, risk reduction, security best practices.

In large-scale scanning scenarios, recovering 3D data from 2D images is essential for efficient use of scanning equipment.  However, as image data volumes increase, so does the time required for data processing. This issue becomes particularly pronounced when using advanced neural networks, which are increasingly employed in 3D data recovery due to their superior performance over traditional methods. In response, we've developed a novel approach that leverages a hierarchical 3D-2D learning strategy to accelerate 3D data reconstruction. This approach uses a hierarchical structure to process data of different resolutions in succession, and also introduces a 3D-2D volume alignment loss to maintain spatial consistency. Furthermore, we introduce a 3D volume decomposition-based data parallelization technique to overcome the computational limitations of large-scale data reconstruction. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in 3D data reconstruction and demonstrates improved processing speed, with significant gains of 2.5x and 3.6x, respectively. Additionally, our method offers increased flexibility in data parallelization, with reduced memory usage and green computing benefits. Our code is now publicly available to support similar research and developments. The Arrovian approach seeks to identify social preference orderings that satisfy specific criteria when applied to diverse sets of individual preferences.  Key to these investigations is a theorem established by Maskin, which reveals that the existence of a sequence of consistent demand functions whose limits satisfy a particular social preference criteria implies the use of unstable limiting processes.  The primary objective of this study is to verify the applicability of this theorem in scenarios featuring non-standard models of individual preference.  Two such scenarios are examined.  The first involves individuals with constant absolute utility, while the second corresponds to those with linearly decreasing absolute utility, and in both cases, our analysis confirms the applicability of Maskin's theorem.  Furthermore, we observe that the limit demand functions resulting from these scenarios fail to be continuous when considered in a particular context.  The study also explores the applicability of Maskin's theorem to standard models of individual preference and reveals that the initial consistency requirement can be satisfied by constructing a sequence of demand functions whose limits consistently converge to a continuous social preference function.  Finally, we examine the scope for expanding the range of Arrow's impossibility theorem to encompass scenarios with a continuum of individual preference functions and demonstrate that any such extension would necessitate the use of non-standard limiting processes.  The study thus contributes to an understanding of the interplay between the concepts of convergence and continuity across diverse applications.  Importantly, our results indicate that this distinction is particularly pronounced in social preference investigations, where it holds almost uniformally across all relevant domains. We introduce Landmark Gabor Filters, a novel image representation method built around a set of carefully designed Gabor filters with distinct orientation markers. These filters serve as a conceptually straightforward image acquisition mechanism for neural network-based vision systems. The use of Landmark Gabor Filters results in stable and consistent low-level feature representations across various orientations, due to their inherent ability to capture images from multiple perspectives as a 3D Gabor function rotates. Experimental evaluations conducted on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the robustness of features derived from Landmark Gabor Filters, particularly in situations involving extreme orientation changes. Moreover, our research showcases the potential of integrating Landmark Gabor Filters with convolutional layers to achieve superior performance across a range of state-of-the-art benchmarks. The effectiveness of this hybrid approach is exemplified by significant enhancements in classification accuracy on the CIFAR-10 dataset and improved robustness of image binocular stereo matching on the KITTI dataset. The full source code and model weights are publicly available on our GitHub repository. Furthermore, our contribution significantly advances the field of steerable image representations by providing a novel low-level feature representation method that outperforms existing baselines in several key aspects. As the research progresses, the potential applications of this method will be expanded to include other challenging computer vision tasks. Classifiers are often ineffective in practical scenarios due to their inability to handle imbalanced data sets. A novel approach, proposed in this research, involves creating a more balanced distribution of positive instances by generating samples from the predicted class boundaries, as determined by a pre-trained imbalanced classifier. Unlike traditional methods, such as over- and under-sampling, this strategy seeks to exploit the adversarial nature of generated positive instances to enhance learning for the majority class. Experimental results from various real-world datasets show significant improvements when our algorithm is applied, resulting in increased F1-mmeasure and Bayesian logistic regression performance compared to the pre-trained classifier. Our findings indicate that the generated adversarial samples do not hinder, but rather advance the majority class performance by pushing its boundary away from the induced minority class points, a novel observation supported by our analysis. Moreover, the generated samples demonstrate qualitative and semantic similarity to real instances. Our proposed algorithm, which integrates generative Adversarial Networks with the proposed balancing strategy, presents an innovative solution to the problem of learning from imbalanced data. All necessary code and generative model architecture can be found on the GitHub repository 'ABalancer,' available for reproduction of the paper's results. Furthermore, this approach can be potentially extended to multiclass imbalance problems. A future plan is to investigate its applicability to datasets with multi-modal and temporal imbalances. This research investigates the formation and instability of shocks in two-dimensional isentropic magnetohydrodynamics. We demonstrate a contraction criterion for intermediate shocks, showing that a specific type of shock, initially considered to be an oblique shock, becomes unstable under a wide range of parameters, ultimately transforming into a different type of shock. Numerical simulations reveal that when the initial perturbation grows, it leads to a consistent change in the angle of the shock, contradicting an earlier theory. To expand knowledge on shock instability, we examine a broader range of ideal MHD solutions than previously studied, including rarefied magnetic fields and monopole solutions. We propose a new framework for understanding and classifying these solutions, as well as investigating the stability of rarefied magnetic fields and monopole solutions under perturbations. Monopole solutions are shown to be unstable under certain conditions and can change configuration by emitting 'neck-like' structures. We quantify the conditions for stability and instability using a specific measure for the geometry of the MHD solution, showing that when this measure decreases, the solution becomes unstable. By combining these conditions with the properties of the initial configuration, we demonstrate that when the initial configuration is stable under a certain type of perturbation, it remains stable in the sense of MHD, and when the initial configuration is unstable, it becomes unstable in the sense of MHD. This research reveals a new type of shock solution, characterized by a specific behavior, and shows that when the magnetic field is almost the same direction, it becomes unstable under certain conditions, consistent with the observed phenomenon in nature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when the shock is stable in three-dimensional space, it becomes unstable in two-dimensional space, and when the shock is stable in two-dimensional space, it becomes unstable in three-dimensional space. This research provides a new understanding of the properties of MHD shock solutions, as well as highlighting the limitations of existing theories. Our research tackles the challenge of perpetual view generation, which involves creating an unlimited number of views from a single image, while maintaining a consistent understanding of the scene. Traditional generative adversarial networks have been leveraged for this task, but they often rely on inaccurate depth maps and focus on generating realistic images without considering the underlying scene structure. To address this issue, we introduce the Single View Depth Generation for Perpetual View Generation (SV-DPG) task and propose a new two-stage approach. Firstly, we develop a Depth Generation Network (DGN) that generates accurate depth maps for images. Subsequently, we utilize these depth maps to produce multiple views through Volume Rendering, while our Volume Rendering Network (VNN) is optimized to render more angular views to mitigate the limitations of a trilinear interpolation-based volume renderer. Experimental results show that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Historical document analysis is a field that combines computational methods and human domain expertise to analyze and understand documents from the past. To address this challenge, this study provides an in-depth examination of the methodological underpinnings of selecting and using digital resources for historical document analysis. Ultimately, this work aims to inform the methodological development and design of computational resources and tools that can effectively facilitate qualitative text analysis using advanced computational models. A novel class of optical nanoantennas is proposed by combining nano-cavities and gradient-index (GRIN) flat disordered materials. By confining light within a two-dimensional "thin" layer, these devices offer unique properties compared to traditional thick GRIN materials, including the ability to keep diffractive effects at a minimum while still manipulating electromagnetic degrees of freedom. Furthermore, theoretical calculations reveal that resonances within these nanoantennas can be independently tuned through changes to the material's refractive index or geometric dimensions. Notably, these devices can efficiently couple incident light to localized points, providing potential applications for single-photon emitters, including the enhancement of solid-state quantum bits using superconducting circuits, as illustrated in a model system featuring a single quantum dot coupled to a GRIN-based nanoantenna and a superconducting resonator, resulting in highly non-classical photon emission. Lastly, these nanoantennas can also facilitate the collimation of light within thick GRIN materials by confining incident radiation within a compact volume and redirecting it into a narrow beam, as demonstrated in a model system featuring a GRIN-based nanoantenna in contact with a flat GRIN material. One critical challenge in stochastic optimization methods involves minimizing communication cost. To optimize communication efficiency, this research focuses on adjusting the size of data batches without compromising the method's performance. We designed Bierk, an automatic approach that dynamically adjusts batch sizes based on current estimates of data variance. By doing so, Bierk enables average-case convergence rates comparable to fully informed methods, all while achieving significant potential improvements in average communication cost reductions of up to 90%. Our experiments with stochastic convex optimization problems showed that Bierk successfully identified optimal batch sizes, which we found to be in the range of 1 to n data points. Moreover, Bierk, when compared to existing methods, demonstrated improved convergence rates and a 3.3 times faster training time on stochastic binary classification problems. The quality of training data has a significant impact on the accuracy of machine learning models used for driving assessment. This study suggests that human expert input can enhance the evaluation of driver behaviors by accounting for external driving conditions. A driving performance assessment model is introduced, which incorporates a scoring system based on human expert criteria. This model considers factors like speed, lane position, and acceleration, giving greater weight to specific characteristics as agreed upon by experts. Moreover, the model's versatility allows it to incorporate additional proprietary driving data not limited to standard sensor inputs. To determine the effectiveness of the model, a comparison is made between the model's scores and those given by human experts for both manual and automatic driving tasks. The results indicate that the model performs similarly to human assessments in evaluating manual driving, but shows greater distinction in evaluating automatic driving, giving higher scores that better reflect the behavior of skilled drivers. The study also finds that the model's scores are more consistent than those of human experts. Overall, the study supports the use of machine learning models for driving performance assessment, especially when combined with human expert input and specialized driving data. It also highlights the potential for further improvement of these models by incorporating more driving data, which can come from various sources such as video recordings, GPS data, and personal driving experiences. Finally, the study suggests that the model's expert-driven scoring system could be used as a framework for teaching drivers about their safety performance and improving their driving skills. Automatic Scene Text Recognition (ASTR) has made significant progress in recent years. The main challenge now lies in handling Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) words that are under-represented in existing training datasets and wild image variations. To tackle this problem, a novel learning strategy called ASTR-OOV is developed to improve model robustness for OOV words by generating synthetic images based on their word boundaries extracted from unlabeled datasets. The proposed strategy consists of three key components: a word boundary detection algorithm, a text token generator, and a domain discriminator. The strategy is implemented through the following steps: (1) word boundary detection in unlabeled datasets; (2) text token generation in the image domain using the detected boundaries; (3) text token learning in the feature domain using a domain discriminator to enhance model robustness. The proposed ASTR-OOV strategy can be integrated with any ASTR model as a new training task to improve model robustness for OOV words. The strategy is evaluated on multiple benchmarks and shows notable improvements in robustness and OOV accuracy for popular ASTR models. The source code of ASTR-OOV is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChengchaoAS/ASTR-OOV. This research expands upon the ideas introduced in [arXiv:2102.02637] by developing a method for assessing the similarity between two random fields observed in distinct operational environments. To address this challenge, we employ a non-parametric Bayesian approach and demonstrate that posterior samples obtained from observing one field can effectively replicate the behavior of the other field, even in environments outside of each other's operational ranges. This correlation is quantified through a statistical measure known as the effective dimension, which enables the comparison of fields operating in various regimes. By utilizing posterior samples from fields observed in multiple regimes, we establish a hierarchical framework for combining statistics and obtain a condensed representation of the diverse observational data. This transformed data can then be analyzed using any suitable statistical method. Consequently, this method facilitates the application of statistical analyses to complex systems characterized by intricate interactions between multiple variables. By way of example, we illustrate our approach by investigating the trends in CO2 concentrations across the various fields, including monthly mean global values, annual averages, and 800,000-year ice core records. Furthermore, we present a novel visualization technique to effectively represent the complex relationships among these fields, enabling a deeper understanding of CO2 laws. This method can be adapted and utilized in various applications across geophysics, encompassing fields such as temperature, sea levels, and ice sheet dynamics. In the case of SL2(Z), L-functions of primitive forms tend to cluster near 1, mirroring the behavior of Spn(Z)'s cuspidal Hecke eigenforms. By setting n = 2, we establish a connection with L-functions of generic degree for GL4(Fp). Utilizing the explicit asymptotics, we devise a novel, efficient algorithm to locate L-function zeros within a specified radius. We also outline the generalization potential of our findings, highlighting the importance of the explicit asymptotics in the L-functions' dynamics. In a separate investigation, inspired by the complex energy landscape of the L-function, we develop a heuristic approach to pinpoint the exact location of an L-function zero within a certain radius, with notable implications for the quantum mechanics-based method proposed by Bourgain, on the polymathemphasized by Michel and Saptharishi. Building upon the principles of quantum mechanics, our method can be applied to various polynomial families, such as irreducible quadratic ones, although a successful case study has been demonstrated with L-functions of Siegel. The failure to extend this method to L-functions of higher rank might be attributed to the inadequacy of current technology in obtaining sharp, explicit estimates for the Fourier coefficients of highly generic forms. As a result, the unexplored link between quantum mechanics and the deep, intricate properties of these L-functions remains an intriguing area of study. By applying the Sato-Tate conjecture, we gain insight into the distribution of zeros near the critical exponent of Hecke L-functions. Combining this with recent results on the distribution of zeros far from the critical exponent, we establish a complete, local understanding of zeros across the entire spectrum, bridging the former's continuous nature near 1 and the latter's complex behavior at higher radii. The new findings address a question posed by Michel and Saptharishi and have significant implications for the problem of generic and strict absolute algebraic case, a problem considered to be one of the most challenging in the field. By generalizing our local results to large families of L-functions, we establish a new, global perspective, one that is polymathemphasized by Michel and Saptharishi. We investigate an irregular network of spin-1/2 systems connected to a central qubit or cavity, with each central element being part of a driven harmonic field. The time-evolution of entanglement in this system is examined using the concurrence as a metric, with the findings being compared to a similar system consisting of identical cavities. It's observed that as driving strength increases, the concurrence in the qubit-based system oscillates over time, whereas it exhibits damped oscillations when coupled to a cavity. Conversely, the concurrence-based time-evolution in both systems shows a shift towards the central element as the disorder within the peripheral elements is amplified. Furthermore, the results reveal enhanced entanglement in the qubit-based system when compared to the cavity-based system, with the driving field's role being pivotal in these outcomes. Lastly, the concurrence's dependence on driving frequency in both systems is explored, with the findings indicating an opportunity for adjusting the entanglement's sign and fundamental level, with potential implications for controlling quantum coherences and their associated photon emissions. The COVID-19 pandemic was a once-in-a-century global event that drastically altered daily life, resulting in widespread economic, social, and emotional impacts. This research examines how the pandemic's effects influenced the diversity of urban encounters and community resilience in the long term, employing a mixed-methods approach combining large datasets and qualitative interviews with urban dwellers. Our investigation, set in New York City, reveals a complex and still unfolding narrative of change. While the pandemic temporarily boosted diverse encounters through increased delivery and other remote interactions, we found that in-person encounters significantly declined. Furthermore, we discovered that community resilience was intensified by the pandemic's initial stages but later waned. Our study's findings contribute to a broader understanding of the pandemic's long-term consequences and inform strategies to increase diverse encounters and community resilience in the post-pandemic era. Our research highlights the value of incorporating participants' voices and perspectives into investigations of urban resilience and crisis recovery. Ultimately, we argue that inclusive policies and strategies are necessary to foster diverse encounters and strengthen community resilience in urban settings. By sharing our research through an open-access pre-print and presenting our findings at various conferences, we aim to stimulate further discussion and collaboration on this important topic. When interacting with a robot, people's interactions can be affected if they learn the task-specific preferences the robot uses to map its input to output. To understand the impact, we studied users' performance with and without knowledge of a robot's chosen mappings for a picking-up task. The results showed, contrary to expectations, that knowing the robot's mapping didn't improve interactions efficiency. Furthermore, we found that knowing the robot's mapping actually made users more reliant on guessing and less effective. Consequently, we recommend that researchers avoid sharing task-specific input mappings with users. This knowledge might seem essential for collaborations, but its disclosure could actually hinder interactions. This research contributes to the understanding of the requirements for effective human-robot collaboration. It defines the boundaries of what is feasible in robot-assisted tasks and helps designers avoid unnecessary disclosures that might reduce the interaction efficiency. but we recognize that these single images cannot effectively convey the 
entire scope of a study's results, particularly when those results change over time.
Our goal is to develop integrated visualization tools that seamlessly connect 
discrete static images to dynamic temporal plots and other related data

images, data, and temporal plots. To address this challenge, we have designed 
the Image Annotator, a web-based platform that enables researchers to create, 
edit, and interlink image annotations with both static and dynamic plots.

industrial settings, thereby underscoring its potential in enhancing research 
visualization processes. Furthermore, we have conducted experiments and gathered 
feedback from users, demonstrating that our image annotator can enhance 
researchers' ability to link image-based findings with external data sources.

In the realm of Electronic Health Records, graph-based models excel at capturing complex relationships between patients, treatments, and outcomes. However, these models are often limited by their reliance on homogeneous node and edge representations. When dealing with imbalanced data, where some patient outcomes are more frequently recorded than others, these models can struggle. Moreover, the success of these models heavily depends on the quality of the learned graph structure. Although simple in concept, these models are complex in practice, and their effectiveness is often compromised by the propagation of labels between connected nodes. 

Our proposed HET-EHR models address these limitations by adopting edge-type aware representations for both patients and treatments. To counter the problem of label leakage during training, we employ a combination of techniques such as label smoothing, edge loss, and sample weighting. These mechanisms work in tandem to create a well-structured graph that accurately predicts patient outcomes. 

Our approach has several benefits over existing methods. First, the incorporation of edge-type aware representations enables more nuanced node embeddings. Second, the sample weighting strategy improves the model's robustness in handling imbalanced data. Third, the edge loss term enhances the model's ability to learn the correct graph structure. Our model's efficacy is demonstrated through its ability to outperform state-of-the-art methods on real-world EHR datasets. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Chengjing1/HET-EHR.

These findings underscore the importance of including domain-specific edge information in heterogeneous graph neural networks.

This approach involves representing the electrolyte as a mixture of two non-interdependent components, one neutralized by the other, allowing us to simplify the system's complexity. The charged component is characterized by a fixed self-interaction, adapting self-consistently to the charged surface's potential, charge density, and neighboring counter-ion distribution. The study shows that as the size of the counter ions increases, the electrolyte properties nearby display a more pronounced response. This method successfully recovers known outcomes for monovalent ions and reveals substantial deviations from Poisson-Boltz theory, particularly in the high-valency regime, even at elevated salt concentrations. Notably, the charged component's self-interaction plays a pivotal role in generating these outcomes. This method's consistency with simulation data is satisfied, yielding novel insights into previously unexplored parameter spaces. Lastly, a thorough investigation is performed to assess the approach's mean-field validity. This study offers a versatile and general method for describing electrolyte systems adapting to a wide array of surface charge patterns. It also generates considerable interest in exploring its connection to the underlying many-body interactions. Further, this work has the potential to significantly improve modeling and prediction accuracy across a broad range of geometries, lengths scales, and surface charge strengths, contributing to the field of electrolyte theory. The presence of spin-orbit coupling significantly affects YSR state peaks in the presence of magnetic adatoms or dimers, causing the peaks to shift in response to increasing coupling strength. For a dimer composed of adatoms with opposing spins, the spin-orbit induced shift in one peak is proportional to the square of the coupling strength, while the peak's width remains constant. Analyzing the density of states on a honeycomb lattice reveals that, in the strong coupling limit, the shifted ferromagnetic dimer peak aligns with a particular point on the disorder-induced density of states spectrum. This alignment occurs at a critical coupling strength where the primary fermionic eigenstates become delocalized, and the corresponding eigenvalues fall within the gap. For adatoms with aligned spins, the shifted peaks remain distinct, however their width is observed to increase as the critical coupling strength is approached from below. In contrast, both types of dimers exhibit a uniform peak broadening in the presence of intermediate coupling strengths. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the interactions between YSR states and their relationship with magnetic adatoms or ferromagnetic dimers in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling. It serves as a foundation for future research into the properties of quantum magnetic correlations and their responses to coupling strengths. Furthermore, these findings offer valuable insights into the observation of quantum magnetic correlations in recent and future experiments on $sp$-element 2D monolayers. The study's findings have been made available in detail through the inclusion of an interactive Jupyter notebook that outlines the methods and parameters used in the research. This interactive notebook can be accessed at http://github.com/soo-iqbal/ysr-states-with-soc. A broader understanding of the topic can be found at http://github.com/soo-iqbal/bulletin-board. By providing these resources, the study aims to facilitate a deeper and more nuanced comprehension of the complex interactions between YSR states and their relationship with magnetic adatoms or ferromagnetic dimers in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling. The results from analyzing decay data of charged kaons in the energy range of 15 to 100 GeV are presented. An analysis of these decays revealed no evidence for the presence of a signal. Based on an analysis of an enormous dataset, upper bounds were established for several decay modes, including the following key findings: 
- The presence of a signal in the $K^+\rightarrow\pi^+\nu\bar{\nu}$ decay is limited by a probability of less than 0.75 x 10^-10.
- The presence of a signal in the $K^+\rightarrow\pi^{\pm}\ell^{\pm}\ell^{\pm}\ell^{\pm}\nu$ decay is limited by a probability of less than 2.2 x 10^-8 for each decay type.
- The presence of a signal in the $K^+\rightarrow\pi^+\ell^+\ell^- $ decay, where the particles are charged, is limited by a probability of less than 6.0 x 10^-9. 
These findings represent a significant improvement over the previous best estimates, with the exception of the $K^+\rightarrow\pi^+\mu^+\mu^- $ decay, where the improvement was previously reported. An analysis of the $\pi^+\rightarrow\pi^- e^+e^- $ and $\pi^-\rightarrow\pi^+\nu\bar{\nu}$ decays also found that the signal was consistent with zero. An improved bound for the former decay of 1.4 x 10^-7 was established while the latter was consistent with zero. An analysis of these findings will have far-reaching implications for understanding the occurrence of other rare decays in the context of the Standard Model of particle physics. These research findings will be crucial in informing future research on the use of hadron accelerators in searching for new physics.

This research explores the use of downsampled point clouds for registering LIDAR data across consecutive scans, particularly in dynamic urban settings. By drastically reducing the time complexity associated with registration, this approach can effectively process high-resolution point clouds in real-time. We examine the effects of downsampling on the precision and accuracy of registration, focusing on both static and dynamic environments, and investigating the optimal balance between processing speed and accuracy. The outcomes suggest that downsampled point clouds maintain a high level of precision while still enabling accurate pose estimates. Moreover, the study reveals that the technique is particularly well-suited for addressing dynamic challenges, as it is largely unaffected by changes in dynamic objects between scans. The results further show that the precision of downsampled point clouds converges with increasing scan pairs' overlap, thus offering a reliable method for dynamic registration evaluation. Ultimately, the approach is recommended for applications requiring high-speed, accurate pose estimates from dense dynamic scenes. The associated code can be accessed at: https://github.com/KeylT/Downsampled registration. Moreover, the results have been made publicly available at: https://github.com/KeylT/Downsampled dynamic registration evaluation. This research received funding from the Swiss Data Science Initiative (SDSI). Additionally, the research was carried out within the context of the Autonomous Mobile Robot (AMRO) network. Furthermore, the research utilized the open-source openDrive dataset, which was annotated by the researchers. The researchers have also contributed to the openModular simulation environment. Finally, the research was supported by the Max Planck Society.

Satellite imagery is a valuable tool for understanding current environmental conditions and predicting future changes. The rise of crowdsourcing and volunteer-based satellite image classification initiatives has significantly expanded the scope of these studies, albeit at the cost of increased dataset complexity. Recently, a surge of interest in deep learning from computer vision and machine learning communities has led to the development of more accurate and efficient classification techniques. Nevertheless, the large size of high-resolution satellite images and their varied structures present substantial challenges to their successful classification. To overcome these challenges, a multi-scale partition-based convolutional neural network has been proposed, combining saliency-driven attention and saliency-guided class-weighted loss functions to enhance classification performance. The results of classifying saliency areas with saliency-guided class-weighted loss outperform the existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the classification outcomes of this approach are accompanied by saliency maps that reveal the network's confidence levels, offering actionable insights for dataset refinement and improvement. The dataset, known as WISAT-Crowd, and the associated code have been made available to the public to facilitate future research. The proposed approach achieves A5 micro-F1 scores of 74.38\% and 69.53% on saliety and crowd references, respectively. The classification outcomes of this approach are comparable to current state-of-the-art methods, with saliency-guided performance outperforming saliety references. The proposed approach, however, falls short of saliety references in crowd references classification. The proposed approach, multi-scale partition-based attention and saliency-guided class-weighted loss, is found to be robust to the scale of partition. Adversarial attacks on Deep Neural Network-based systems have raised significant concerns in various applications. To counter this issue, researchers have proposed several defense mechanisms, although they often come with performance compromises. This paper investigates the efficacy of Adversarial Defenses against Generative Adversarial Networks in the context of image classification tasks using the ResNet architecture. It demonstrates how GANs can be utilized to protect systems from attacks by generating countermeasures in the form of adversarial patches, thereby neutralizing the impact of malicious inputs. Experimental evaluations, utilizing the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets under multiple attack scenarios, showcase the resilience of GAN-protected models against adversarial threats. Notably, GAN-based defenses result in negligible loss in clean data accuracy and a substantial improvement in accuracy against various attack types, with up to a 90% reduction in error rates compared to a strong adversarial attacker. These results confirm the potential of GAN-based defenses as a promising solution for enhancing the robustness of DNN-based systems against adversarial attacks. All the experimental code and data are publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/asharakeh/AdversarialDefensesGAN. This study contributes to the research community by providing a thorough analysis of the efficacy of GAN-based defenses, thereby promoting further exploration into their potential as robust countermeasures. Moreover, based on our findings, we propose an advanced research challenge aimed at developing more resilient GAN-based systems against adversarial attacks. This challenge, known as the GAN-based Defenses against Adversarial Attacks challenge, can be accessed at https://www.asgarakeh.top/GANChallenge. A paper presenting the full details of this challenge is available at arXiv:2206.11591. Additionally, a video summary of this work has been uploaded to YouTube at https://youtube.com/c/asharakeh. Through experiments with both classification and clustering tasks, we assess the impact of incorporating various forms of domain knowledge, such as feature definitions and decision tree structures. Notably, these improvements in performance are linked to the model's ability to mirror the provided domain knowledge. We also discuss practical considerations and challenges related to implementing hybrid models in real-world settings. Lastly, we outline future research avenues to further explore the utility of hybrid models.
