Researchers in computer vision and natural language processing have made significant strides in developing networks that directly produce an image's semantic description, as well as those that focus on the intermediate representations' characteristics. Meanwhile, the underlying convolutional neural networks' visual features mappings remain largely unexplored. Our goal is to identify the relationships between these intermediate representations and their corresponding class descriptions using these visual features. To this end, we have developed the LaViSE model, which employs a transformer-based encoder to capture the structural patterns of LaVIE representations, and a subsequent decoder to generate class descriptions based on these captured features. Through our experiments, we have shown the effectiveness of LaViSE in multiple scenarios, and highlighted its value as an analysis tool for delving into the inner workings of convolutional neural networks. Our code and datasets are available on the LaViSE GitHub repository at https://github.com/AdityaCrato/LaViSE. Additionally, we have included a LaViSE-based evaluation of the backprop through the lens of natural language processing study, and our findings can be found at https://adityacrocrato.github.io/LaViSE_BPTLNP. Our paper is organized as follows: Section II covers the related work, Section III introduces LaViSE, and is divided into three sub-sections: (i) the feature encoder, (ii) the class description embedding, and (iii) the description generator. Section IV presents our empirical results, and Section V concludes the paper and outlines future directions. The remaining content can be viewed at https://doi.org/10.1109/TNNLS.2022.9981029. Another factor influencing decision-making is the frequency and flexibility of visit scheduling, which can impact patients' actual visit decisions. This has the consequence that, given certain conditions, every method converges to a Nash equilibrium in multi-player games where the objective functions are prox-regular. To illustrate this, we demonstrate that Bregman prox-methods always converge to a Nash equilibrium under suitable conditions. These results are particularly relevant in the context of variational inequality problems involving non-smooth, monotone functions. Furthermore, for non-prox-regular mappings, we develop a criterion ensuring that, under certain assumptions, its fixed points correspond to equilibria of related equilibrium problems. This criterion is then applied to non-prox-regular monotone composite mappings, yielding a novel characterization of their fixed points in terms of Nash equilibria of multi-player equilibrium problems. This work showcases the utility of regularity properties in dynamics for Nash equilibrium problems. To establish these results, we draw upon key tools from our previous research, as well as recent findings in our papers. The limitations of deep learning predictive models can be quantified by using Bayesian methods to assess uncertainty. However, most approaches thus far have focused on the predictive predictive predictive predictive distribution without considering the uncertainty of the predictive function itself. We present a novel non-asymptotic bound for the posterior predictive distribution that is based on the uncertainty of the predictive function. We derive this bound by using McAllester's complexity measure and apply it to binary classification and density estimation. Our results show that, unlike existing methods, this bound accurately reflects the uncertainty of the predictive function when applied to new data. We support this with empirical evidence and show that this bound can be used to quantify model selection uncertainty. Furthermore, by using the posterior predictive distribution with the constraint of the bounded uncertainty of the predictive function, we develop a novel post-processing technique for binary classification and density estimation tasks. We found that this technique, which we call predictive function regularization, enhances the accuracy of predictive uncertainty and improves predictive performance by approximately 16% and 23% for binary classification and density estimation, respectively, when evaluated on various unsupervised and supervised datasets. Recently, the combination of a dense retrieval model and a sequence generation transformer, known as Retrieval Augment Generation (RAG), has been developed and made public by Google, leading to a range of applications. In this paper, we explore the potential of RAG as a versatile platform for open-source adaptive machine learning. In our study, we address several key challenges in fine-tuning RAG models, including model size and complexity, limited training data, and the scarcity of annotated examples. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a step-by-step approach to fine-tuning RAG models and present three innovative applications: (i) extracting key information from complex documents, (ii) generating informative articles based on given data, and (iii) identifying the primary piece of information within a document. In each of these domains, we compare the performance of RAG with that of a BERT model and observe that RAG surpasses BERT in several benchmark tests. In addition to our empirical evaluations, we present two real-world applications where the RAG model is used to automatically gather data: (i) detecting when the knowledge transfer from RAG to the task of interest has been sufficient, and (ii) determining whether it is worthwhile to continue fine-tuning RAG models based on their current level of performance. These supplementary results reveal that RAG is well-suited to the domain of adaptive machine learning in contrast to the commonly used BERT model. Text-video retrieval has received significant attention in recent years, with a growing number of studies aiming to enhance general video representations through specialized models for specific queries. However, existing approaches still fall short in expectations due to their limited generalization capabilities and reliance on handcrafted features. This paper proposes TS2-Net, a learning method for video representations that utilizes self-supervised learning based on temporal contrastive learning. By incorporating temporal information into the framework, TS2-Net addresses information loss in text-video retrieval and enables the learning of general video representations through two key components. The framework consists of a video-caption matching branch and a video similarity mining branch. The video-caption matching branch involves predicting video and caption pairs using noise-perturbed short-term memory, while the video-similarity mining branch involves predicting video similarity using a transformer encoder with a similar architecture to BERT. This allows TS2-Net to learn a robust and general video representation that outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Experimental results demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves superior performance on several text-video retrieval datasets, including Activity, VGG, Kinetics, ActivityNet, and YTC, outperforming top methods by 6.8%, 6.3%, 4.8%, 9.0%, and 9.2% respectively. This counter-intuitive phenomenon could have significant implications for the development of reliable high-dimensional AI-based classification systems. By applying these "linear classifiers" as post-training regularization methods, designers may be able to prevent accuracy degradation when deploying these systems. Furthermore, this concept could also facilitate the accurate analysis of AI system failures in complex classification tasks. This research may also inspire the development of novel machine learning architectures that effectively correct errors in high-dimensional spaces. Finally, our findings could also lead to the creation of noise-free surrogate models that aid in the development of robust AI-based classification systems. Designing muon colliders requires the large-scale production of muons, which inevitably experience decays while in flight during the muon storage and cooling stages. Muons that reach detector sites will undergo in-flight decay before being measured, significantly reducing the detector's effective sensitivity due to the loss of momentum and energy. This limitation can be mitigated through the implementation of specific detector designs featuring multiple, closely spaced centers or dense detector components with minimal material. In a muon collider, the likelihood of in-flight decays is particularly concerning during the muon distribution stage but can also be a concern during the muon compression stage. This study provides a comprehensive mathematical model of in-flight decay loss and proposes tailored detector designs to minimize this loss, focusing on specific muon collider configurations such as a 10 GeV muon collider with a single detector and a 20 GeV muon collider with twin detectors, both of which require a muon storage ring for efficient injection, accumulation, and focusing. In the first configuration, in-flight decay loss can be reduced from 55% to 20% through a specially designed detector featuring a muon collider-specific layout featuring rounded edges and a muon-target distance of 20 meters, which would feature a target radius of 15.5 meters and a muon beam spot size of 0.2-0.4 mm. In the second configuration, in-flight decay loss can be reduced from 65% to 25% through a specially designed detector featuring a muon collider-specific layout featuring a targeted location at the center of a dual-collider setup with a 32.5 meter distance, which would feature a target radius of 16.25 meters and a muon beam spot size of 0.6-0.8 mm. These optimized designs feature a dense focusing system consisting of a heavy liquid target surrounded by sensitive materials, which effectively transfers momentum to the target through a focused muon beam, resulting in minimal target material density and thus minimal additional decay loss. This novel design concept significantly minimizes in-flight decay loss and holds great potential for improving the overall efficiency of muon colliders. Although research has identified several types of test smells, there is a lack of understanding about how developers perceive their severity and the impact they have on the maintainability of test code. To investigate this, we conducted a survey of developers involved in maintaining open-source projects, asking them about the severity of test smells and how they affect test code. The results showed that developers consider test smells to be less severe than system failures and that they believe test smells negatively affect project maintainability. Additionally, we found that developers have different opinions on how to prioritize and fix test smells, with some viewing them as minor issues that do not require immediate attention. Our study suggests that developers need guidance on how to identify and fix critical test smells. Based on these findings, we propose new research directions that focus on developing practical guidelines for identifying and fixing critical test smells. Furthermore, we suggest exploring the effectiveness of introducing practical guidelines to developers through continuous integration systems. By targeting critical test smells, we can improve the quality of test code and reduce the maintenance costs associated with test code. A practical guide that helps developers identify and fix critical test smells can facilitate the hard task of maintaining large test repositories. By integrating this guidance through continuous integration systems, we can make the learning process easier for developers and provide them with cost-effective solutions for improving test code quality. A secondary goal of this research is to investigate the impact of introducing practical guidelines on the evolution of test smells in actual project contexts. The new research directions are: (i) Investigating the effectiveness of introducing practical guidelines on the evolution of test smells in actual project contexts, (ii) Targeting critical test smells that developers consider to be severe enough to warrant immediate attention, (iii) Introducing the practical guidelines through continuous integration systems to facilitate the learning process and reduce the implementation costs, (iv) Developing cost-effective solutions for improving test code quality, and (iv) Facilitating the hard task of maintaining large test repositories. A total of 429 developers participated in the study and provided valuable insights that can inform the design of new methods to identify and fix critical test smells. The study collected novel metrics that can be used to investigate the impact of introducing the practical guidelines on the evolution of test smells in actual project contexts. The data collected can be accessed at: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2022.111203. A newly upgraded version of the $K\overline K$ production Monte Carlo algorithm, known as $K\overline K$MC, has been developed. This upgraded version, called $K\overline K$MCee, includes the ability to accurately simulate the production of pairs of electron-antilepton and muon-antilepton by incorporating the latest high-precision data from the $K\overline K$ mass book. Compared to its predecessor, $K\overline K$MCee offers a significant $10$ to $100$ times speed increase due to its use of the $io$ library. This version also accounts for the effects of pair production in the final state and includes a new phase space parametrization that has improved the program's overall accuracy. In order to validate the accuracy of $K\overbar K$MCee, a detailed comparison was made between its predicted and actual $K\overbar K$ transverse momentum spectra. It was also used in precise predictions for the LHC's $\Delta \alpha_{\rm had}$, a quantity that was predicted with a precision of $0.00037\times(78{\rm TeV}/m_{W})^2$. In addition, a detailed analysis was made of the LHCb experiment's sensitivity to the $K\overbar \mu$ mass difference, yielding a precision of $0.074$ meV/c$^2$. In particle physics research, a newly proposed method for precision studies of the $g-2_{\mu}$ is suggested, which relies on the $\mu^+\mu^-$ production process in the $LHC$. It was predicted that the $LHC$ could achieve a precision of $0.050$ times $10^{-10}$ in its measurement of the $\mu^+$ and $\mu^0$ masses. In the area of precision hadron physics, a newly proposed method for precision studies of the $e^-e^-$ production process is suggested, which relies on the $e^-e^-$ production process in the $LHC$. It was predicted that the $e^-e^-$ production rate would be $1.3\times 10^{12}$ times $10^{-8}$ per year. In the area of precision lepton studies, a newly proposed method for precision studies of the $\tau$-lepton production process is suggested, which relies on the $\tau$-lepton production process in the $LHC$.

Real-world graphs are often dynamic, with nodes and edges that appear, disappear, and form new connections over time. While static graph deep learning has made significant progress, the research on dynamic graph learning is still in its early stages. A major obstacle is the lack of suitable graph representation that captures both the structural characteristics and the temporal changes effectively. This work proposes an innovative method of transforming sequential edge data into a consistent, fixed-dimensional format by representing it as a series of vectors and determining the optimal number of vectors through an attention mechanism. We present two variants of this method, called Edge4Seq and Edge4Seqat, which differ in their handling of the attention mechanism's output. Edge4Seqat further improves the format of the transformed edge data by using an attention mechanism to determine the optimal subsequence length for each edge. We evaluated the Edge4Seq and Edge4Seqat methods on unsupervised and semi-supervised node classification tasks, and the results demonstrate their superiority over existing techniques. Moreover, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the proposed methods to gain a deeper understanding of their performance. Deep learning techniques have significantly improved image recognition from various perspectives. In the field of computer vision, a conventional approach to camera calibration involves minimizing the re-projection error. This method, although widely used, has its limitations. Notably, the error function may have non-linear relationships with some calibration parameters, and the error measure can be ambiguous across different datasets. To address these issues, we propose a direct regression approach that eliminates the need for a specific loss function. We train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict all 66 pose parameters of a standard matrix simultaneously. The results show that our method compares favorably to established techniques when evaluated using the eigen decomposition quality metric. We further conduct an in-depth analysis of the direct regression method and discuss its potential applications in the field of camera calibration. In many real-world reinforcement learning tasks, direct rewards are scarce and infrequent, making it necessary to avoid actions that might result in adverse consequences. To tackle such tasks, an agent can learn the rules that govern its environment by discovering the underlying constraints that dictate its actions. This research delves into the possibilities of incorporating the constraints learned by a constraint-abiding agent into a separate agent that seeks to optimize its performance. We examine both cases where the constraint agent is optimized for constraints and those where it is optimized for a combination of constraints and rewards. To achieve this, we propose a novel training framework that enables the coordination and simultaneous learning of the constraint agent and the optimization agent. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach allows the constraint agent to adapt its constraints over time, resulting in more effective and efficient performance. Our results are illustrated through experiments in complex environments that require the avoidance of suboptimal states. Subsequently, we evaluate the key properties of our constraint framework using a simplified symbolic grid-world scenario. This research offers significant contributions to the field of constraint-based reinforcement learning, highlighting the practical value of our approach in various applications. To facilitate replication and ease access to our research, we have developed an open-source constraint-based reinforcement learning framework that incorporates the key components and can be utilized in future studies. This framework is available online. To verify the feasibility of our approach, we have conducted a comprehensive empirical analysis that covers the learning capacity of our constraint-based agent in a simplified symbolic grid-world scenario, the adaptability of the constraints learned by our approach, and the performance benefits of our method in complex environments. Our findings corroborate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. Moreover, we have performed an in-depth ablation study that assesses the impact of our method on reinforcement learning by comparing its performance with that of state-of-the-art constraint-based methods. Our results indicate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in several key aspects. To facilitate the understanding and replication of our research, we have presented a step-by-step explanation of our method based on a simplified symbolic grid-world scenario and provided publicly accessible implementation details. Our code is available online. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of our findings, we have conducted a comprehensive series of experiments that cover various complex and challenging tasks. Our results demonstrate the superiority of our method in several key aspects. A persistent issue in analyzing a node's clustering behavior involves defining a continuous clustering coefficient that can be applied to large-scale networks where complete cluster data is not available. In this study, we compare the current continuous clustering coefficient proposed by Zhang and Horvath in 2015 with an alternative metric developed by Fortunato in 2010. We examine the performance of both coefficients under various network scenarios, including the effects of different node connection probabilities and the presence of errors. A new method to compute the Zhang--Horvath clustering coefficient efficiently is also presented, which enables its calculation and comparison with the Fortunato clustering coefficient across a range of random and complex networks. The results indicate that the performance of the two clustering coefficients differs significantly, even for the same type of random networks, and that the Zhang--Horvath clustering tends to be more sensitive to errors and particularistic network structures. The proposed efficient computation method is a valuable addition to the field. Analytical expressions for the expected clustering coefficients are derived for Erdos--Reneyi networks with a constant node connection probability, which helps to validate numerical simulations and real-world network data. The findings highlight the importance of carefully selecting a clustering coefficient that is suitable for a given type of network and data quality. The study also suggests potential applications of the continuous clustering coefficient in analyzing the effects of different node communication probabilities and the impact of errors on this behavior. Finally, the work includes an examination of the continuous clustering coefficient's performance in a specific type of network, the "heterogeneous out-of-range" model, which is characterized by a power-law distribution of nodes' average connection probabilities with a given neighbor. In this type of network, the behavior of the clustering coefficient varies significantly with the exponent governing the power-law distribution, and a method to compute the Zhang--Horvath clustering coefficient efficiently is developed for this specific type of network as well. The results show that the clustering coefficient tends to be more sensitive to errors in cases where the exponent is larger. The study's outcomes offer valuable insights into the performance of different clustering coefficients under various network conditions, which may have far-reaching implications in practical applications. The work's findings are illustrated using real-world network data from the Delis-Katzenelson network and the Facebook social network. The results show that the performance of the clustering coefficient is more pronounced in cases where the network is divided into distinct clusters. Researchers across various fields continuously build and expand their ontology resources, which have evolved into comprehensive data management systems with complex structures. Visual aids, like class diagrams, help to organize and understand these ontologies, although existing tools have limitations in presenting layered relationships and cluster hierarchies. Furthermore, it is crucial to clearly present the hierarchical organization of clusters to allow users to filter and manage ontologies, which has previously been addressed by a few proprietary solutions. The results show that OntoPlot outperforms other tools in terms of visualization features, user engagement, and cognitive load. The study also highlights OntoPlot's capabilities in managing complex data, error tolerance, and visual complexity. Recent research suggests that pre-trained language models are capable of handling a wide range of tasks, and their capabilities can be leveraged for tasks such as essay grading. However, developing an accurate essay-grader requires a massive amount of text data and extensive manual scoring by human evaluators. To overcome this challenge, we created an auto-correcting essay-grader based on the pre-trained Transformer model, BART, which adjusts its performance through the data it processes. Our study compares the performance of fine-tuned models with smaller and larger pre-trained models on three different essay-grading challenges. The results show that a well-designed small pre-trained model outperforms the top-ranked system in the 2020 competition as well as surpasses a more complex pre-trained model. Moreover, we investigated how an external knowledge source, specifically a chemistry-based model, can influence the bias in the essay-grader's assessments and found that the control over bias is a trade-off between model complexity and performance. The research also highlights the potential for the essay-grader to serve as a tool for examining the bias in the models it uses, similar to programs like @BiasEval, which evaluates the bias in models such as BART and BERT. The challenge of distinguishing signal from noise in predictive models can often 
cause learned representations to favor instances with higher instance counts.
To address this issue, we propose a novel method for learning how to effectively 
re-rank predictive outcomes without the need for manual supervision.
By recasting the problem of suppressing false positives as an optimized 
re-ranking task, and further simplifying it as a set of independent binary 
classification issues, we create a highly manageable learning environment.
This approach's key feature is the creation of a primitive representation that 
retains the essential characteristics of the original data, allowing for accurate 
decision-making in the re-ranking process.
Using this method on two public datasets, we show that our framework can 
significantly enhance the accuracy of predictive models and observations.
Most notably, the improved version of the well-known Deep Neural Network 
architectural design achieves a 6.9% increase in top-1 classification precision 
on the ImageNet dataset. 
This elevated performance is achieved without the traditional high computational 
costs associated with this design, as a result of the reduced number of neurons 
required in the final classification layer. 
Furthermore, we observed that the re-ranked model's ability to classify images 
at a higher level of abstraction also facilitates the discovery of more accurate 
semantic relationships between words, as measured by the enhanced precision of 
word-image pairings. 
To validate this finding, we successfully applied our framework to a range 
of diverse tasks, including word and sentence level classifications, 
while achieving positive results. 
We believe that our framework offers a novel approach to addressing 
noise-related challenges in machine learning. 
To the best of our knowledge, the use of noise filtering as a 
set of independent re-ranking tasks has not been explored before.

Typically, this involves adjusting parameters step by step using various fitting methods, such as maximum likelihood fitting. In this work, we explore an alternative approach called adaptive genetic algorithms, which starts by generating a population of many different parameter sets, then gradually evolves these parameters towards a best fit. We discuss the basics of this method and provide examples of its application for analyzing both continuous and discrete data, along with demonstration examples of its use for simulating various types of real-world radiation damage according to the NRT and NRT2 models. Furthermore, we compare the performance of this method with traditional maximum likelihood fitting techniques for fitting normal and skewed distributions. Our results indicate that adaptive genetic algorithms can provide robust results even for complex data distributions, while offering some benefits in terms of flexibility and capability to handle edge cases. As such, this method could be a valuable tool for analyzing data from experiments on radiation damage, particularly in high-energy physics. In addition to discussing the implementation of this method, we also examine some general issues that need to be considered when adjusting parameters, such as proper accounting for measurement uncertainties and accounting for systematic uncertainties when they are present. Finally, we highlight some potential future areas for improvement of this method, including its adaptation to analyze data in high-dimensional spaces and development of more sophisticated algorithms based on machine learning techniques. Overall, our work provides a useful overview of various parameter adjustment methods and serves as a foundation for future advancements in this field. As such, this method could be a valuable tool for analyzing data in various fields of science and engineering. High-frequency wave propagation in domains with small holes is analyzed through the multi-scale method in geometrical optics. Formulations are developed for arbitrary numbers of small scales and various support sizes, yielding improved asymptotic relations for potentials limited to compact support. By utilizing this approach, we can accurately study the behavior of waves in nearly empty domains with complex structures, such as highly porous materials. Numerical schemes are then created for two-scale geometrical optics problems, resulting in efficient and simple to implement methods for computing full-scale solutions. A particular scheme is introduced, which for potentials, involves computing an oscillatory counter-term to obtain the correct full-scale limit from the asymptotics of the sum over small scales. This approach is applicable to general potentials, but for geometrical optics, it requires modifications to account for non-diffraction phenomena. Neural architectures based on the teacher-student framework, specifically including transmutation and mixture mutations, have shown potential in enhancing the robustness and performance of machine learning models through class label transformation and mixing features. However, their potential benefits for audio classification remain unexplored. This study investigates the effectiveness of these mutations as regularization methods in deep neural networks for mislabeling or feature mixing, focusing on the tasks of music emotion recognition and bird species identification. We evaluate and compare the mutations at three levels: as regularizers during model training, as predictions on test data for uncertainty measurement, and as refined models using the predictions as ground truth. The results indicate that transmutations and mixture mutations can improve test accuracy and decrease uncertainty, with mixture mutations being more effective as a regularizer and transmutations performing better in the refined model setting. Ultimately, the study finds that strong teacher-student architectures based on these mutations do not necessarily lead to superior audio classification performance when used alone, but can be a valuable addition to ensemble approaches. The code and model weights for this study are available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/jmvalero/TransmutationMixture.

Despite this, there are ongoing concerns about whether these methods reliably produce consistent results, a question we seek to answer in this study. Our findings indicate that KD consistently outperforms PQ and that high-quality teacher models can significantly improve the distillation process. Moreover, we observed substantial improvements, approximately 21-24%, in the performance of the models when fine-tuned using KL Divergence loss or sequence-level categorical cross-entropy, two optimization methods we experimented with. Finally, the top-performing models we developed achieved an accuracy of 85.68, a significant improvement over the 73.47 achieved by the best model in XLSUM at CoNLL 2020. We take this research further by proving a more general version that allows the density of the binomial expansion to be defined by expressions with positive summands. We also prove a similar result for infinite binomial expressions that are defined by positive sums. These findings provide strong counterexamples to previous conjectures regarding Turán numbers of specific graph structures. We also discuss the limitations of our work, pointing out gaps in current theoretical knowledge. Furthermore, we address a possible 'finite version' of a previously established result from Erdős and Gallai by proving that complete $r$-partite graphs with four distinct parts are among the structures that achieve the original density of the binomial expression. We achieve this by translating the problem into a more manageable form and applying graph embedding techniques, such as edge-colouring and list-coloring. We further generalise these results to $r$-partite graphs with an arbitrary number of parts by applying similar graph embedding techniques, such as edge-colouring, list-coloring and Hall-type theorems. We also find that for graphs with specific degree properties, we can find $r$-uniform subgraphs that have the same density as the original binomial expression. Secondly, we utilized a task-specific pre-training approach, prompt learning reconstruction, to leverage the extensive labeled data in image datasets. Our experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of our methods, as they significantly improved the performance of PPLM on image captioning datasets and other tasks, such as visual question answering and zero-shot object detection. Causal thinking lies at the core of how humans evaluate action consequences, a concept
research has been actively exploring in recent AI developments. Notably, prior approaches
focusing on causal prediction often overlooked the subjective nature of human decision
making, specifically how humans assess harm. In contrast, we introduce a novel framework
that captures a person's point of view when evaluating negative outcomes. Using this
perspective, we show that measuring harm involves comparing an individual's well-being
before and after an experience, and that contrastive causation, a key aspect of causal
thinking, contributes to different types of harmful effects. Through applications and
analyses, we highlight the significance of understanding the diverse range of adverse
outcomes and focusing on the victim's utility when assessing harm. This work paves the
way for further studies on cause-and-effect thinking in the context of victim-centered
evaluation, a crucial step in developing responsible AI technologies. As such, our work
envisions these theories to inform the next generation of AI systems that integrate
causal reasoning and empathy. Ultimately, our research aims to foster a deeper
appreciation for the intricate nature of human causal thinking and assessment of
adverse consequences. A publicly accessible implementation of our model can be found
at https://github.com/atchekhova/cause- harm.

These equations generalize the standard Fourier heat conduction equation, with the non-linear relationship between heat flux and temperature motivated by thermoviscous action. We draw on principles from non-linear solid mechanics to explore the well-posedness of initial-boundary value problems for these equations, and our analysis focuses on specific equation types derived from the Maxwell-Cawley, Mindlin-Eringen, and Green-Lindsay models. By applying energy inequalities and the Lax-Milgram theorem to demonstrate uniqueness and stability, the existence of weak solutions is confirmed. Furthermore, as the Maxwell-Cawley model corresponds to the Leslie equations in liquid crystals, our findings also apply to the latter. Unlike traditional heat conduction equations, the models we study lack maximum principles, so an alternative approach is employed to obtain the desired solutions. This work differs from previous studies, which either relied on regularity of the temperature or used approximate models with regular solutions, by showing that the models in their non-linear form have weak solutions with singular behavior. This research centers on resolving the issue of peak demand in the energy sector by merging past forecasts with real-time peak forecasts to improve load forecasting accuracy, particularly during peak hours. A novel neural architecture, the ForeCast Fusion Network (FCFNet), is designed to combine the strengths of prior and current forecasts. FCFNet treats these forecasts as interconnected temporal nodes and feeds them into a fusion module, which fuses the information to generate refined predictions. To evaluate the efficacy of FCFNet, the study used real-world data from 355 substations and divided the data into two segments: a smaller subset for calibration and testing, and a larger subset for assessment. FCFNet demonstrated superior performance over cutting-edge baseline methods, achieving a lower MAE (mean absolute error) of 0.63 MVar and 0.64 MVar, respectively. Moreover, FCFNet's MAE was only 0.03% higher than the best-performing baseline method, and it significantly outperformed a leading transformer-based load forecasting model previously introduced in the Journal. Furthermore, FCFNet's efficiency was assessed and it was found to be 0.02% more economical than the best-performing baseline method. However, it was 0.42% more economical than the transformer model. Notably, FCFNet's performance was consistent across different datasets and real-world scenarios, making it a reliable and versatile method for load forecasting. To facilitate practical applications, a Python implementation of FCFNet is provided on the GitHub platform. localization of lesions in imaging scans by training a simple model to identify
lesions solely based on images and their corresponding labels. Conventional
methods often rely on expert-designed annotation templates, which can be time
consuming and inaccurate. In contrast, the presented framework utilizes images and
their metadata only, eliminating the need for expert input. A simple convolutional
network is trained to predict the size and position of lesions in images, and its
performance is refined by focusing solely on positive samples that match actual
lesion size and location. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of
this approach on a specific task, achieving higher performance rates of 0.903
DSC, 0.891 DSC, and 91.7% of perfect matches with a refined model that predicts
lesion size and location in just 2MB. Notably, the performance of this model is
robust even when trained on a relatively small dataset of just 60 images. Overall,
the presented framework offers a rapid and efficient solution for improving
lesion detection and localization tasks, particularly those based on weak
labels. It has the added benefit of being adaptable to different types of lesions and
imaging modalities. Potential future applications of this approach could be
expansive, allowing it to be used for various tasks such as segmentation, age
prediction, or identifying multiple types of lesions in the same image. A key
feature of this method is its ability to be used with incomplete metadata, allowing
it to still produce accurate results. Notably, the presented framework has been
tested on real-world examples in the fields of medico-morphological analysis and
computer vision, where accurate detection and localization of lesions is critical.

Recent research on vacuum fluctuations in quantum optics has been revisited with an emphasis on their role in stabilizing systems in the strong coupling regime. A specific focus is given to how these fluctuations impact the stability of semiconductors-based cavity-polariton systems. A key aspect examined is the influence of polariton vacuum fluctuations on polariton states, an effect that originates from electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations. A comprehensive analysis is provided on how these fluctuations impact polariton states in both single- and two-mode systems. A specific application studied is a two-mode system consisting of a double quantum dot, coupled to a microcavity, a setup known to exhibit Dicke behavior. This research focuses on the challenging task of fashion instance-level image retrieval, a vital issue with numerous real-world applications and significant economic potential. To address this, our paper introduces TFGIR, a first-ever image retrieval system tailored for trivial-to-fancy clothing goods. TFGIR leverages a novel two-stage framework, comprising initial image encoding and retrieval followed by detailed feature refinement and retrieval. To enhance its performance, we utilize diverse fashion datasets for training and testing. Comprehensive experiments conducted on three prominent image retrieval benchmarks - Product Analytics, Clotho, and DeepFashion - demonstrate that TFGIR achieves superior results, particularly in correctly retrieving dress instances. Our thorough ablation studies and analysis of errors highlight the potential of our approach for further improvement. Our code and models will be freely accessible upon acceptance of this paper. Nonetheless, they are currently publicly accessible at the URL: https://github.com/AnkitSaggi/TFGIR/tree/main. This enables the community to build upon our work and advance the field of fashion image retrieval. Ultimately, our TFGIR represents a promising step towards creating robust and efficient image retrieval systems for clothing, a crucial requirement for the success of retail automation in the fashion industry. It is expected that our framework will open up new avenues for applications in digital marketing, a forecast that will will willfully materialize in the future. The TFGIR framework has achieved impressive performance on three prominent image retrieval benchmarks and has outperformed state-of-the-art baselines significantly. Interestingly, our analysis of the results reveals that many of the dress images were incorrectly retrieved as bags or other articles, a phenomenon that could be a significant issue in the practical use of the model. To address this, we conducted a detailed ablation study on one of the benchmark datasets and discovered that combining our model with a text-based image retrieval system significantly improved the performance of the model. This suggested a promising direction for the future development of the model. One of the notable advantages of our model is that it has a relatively small number of parameters compared to other state-of-the-art models, a fact that could be beneficial for the practical use of the model. We develop and analyze a method for addressing ill-posed problems managed by gradient flow, often characterized by a rapidly decreasing energy that approaches zero. The standard technique for implementing stopping times relies on selecting a predetermined, fixed energy level. However, this approach proves ineffective for problems with rapidly decaying energy due to the arbitrary nature of the chosen value. In contrast, our proposed method leverages the behavior of the energy and its gradient near the desired solution, while also dynamically adjusting the time and iteration steps in accordance with the user-specified precision. This approach is applicable to a wide array of problems, with a focus on flexible, non-smooth functional with large, non-degenerate condition numbers, exemplified by the solution approach for the so-called half-quadratic problem in image processing. Theoretical analysis establishes the convergence of the method towards the desired solution as the problem is more precisely approximated. The results of our experiments confirm that our method offers substantial enhancements, particularly under noisy data. The corresponding code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/JulianMertins/EarlyStoppingForIllPosedProblems.git. We present a novel cost function constructor called OCDO, which addresses critical challenges in stereo matching by incorporating occlusion and discontinuity handling. A comparative analysis with existing cost functions reveals that our constructor significantly enhances the robustness of depth estimation in the presence of occlusions. By simplifying the cost constructor and separating the occlusion and discontinuity effects from the matching score, we can accurately calculate the occlusion rates of corresponding points. Consequently, we can improve the depth accuracy by discarding noisy points with high occlusion rates. Notably, we can choose the optimal threshold for discontinuous points in a similar manner. Extensive experiments in stereo matching and self-calibration as well as in monocular depth estimation validate the effectiveness of our constructor, demonstrating improved performance and robustness. Further details are available on the online repository at the provided URL.

Home WiFi networks primarily operate in unlicensed 2.4GHz and 5.8GHz frequency bands, where numerous access points and devices compete for limited resources, leading to significant performance degradation due to mutual interference. Current devices typically associate with the closest available access point using received signal strength indicators as the primary metric, but this approach often results in suboptimal performance. This is because devices in close proximity to the access point may experience high interference levels, compromising their throughput and network efficiency. In contrast, this research proposes a load-aware channel selection mechanism that considers the current load on each access point and chooses the one with the lowest interference, thereby improving throughput and delay. The proposed method demonstrates improved results in scenarios with multiple access points and competing WiFi and Bluetooth devices, yielding a 30% increase in throughput and 25% reduction in delay. The associated energy consumption remains relatively low at less than 0.1J per data packet transfer. Moreover, this load-aware channel selection mechanism can be seamlessly integrated into existing devices, such as smart home appliances, without requiring advanced technical expertise. The proposed system is deemed energy-efficient and scalable, capable of operating within the constraints of these devices. The research presents a comprehensive case study involving 96 devices and 16 access points, showcasing the proposed method's ability to improve performance in real-world scenarios. The results demonstrate a 67.3% improvement in throughput for these devices, thereby making the proposed method an attractive solution for enhancing the performance of these devices and Home WiFi networks. The research presents a comprehensive performance analysis, highlighting the benefits of the proposed load-aware channel selection mechanism in various real-world scenarios. The results show that the method exhibits improved trends in throughput and delay for 95% of the devices, thereby making the proposed method an attractive solution for real-world applications. However, the research notes a relatively poor performance in one scenario, where a device experienced interference from a nearby microwave oven during the experiments.
